questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein is a major component of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal casts

Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein forms a major component of the organic matrix of renal casts.

Tamm-Horsfall protein, also known as uromodulin, is the most common protein present in urine and is produced in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. They are membrane-bound, glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored proteins that are released by proteolytic cleavage at the apical membrane. It is secreted as the most abundant protein in normal human urine (20 to 100 mg/day) and is not expressed by macula densa cells or the downstream distal convoluted tubule (DCT)

They form the major organic matrix of all renal casts and play a role in the modulation of innate immunity in the kidney and inflammation during kidney injury. Uromodulin is coded by the UMOD gene, and mutation of this can lead to medullary cystic kidney disease (MCKD II) and familial juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy.

Casts are cylindrical structures that are formed in the DCT and collecting ducts. They assume the shape and size of the lumen in which they are formed. Several factors favor cast formation, such as urine stasis, low pH, and high concentration. All casts have an organic matrix composed primarily of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein. Casts are the only elements in urine sediments that are specific to renal origin.

Other options:

Option A: Thrombi occurring in heart chambers or the aortic lumen are designated mural thrombi. Thrombi often have grossly and microscopically apparent laminations called lines of Zahn, which are pale platelet and fibrin deposits alternating with darker red cell–rich layers.

Option B: Curschmann spirals are a characteristic finding in sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage specimens of patients with atopic asthma formed due to the extrusion of mucus plugs from subepithelial mucous gland ducts or bronchioles.

Option D: In multiple myeloma, the malignant plasma cells often secrete free, unpaired κ or λ light chains which are referred to as Bence-Jones proteins.

Pearl PF0892: Urinary Casts and Their Significance

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is a formal thought disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Derailment

Derailment is a formal thought disorder.

It is a breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of being goal-oriented. It is generally identified in schizophrenic patients as a generalized loosening of associations.

For example, a person with derailment thought disorder might jump from talking about rabbits to the hair on their head to your sweater. They talk in chains of semi-related ideas. Their communication style has a generalized loosening of associations. Their ideas often fall further and further from the topic.

Formal thought disorders are:

• Circumstantiality is the overinclusion of trivial or irrelevant details that impedes the sense of getting to the point.
• Clang association is an association of thoughts with the sound of words rather than by their meaning (e.g., through rhyming).
• Derailment is the breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of goal-directedness. The words make sentences, but the sentences do not make sense.
• Flight of ideas is a succession of multiple associations so that thoughts seem to move abruptly from idea to idea, through rapid, pressured speech.
• Neologism is the invention of new words or phrases or the use of conventional words in idiosyncratic ways.
• Perseveration is the repetition of out-of-context words, phrases, or ideas.
• Tangentiality is responding to a question, that is appropriate to the general topic without actually answering the question.
• Thought blocking is a sudden disruption of thought or a break in the flow of ideas.

Other options:

Option A - An obsession is a recurrent and intrusive thought, feeling, idea, or sensation.

Option C - A delusion is defined as a false belief based on incorrect inference about external reality that firmly sustains despite evidence to the contrary.

Option D - Thought insertion is a type of delusion where the patient believes that thoughts are not his/her own and have been inserted into his/her mind.
questions.learning: Derailment Derailment is a formal thought disorder. It is a breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of being goal-oriented.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is not given in status epilepticus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ethosuximide

Status Epilepticus:

• Continuous seizure activity >5 minutes OR
• Recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness

It’s a neurological emergency → risk of:

• Neuronal injury
• Hypoxia
• Death

1. Immediate suppression (fastest acting)

→ Benzodiazepines (IV Lorazepam)

2. Stabilization (prevent recurrence)

→ Longer-acting anticonvulsants

3. Refractory phase

→ Anesthetics (propofol, midazolam infusion)

Ethosuximide Fails in SE

• Works on thalamic pacemaker activity
• SE involves diffuse cortical excitation
• Ethosuximide → ONLY absence seizures

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 13-year-old boy collapsed while playing football. ECG showed V5, V6 inversion and prominent inverted T-waves. 2D echocardiography showed systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve leaflet. Which of the following features will be seen on clinical examination and which of the following are true regarding the management?

Clinical findings
Management

a. Pulsus bisferiens
1. Beta-blockers are given

b. Pulsus alternans
2. Beta-blockers are contraindicated

c. Ejection systolic murmur
3. ICD is indicated

d. Murmur increases on standing
4. ICD is contraindicated

e. Murmur decreases on standing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 & 3, a, c, d

The given clinical scenario of a young patient with a history of sudden collapse following physical activity along with ECG findings of V5, V6 inversion, and prominent inverted T-waves, and 2D echocardiography showing the systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve leaflet point toward a diagnosis of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HCM).

In HCM, clinical examination may reveal pulsus bisferiens and an ejection systolic murmur that increases on standing.

Beta-blockers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICD) are used in the management.

HCM is a leading cause of sudden death in young. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance. HCM is characterized by the thickening of the septal myocardium below the aortic valve leading to obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract.

Symptoms:

• Exertional dyspnea
• Syncope
• Angina, palpitations, cardiac arrhythmias
• Sudden cardiac death (particularly during or after intense physical activity)

Examination:

• Systolic ejection murmur best heard at the apex or lower left sternal border

Parameters
Murmur intensity increased
Murmur intensity decreased

Preload

Valsalva

Standing

(↓preload = ↑obstruction)

Squatting

Passive leg raising

(↑preload = ↓obstruction)

Force of contraction

Exercise

(↑force = ↑obstruction)

Afterload

Vasodilators

(↓afterload = ↑obstruction)

Isotonic handgrip

Squatting

(↑afterload = ↓obstruction)

• Holosystolic murmur from mitral regurgitation
• Sustained apex beat
• S4 gallop
• Paradoxical split of S2
• Pulsus bisferiens: LV outflow obstruction causes a sudden quick rise of the pulse followed by a slower longer rise.

ECG findings:

• Left axis deviation
• P wave abnormalities
• Prominent abnormal Q waves
• Deeply inverted T waves

Echocardiography findings:

• LV wall thickness ≥15 mm
• Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve leaflet
• Mitral regurgitation

Treatment:

• Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are the first-line treatment
• Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) - indicated when the history of cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular tachycardia is present

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman suddenly develops facial asymmetry, slurred speech, and weakness in her right arm. The symptoms gradually improve and completely resolve within 48 hours. On cardiac examination, a mid-diastolic murmur is heard on the left side of the heart, and her heart rhythm is irregular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with sudden focal neurological deficits—facial asymmetry, slurred speech, and right arm weakness—suggestive of a cerebrovascular event. The key feature in this case is that the symptoms completely resolve within 48 hours, which is characteristic of a Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA). A TIA is defined as a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by temporary cerebral ischemia without permanent infarction. Most TIAs resolve within minutes to hours, but by definition, no residual deficit remains. The presence of a mid-diastolic murmur (suggestive of mitral stenosis) and irregular rhythm (likely atrial fibrillation) indicates a cardioembolic source, which is a common cause of TIA. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Thrombo-embolic stroke → Causes persistent deficits (C) Cardioembolic stroke → Would not completely resolve (D) Paradoxical embolism → Requires right-to-left shunt
questions.learning: The patient presents with sudden focal neurological deficits—facial asymmetry, slurred speech, and right arm weakness—suggestive of a cerebrovascular event.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug elicits the following response on blood pressure and heart rate as shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Norepinephrine

The above picture shows an increase in systolic pressure, diastolic pressure and mean arterial pressure, and reflex bradycardia. This effect is seen in case of norepinephrine.

Norepinephrine acts on α1 and β1 receptors to increase the peripheral vascular resistance and stroke volume respectively. This causes an increase in diastolic, systolic, and mean arterial pressure. Increased mean arterial pressure leads to reflex bradycardia.

Adrenergic drug

Receptors it acts on

Adrenaline

α1 + α2 +β1 + β2

Noradrenaline

α1 +α2 +β1 but no β2 action

Isoproterenol

β1 + β2 + β3 but no α action

Other options:

Option B: Isoproterenol increases systolic blood pressure by increasing contractility and increases heart rate due to its β1 action. The β2-mediated vasodilation, results in a decrease in mean arterial pressure and reflex tachycardia.

Option C: On administration of epinephrine, there is an increase in systolic pressure, which is greater than the decrease in diastolic pressure so the pulse pressure increases. Heart rate is increased as a result of direct cardiac stimulation.

A rise in blood pressure occurs when adrenaline is given intravenously at higher concentrations, as its alpha-adrenergic activity dominates.
As adrenaline is quickly metabolised and taken up, its concentration falls, allowing β2-adrenergic effects to become dominant. Hence, a fall in BP is seen. This is referred to as the biphasic reaction of epinephrine.

Option D: At higher concentration, dopamine usually increases systolic blood pressure and pulse pressure and has no effect on diastolic blood pressure or increases it slightly. Tachycardia is less prominent during the infusion of dopamine.
questions.learning: Norepinephrine — The above picture shows an increase in systolic pressure, diastolic pressure and mean arterial pressure, and reflex bradycardia. This effect is seen in case of norepinephrine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Nasal polyps are commonly associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intrinsic asthma

Nasal polyps are associated with intrinsic asthma.

Intrinsic asthma is characterized by the presence of asthma with negative skin prick tests for common antigens. The association of nasal polyps with asthma is described by Samter’s triad (intrinsic asthma + aspirin hypersensitivity + nasal polyposis). Asthma is usually severe, persistent, and adult-onset.

Other options:

Option B: Brittle asthma refers to a severe variant of asthma where patients have very serious and often, life-threatening attacks despite appropriate therapy.

Option C: Extrinsic asthma is also referred to as atopic asthma. It is allergen mediated.

Option D: Exercise-induced asthma is airway narrowing due to strenuous physical activity. Symptoms typically start after the exercise has ended and last for around 30 minutes.
questions.learning: Intrinsic asthma Nasal polyps are associated with intrinsic asthma. Intrinsic asthma is characterized by the presence of asthma with negative skin prick tests for common antigens.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the plant shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parthenium hysterophorus

The image shown is of the weed Parthenium hysterophorus.

Parthenium hysterophorus is an invasive weed that colonizes and causes environmental, agricultural, and medical hazards. They grow very quickly and colonize among other plants causing disruption of the ecosystem. The chemicals like parthenin, hysterin, hymenin, and ambrosin present in the plant, disrupt the growth of the surrounding crops.

In terms of the medical hazards, the pollens and other parts of these plants are shown to cause bronchitis, asthma, contact dermatitis, hay fever, and other allergies.

The contact dermatitis caused by it is called 'Parthenium dermatitis'. An image of the most common type of 'Parthenium dermatitis' called 'airborne contact dermatitis' is shown below:

Parthenium is also believed to have some health benefits and is used by alternate systems of medicine in conditions like rheumatic pain, diarrhea, urinary tract infections, dysentery, malaria, and neuralgia.

Calotropis gigantea

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines is C/I in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines, such as the Varicella vaccine, are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to the potential risk of fetal infection and congenital varicella syndrome. Other live vaccines to avoid include MMR and Yellow Fever. In contrast, inactivated influenza (Option A) is recommended to protect both mother and newborn. Rabies vaccine (Option C) is safe and mandatory for post-exposure prophylaxis as the disease is fatal. TDaP (Option D) is recommended during the third trimester to provide passive immunity to the infant against pertussis. Therefore, while killed vaccines and toxoids are generally safe, live viral vaccines like varicella pose a theoretical risk to fetal development and must be administered either before conception or postpartum

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the part marked 'A'?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Edge

The edge of an ulcer is is represented by 'A'.

An ulcer is defined as a break in the continuity of the epithelium or mucous membrane with molecular death. Classically an ulcer is described to have four parts which are:

* Margin

* Edge

* Floor

* Base

The margin is defined as the junction between the normal epithelium and the ulcer.

The edge is defined as the part between the margin and the floor. Five types of ulcer edges are commonly described as follows:

The floor is defined as the exposed surface of the ulcer. It is better seen than felt, and may contain granulation tissue, discharge or slough. Trophic ulcers have bone as the floor due to their depth.

The base is defined as the structure on which the ulcer rests, eg, bone or soft tissue. It is better felt than seen.
questions.learning: Edge — The edge of an ulcer is is represented by 'A'. An ulcer is defined as a break in the continuity of the epithelium or mucous membrane with molecular death.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a common feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distal bronchiectasis

Central bronchiectasis is a typical feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), not distal bronchiectasis.

ABPA is an eosinophilic pulmonary disorder caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to the colonization of airways by the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus. It occurs almost exclusively in patients with asthma (~2.5% of patients) or cystic fibrosis (up to 15%). In chronic cases, repeated episodes of bronchial obstruction, inflammation, and mucoid impaction can lead to bronchiectasis, fibrosis, and respiratory compromise. While central bronchiectasis is characteristic, some patients can develop chronic cavitary lesions.

With the development of ABPA, asthma or cystic fibrosis typically worsens and may manifest with a new or worsening cough or an increase in sputum production or wheezing. Many patients report coughing up thick sputum casts. The presence of hyperattenuating mucus in the airways is highly specific.

ABPA is diagnosed serologically, based on the presence of:
Serum IgE > 1000 IU/ml
Positive skin prick test or IgE levels against A. fumigatus extract
Detection of Aspergillus-specific antibodies
Eosinophilia >500 cells/μL

Treatment - The use of systemic glucocorticoids is indicated for ABPA, but the course should be tapered by 3-6 months. Antifungal agents like itraconazole, voriconazole, and newer azoles can be used for over 4 months to control disease activity. Monoclonal antibodies against IgE, IL-4, and IL-5 receptors can be used for severe refractory cases.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with a rare homozygous recessive condition presented with ectopia lentis. In the peripheral smear, there was no megaloblastic anemia. Later, he was found to have elevated homocysteine levels in the blood. Which of the following supplementations will help the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyridoxine

The vitamin that can be used as supplementation in this patient with homocystinuria is pyridoxine (vitamin B6).

Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease most commonly caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi. The skeletal features of homocystinuria often mimic Marfan syndrome. Folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiency can also lead to homocystinuria with megaloblastic anemia.

Demonstration of elevated total homocysteine in the blood confirms the diagnosis. 50% of the cases of homocystinuria are termed pyridoxine-responsive because large doses of pyridoxine can enhance the activity of deficient enzymes in these patients. Administration of large doses of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) restores the activity of the deficient enzyme in half of all cases of homocystinuria.

Folate supplementation is also added to overcome any folate deficiency that might occur due to increased conversion of homocysteine to methionine. For the other 50% of the patients, the treatment consists of methionine restriction and cysteine supplementation. In addition, betaine (methyl group donor), folate and vitamin B12 may be added.
questions.learning: Pyridoxine — The vitamin that can be used as supplementation in this patient with homocystinuria is pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease most commonly caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is deficient in a patient with phenylketonuria with normal phenylalanine hydroxylase levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dihydrobiopterin reductase

In a patient with hyperphenylalaninemia but normal phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), the defect lies in the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) metabolism.

Key enzyme involved: Dihydrobiopterin reductase (DHPR) Deficiency → ↓ BH₄ availability

• Impaired phenylalanine → tyrosine conversion → ↑ phenylalanine
• Also affects neurotransmitter synthesis:

o    ↓ dopamine (tyrosine pathway)

o    ↓ serotonin (tryptophan pathway)

Clinical importance:

• More severe than classical PKU
• Presents with neurological deficits due to neurotransmitter deficiency

Why other options are incorrect:

• Tyrosine transaminase: Involved in tyrosine metabolism (tyrosinemia)
• Dopa decarboxylase: Involved in dopamine synthesis, not primary cause here
• Tyrosine hydroxylase: Requires BH₄ but is not the defective enzyme in this condition
questions.learning: Dihydrobiopterin reductase — In a patient with hyperphenylalaninemia but normal phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), the defect lies in the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) metabolism.

↓

↓

↓

↓

Progestasert (progesterone IUD) / Copper T/ progesterone implant are not ideal in someone already having bleeding problems. Mala N (combined oral contraceptive) is not recommended in a lactating female as estrogen affects the milk output.  Some sources say an 18-month period of lactation justifies COCPs since the child would be on complementary feeds. The best answer hence remains controversial.

A) Progestasert

B) Copper-T 380A

D) Norethisterone enanthate depot

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a patient with a corneal scar whose visual acuity improves when tested with a pinhole, what is the most likely cause of the reduced vision?
questions.explanation: When a patient's visual acuity improves during the pinhole test, it definitively indicates that the vision loss is due to a refractive error rather than primary organic pathology. The pinhole works by blocking peripheral distorted light rays and allowing only central parallel rays to reach the macula. In a patient with a corneal scar, the surface of the cornea becomes uneven, leading specifically to irregular astigmatism (Option C). This type of astigmatism cannot be corrected by standard glasses but is partially bypassed by the pinhole. Vision loss from Glaucoma (Option A), which involves optic nerve damage, would not improve with a pinhole. Malingering (Option B) is a psychological state where the patient purposefully feigns loss. A Cataract (Option D) involves a clouded lens; while some cataracts allow minor improvement with a pinhole, the direct link between a corneal scar and distorted light makes irregular astigmatism the most accurate clinical cause. Rigid gas permeable contact lenses are the preferred correction for this condition
questions.learning: When a patient's visual acuity improves during the pinhole test, it definitively indicates that the vision loss is due to a refractive error rather than primary organic pathology.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman develops difficulty in producing high-pitched sounds after undergoing thyroid surgery. Injury to which of the following nerves is the most likely cause?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) supplies the cricothyroid muscle, the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

The cricothyroid tenses and elongates the vocal cords, enabling the production of high-pitched sounds. Because the EBSLN runs close to the superior thyroid artery, it is particularly vulnerable during thyroid surgery, resulting in difficulty producing high-pitched sounds and voice fatigue.

Why not the other options?

• A. Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. Injury causes hoarseness, weak or breathy voice, and bilateral injury may cause airway obstruction, but isolated loss of high-pitched phonation is characteristic of EBSLN injury.
• B. Internal laryngeal nerve: Provides sensory innervation above the vocal cords. Injury causes loss of the cough reflex and increased risk of aspiration, without affecting voice pitch.
• D. Glossopharyngeal nerve: Supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle and sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue and pharynx; it is not involved in phonation.
questions.learning: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve — The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) supplies the cricothyroid muscle, the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct method for measurement of nasogastric tube?
options: Tip of nose to ear lobule to xiphisternum
Angle of mouth to tragus to xiphisternum
Ala of nose to angle of mandible to xiphisternum
Angle of mouth to ear lobule to umbilicus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tip of nose to ear lobule to xiphisternum

The correct method for measuring a nasogastric tube (Ryle's tube) is from the tip of the nose to the ear lobule to the xiphisternum.

Nasogastric (NG) tubes play a role in treating intestinal obstruction and can also be used to provide nutritional support. The commonly used method to determine the length of a nasogastric tube (NG tube) is the NEX method, which involves measuring from the tip of the nose to ear to xiphisternum. The approximate length to be inserted is 55cms.

Ideally, Ryle's tube is inserted in the sitting position with the neck slightly flexed. Confirmation of the correct position is done by the following:

• Auscultation in the epigastric area while injecting a bolus of air
• An abdominal radiograph is the best way to confirm the location of the tube

An NG tube placed for suction should ideally be located within the stomach to avoid potential damage to the duodenum. For decreased risk of aspiration, the ideal location for an NG tube is postpyloric (55-60cm).

Indications for NG tube :

Drainage purposes:

• Conservative management of bowel obstruction and postop paralytic ileus
• Gastric decompression prior to emergency surgery
• Aspiration of gastric fluid

Feeding purposes:

• Nutritional support in patients in motor neuron disease, stroke, and following upper aerodigestive tract procedures
• Administration of medication

Contraindications:

Absolute:

• Severe midface trauma
• Recent nasal surgery

Relative:

• Coagulation abnormality
• Esophageal varices
• Recent banding of esophageal varices
• Anastomoses in the stomach and esophagus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy develops bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. The bacteria isolated from the stool specimen fermented lactose and produced colorless colonies on sorbitol MacConkey agar. The most likely etiological agent in this case is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Shiga toxin-producing E.Coli

The given clinical scenario of a boy with bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps with the isolated bacteria fermenting lactose and forming colorless colonies on sorbitol MacConkey agar is suggestive of infection by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) O157: H7, also known as Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC).

O157: H7 is the most common type of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC). Unlike most other E. coli serotypes, the STEC O157: H7 does not use sorbitol and produces clear colonies on the Sorbitol MacConkey agar. The non-STEC produces pink colonies. All species of E. coli are lactose fermenters and produce pink colonies.

They produce two antigenic forms of the cytotoxic toxin known as Shiga-like toxin 1 and Shiga-like toxin 2. Shiga-like toxin 1 is identical to the Shiga toxin of Shigella dysenteriae type 1. E. coli O157:H7 has a small infective dose (around 100 bacilli) and spreads easily from child to child by the feco-oral route.

It can cause mild non-bloody diarrhea to hemorrhagic colitis, or a severe form of diarrhea, with hemolytic uremic syndrome, a disease resulting in acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in the world is E.coli O157:H7. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in India is Shigella dysenteriae type I.

Other options:

Option A: Campylobacter is a slender, spirally curved, gram-negative bacillus. They grow at a slower rate and thus require selective media containing antibiotics like Skirrow's media for culture.

Option B: Yersinia enterocolitica causes diarrhea with symptoms resembling appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis). The patients present with abdominal pain which can be localized to the right iliac fossa, thus mimicking appendicitis. Additionally, it is a non-lactose fermenter.

Option D: Shigella dysenteriae type 1 can produce the Shiga toxin and result in a clinical profile similar to EHEC. But Shigella is a non-lactose fermenting organism, unlike E. coli, and will form pale colonies on MacConkey agar.

Enterobacteriaceae family is classified based on their action on lactose present in MacConkey's medium as,

Lactose fermenters

Escherichia, Klebsiella,Enterobacter

Late lactose fermenters

Shigella sonnei, Serratia, Citrobacter, Erwinia

Non-lactose fermenters

Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus

Mnemonic to remember Non-lactose fermenters: SPY PSM

* Salmonella

* Proteus

* Yersinia

* Providencia - late fermenter

* Shigella (Except S sonnie which is a late lactose fermenter)

* Morganella

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Conducting a village-based session on wound care after a dog bite by demonstrating it through enactment represents which method of health communication?
questions.explanation: In health communication and community education, Demonstration is a highly effective method involving the physical enacting or showing of a specific skill or procedure. By acting out the steps of wound care after a dog bite (e.g., washing with soap and water for 15 minutes), the health worker provides a visual and practical model that is easier for villagers to understand and replicate than verbal instructions alone. A Lecture (Option A) is a one-way verbal communication of information. A Group discussion (Option B) is a multi-way exchange of ideas among a small group. Flash cards (Option C) are a visual aid used to support a presentation but are not the primary mode of enacting a skill. Demonstration is based on the principle of "learning by seeing and doing." It is particularly useful in rural public health for teaching life-saving skills like ORS preparation, hand-washing techniques, or immediate first aid for common injuries, significantly improving the community's health literacy and emergency response
questions.learning: In health communication and community education, Demonstration is a highly effective method involving the physical enacting or showing of a specific skill or procedure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A severely fatigued patient with markedly reduced responsiveness is brought to the emergency department. He has had a progressive loss of muscle strength over the past two days. A CT scan is performed, and the image is shown below. Which blood vessel is most likely occluded by a thrombus?
questions.explanation: The CT scan reveals a large area of hypodensity (darkness) involving the cortical and subcortical regions of the right cerebral hemisphere. This distribution is characteristic of an ischemic stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). The MCA is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery and supplies the majority of the lateral surface of the brain, including the motor and sensory areas for the face and upper limbs. A blood clot (thrombus or embolus) in the MCA results in dense contralateral hemiplegia and sensory loss. The anterior cerebral artery (Option B) supplies the medial surface (lower limbs), and the posterior cerebral artery (Option A) supplies the occipital lobe (vision). The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (Option D) supplies the cerebellum and lateral medulla. Given the widespread hemispheric involvement, the middle cerebral artery is the vessel occluded
questions.learning: The CT scan reveals a large area of hypodensity (darkness) involving the cortical and subcortical regions of the right cerebral hemisphere. This distribution is characteristic of an ischemic stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old male is diagnosed with a tumor in the left lobe of the liver, and a left hemi-hepatectomy is planned. Which anatomical segments (lobes) of the liver will be resected in this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 3 and 4

Left hemi-hepatectomy removes segments 2, 3, and 4 (4a/4b) supplied by the left portal pedicle. Segment 1 is independent and usually preserved. Segments 5–8 belong to the right hemiliver.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Left hemi-hepatectomy removes segments 2, 3, and 4 (4a/4b) supplied by the left portal pedicle. Segment 1 is independent and usually preserved.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In conventional oxygen therapy, which device will deliver highest FiO2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non rebreathing mask

Non rebreathing masks provide highest FiO2 during conventional oxygen therapy.

The non-rebreather mask is a low flow device that can be used to deliver oxygen at higher concentrations (FiO2 80-95%). It uses a reservoir bag to let the oxygen get concentrated while a one-way valve doesn't allow to breathe in expired air.

This type of masks are used in patients with significant hypoxia, with relatively normal ventilation, such as victims of trauma or carbon monoxide exposure.

Other options:

A) Venturi mask:

• Venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance oxygen delivery system and the highest oxygen concentration (FiO2) delivered is 60% at a flow rate of 15 L/min.
• It is based on the Bernoulli Principle, which states that in order to maintain a constant flow, a fluid must increase its velocity as it flows through a constriction.
• It is available in different colors, with the green valve venturi mask providing 60% FiO2.
• This is useful with patients who require greater FiO2 such as COPD patients, where it is important to provide controlled oxygenation.

B) Hudson mask:

• Also known as simple face mask
• Low-flow, variable performance device
• They provide an oxygen flow rate of up to 5-10 L/min and provide a variable FiO2.
• The body of the mask functions as reservoir for both oxygen and expired carbon dioxide.
• Used in patients who require oxygen therapy for shorter periods of time.

D) Nasal cannula:

• They are low-flow, variable performance devices, with flow rate of 1-4 L/min.
• Used in patients who require low supplemental oxygen.
• Nasopharynx acts as the reservoir in such cannulas.

Indications of a nasal cannula and other low-flow oxygen delivery systems include

• Minute ventilation < 8–10 L/min
• Breathing frequencies < 20 breaths/min
• Normal inspiratory flow (10–30 L/min).
questions.learning: Non rebreathing mask Non rebreathing masks provide highest FiO2 during conventional oxygen therapy. The non-rebreather mask is a low flow device that can be used to deliver oxygen at higher concentrations (FiO2 80-95%).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman with a history of multiple pregnancies presents with grade II/III uterine prolapse and cystocele. She reports involuntary urine leakage when coughing or sneezing. What type of urinary incontinence does she most likely have?
questions.explanation: The involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure—such as coughing or sneezing—is the defining symptom of Stress Incontinence . In this patient, the history of multiple pregnancies and the presence of a cystocele (bladder prolapse) and uterine prolapse indicate a significant weakening of the pelvic floor and the urethral support structures (hypermobility). Urge incontinence (Option B) involves a sudden, uncontrollable need to void and is caused by detrusor overactivity. Overflow incontinence (Option A) results from an overdistended bladder due to obstruction or nerve damage, leading to continuous dribbling. Neurogenic bladder (Option D) results from specific neurological lesions (e.g., spinal cord injury). Because the leakage is strictly associated with mechanical "stress" on the bladder in a patient with documented pelvic floor laxity, stress incontinence is the definitive diagnosis. Management often includes pelvic floor exercises or surgical "sling" procedures
questions.learning: The involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure—such as coughing or sneezing—is the defining symptom of Stress Incontinence .

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Choose the correct options from the given statements of the enteric nervous system-

1. Vagus is the only afferent from the gut
2. Functions independent of the Brain and Spinal Cord
3. Myenteric plexus in the lamina propria
4. Exclusively under the influence of nerves
5. Only parasympathetic connects the enteric to the CNS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2

The enteric nervous system functions independently of the brain and spinal Cord. (Statement 2)

Statement 2: Functions independent of brain and spinal cord: The enteric nervous system is often referred to as the "second brain" because it can function independently of the central nervous system (CNS). It has its own reflex circuits and can control gut motility, secretion, and blood flow without input from the brain or spinal cord, although it can be influenced by them.

Statement 1: The vagus is the only afferent from the gut: While the vagus nerve does provide significant afferent (sensory) input from the gut, other nerves, such as those from the pelvic splanchnic nerves, also contribute to afferent pathways. Therefore, the vagus is not the only afferent nerve.

Statement 3: Myenteric plexus in the lamina propria: The myenteric plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers of the gut, not in the lamina propria (which is part of the mucosal layer of the gut).

Statement 4: Exclusively under the influence of nerves: The enteric nervous system is influenced by nerves, but it also responds to hormonal and immune system signals. Therefore, it is not exclusively under neural influence.

Statement 5: Only parasympathetic connects enteric to CNS: Both parasympathetic and sympathetic connect the enteric nervous system to the central nervous system. Not just the parasympathetic.

The enteric nervous system consists of submucosal and myenteric plexi. This Plexi can function independently and is often referred to as the ‘little brain’. The enteric nervous system regulates gastrointestinal (GI) function and is connected to the central nervous system by parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers.

The myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus is present between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers. It innervates both these layers along the entire length of the GI tract. It primarily controls GI motility. On stimulation, it has the following effects:

• Increased tone of the GI wall
• Increased intensity and rate of rhythmic contractions
• Increased velocity of excitatory wave conduction

Some of the myenteric plexus neurons primarily release vasoactive inhibitory peptide (VIP), which causes the relaxation of the GI sphincters.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is found between the mucosa and the circular muscle layers. It innervates the GI glands, endocrine cells, and submucosal blood vessels. It primarily controls GI secretions, absorption, and local blood flow.

The parasympathetic innervation of the plexi is from the vagus and pelvic nerves. They release either acetylcholine or substance P. It generally increases GI motility and secretion.

The sympathetic innervation is from the celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, and hypogastric sympathetic ganglia. It generally inhibits GI motility and stimulates sphincteric contraction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All are features of postganglionic lesions, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Positive histamine test

A postganglionic lesion refers to nerve damage distal to the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), affecting the peripheral nerve after the sensory neuron cell body.

Features of postganglionic lesions:

• Occur distal to the dorsal root ganglion.
• Better prognosis because peripheral nerves can regenerate.
• Surgical repair may be possible in cases of nerve injury.

Histamine test:

• Used to assess integrity of sensory nerve fibers.
• In postganglionic lesions, the axon reflex is lost, so the flare response is absent → negative histamine test.

Therefore, positive histamine test is not seen in postganglionic lesions, making it the incorrect statement.
questions.learning: Positive histamine test — A postganglionic lesion refers to nerve damage distal to the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), affecting the peripheral nerve after the sensory neuron cell body.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for severe acne?
questions.explanation: Oral isotretinoin is the most effective and appropriate treatment for severe, nodulocystic, or treatment-resistant acne. It is a systemic retinoid that addresses all four pathogenic factors of acne: it reduces sebum production, normalizes keratinization, inhibits bacterial colonization (P. acnes), and has anti-inflammatory properties. Regarding the other options, topical tretinoin (Option A) is suitable for mild comedonal acne but is insufficient for severe cases. Systemic steroids (Option C) are not used to treat acne and can actually induce "steroid acne" as a side effect. While antibiotics (Option D), such as doxycycline, are useful for moderate inflammatory acne, they do not provide the long-term remission required for severe, scarring disease. Given its potency and ability to prevent permanent scarring, isotretinoin is the gold standard for severe presentations, despite its required monitoring for side effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
The table below gives the AUC of drug B alone and that of drug B when combined with another drug A. If the 𝑝 value is <0.01, then which of the following statements is true?

Drug
Area Under Curve (AUC)

Drug B
570 seconds ± 127 seconds

Drug B + Drug A
820 seconds ± 124 seconds
options: Drug A decreases intestinal absorption of Drug B
Drug A reduces first pass metabolism of Drug B
Drug A increases the metabolism of Drug B
Drug A increases renal elimination of Drug B
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Drug A reduces first pass metabolism of Drug B

Drug A reduces the first-pass metabolism of Drug B.

The area under the plot of plasma concentration of a drug versus time after dosage is called the area under the curve or AUC. It can be used as a measure of the bioavailability of a drug and to calculate its clearance rate from the body.

Bioavailability refers to the extent to which an administered dose of the drug reaches its site of action; if the metabolic and excretory capacity of the intestine or liver for the drug is large, bioavailability is reduced substantially and this is called the first-pass metabolism whereas bioavailability is increased if intestinal absorption of the drug is increased.

The greater the AUC, the greater is the bioavailability of the drug.

In the question, is observed that when drug A was given along with drug B, the total AUC has increased (820 seconds ± 124 seconds) when compared to the AUC when drug B is administered alone (570 seconds ± 127 seconds).

The null hypothesis for the above question would be that drug A doesn't increase the AUC for drug B and for this to be true, 𝑝 value should be >0.05.

As given 𝑝 value is <0.01, it is significant and the null hypothesis is rejected, which means that drug A has indeed increased the AUC for drug B.

This indicates increased bioavailability of drug B when administered with drug A, which shows that drug A has either increased the intestinal absorption of drug B or has reduced its first-pass metabolism.

Other options:

Option A: If drug A decreased the intestinal absorption of drug B, this would mean that the AUC for drug B, when administered with drug A, would be reduced. This is due to decreased bioavailability of drug B when given with drug A.

Option C: If drug A increases the metabolism of drug B, this would lead to a shorter t1/2 and duration of action of drug B, thereby decreasing the AUC for when drug B and drug A are given together.

Option D: If drug A increased the elimination of drug B, the AUC for drug B when given with drug A would be reduced due to reduced duration of action of drug B.
questions.learning: Drug — A reduces first pass metabolism of Drug B Drug A reduces the first-pass metabolism of Drug B. The area under the plot of plasma concentration of a drug versus time after dosage is called the area under the curve or AUC.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presents with short stature. On evaluation, bone age is found to be 10 years, and the upper segment to lower segment (US:LS) ratio is 1.1:1. There are no dysmorphic features, and the child is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) is a common cause of short stature characterized by delayed bone age with otherwise normal body proportions and health.

• Bone age is delayed compared to chronological age
• Normal upper segment to lower segment ratio indicates proportionate short stature
• No dysmorphic features or systemic illness
• Growth velocity is usually normal, but puberty is delayed

Differentiation:

• Familial short stature: bone age matches chronological age
• Achondroplasia/chondrodysplasia: disproportionate short stature with abnormal body ratios

questions.text: Mr. X enlisted in the Navy in 1997, married Y in 1999, and welcomed their first child, V, in 2002, followed by their second child, M, in 2009. After retiring in 2020 and starting a job at SBI, his parents moved in to live with his family. Which of the following statements accurately describes this family?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2002- Extension

The correct answer is 2002-Extension.

The extension phase begins with the birth of the first child, which is 2002 in this scenario.

Pearl PF0595: The Family as a Social Organization

* A family is a group of biologically related individuals living together under the same roof and eating from a common kitchen.

* It is the most primary and basic unit of all societies.

* The basic and arbitrary model of a family cycle has six phases:

* Types of families:

* A nuclear family or elementary family consists of only the married couple and their offspring while they are dependants.

* The term new family is applied when nuclear families are younger than 10 years and consist of parents and children.

* A joint family or extended family consists of a number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood. All property in joint families is held in common with the family income going into a common pocket. A senior male member is usually the head of the family who makes decisions.

* A three generation family is one where there are representatives from three different generations in one house.

* A communal family is one in which all the members play a part in its management.

* Functions of the family:

* Residence (patrilocal and matrilocal)

* Division of labour

* Reproduction and raising children

* Socialization and social care

* Economic functions

* Problems families are those that lag behind the rest of the community in terms of standard and quality of life of its members.

* Broken families are those in which the parental or family system has been disrupted by separation, divorce or death.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A child is brought to the emergency department after consuming an unknown fruit and shows signs of poisoning. Based on the description of the fruit and the clinical features observed, what type of poisoning is most likely in this case?
questions.explanation: Datura poisoning (also known as thorn apple poisoning) is common in children who ingest the seeds or fruit. The plant contains tropane alkaloids like atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine, which cause a classic anticholinergic toxidrome. Symptoms are often remembered by the mnemonic: "Dry as a bone (no sweat/dry mouth), red as a beet (flushing), blind as a bat (dilated pupils), hot as a hare (fever), and mad as a hatter (delirium/hallucinations)". Poppy seeds (Option A) would cause an opioid toxidrome with pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression. Mushroom poisoning (Option C) usually presents with severe gastrointestinal distress or liver failure depending on the species. Cannabis poisoning (Option D) results in ataxia, lethargy, and a characteristic "stoned" appearance with conjunctival congestion. Datura is a common roadside plant in India, making it a frequent topic in pediatric emergency medicine and forensic toxicology exams
questions.learning: Datura poisoning (also known as thorn apple poisoning) is common in children who ingest the seeds or fruit. The plant contains tropane alkaloids like atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine, which cause a classic anticholinergic toxidrome.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the pharmacological relationship between imipramine and diphenhydramine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both block muscarinic receptors

• Imipramine → Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA)
• Diphenhydramine → 1st generation antihistamine

Different primary roles, but both carry a strong anticholinergic personality

Imipramine (a TCA) and diphenhydramine (a first-generation antihistamine) both have strong antimuscarinic activity. This shared action explains common side effects like dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention.

| Feature | Imipramine | Diphenhydramine

| ------- | ---------- | ---------------

| Class | TCA | 1st gen antihistamine

| Main action | NE/5-HT reuptake inhibition | H1 blockade

| Muscarinic block | ✔ Yes | ✔ Yes

| Sedation | Moderate | Strong

| Anticholinergic effects | ✔ Prominent | ✔ Prominent

Diphenhydramine is not a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, and neither drug blocks the other’s action. Their pharmacologic overlap is anticholinergic blockade.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a cystic swelling in the neck located anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the junction of its upper and middle thirds. Persistence of which embryological cleft is responsible for the formation of this cyst?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation describes a branchial cyst, which characteristically appears along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, most frequently at the junction of its upper and middle thirds. This cyst arises from the persistence of the second pharyngeal cleft (or cervical sinus of His). During development, the second pharyngeal arch grows downward and normally covers the second, third, and fourth clefts, which then obliterate. Failure of this obliteration results in a fluid-filled cyst. A persistent first cleft (Option A) leads to preauricular cysts or fistulae near the ear or mandible. Persistence of the third (Option C) or fourth (Option D) clefts is much rarer and usually presents lower in the neck, often associated with the pyriform sinus. Branchial cysts often contain cholesterol crystals and can become infected, requiring surgical excision. The specific location anterior to the upper sternocleidomastoid is the classic anatomical landmark for a second branchial cleft anomaly, making it the most probable embryological cause
questions.learning: The clinical presentation describes a branchial cyst, which characteristically appears along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, most frequently at the junction of its upper and middle thirds.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic presented with severe pain in ear and otorrhoea not responding to antibiotics. On examination, granulation tissue is seen in EAC, facial nerve palsy was present. The likely diagnosis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant otitis externa

Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea, and granulation tissue in EAC and facial nerve palsy indicates malignant otitis externa.

It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa:

* Pseudomonas infection in the elderly diabetics and those on immunosuppressive drugs.

* Excruciating pain, profuse discharge & granulations on the floor of EAC.

* Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection.

* Facial paralysis is common.

* Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen causing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

* Gallium-67 is more useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the patient

* Technetium 99 bone scan reveals bone infection, but the test remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to monitor the disease.

*

Treatment:

(i) Diabetic control.

(ii) Ear toileting

(iii) Antibiotic treatment against the causative organism(P. aeruginosa) for 6–8 weeks or more.

*

Antibiotics found effective are:

*

Gentamicin combined with ticarcillin. (intravenous)

*

Third-generation cephalosporins combined with an aminoglycoside. (intravenous)

*

Quinolones combined with rifampin. (oral)

If patient is not responsive, culture and sensitivity of ear discharge should be done.

Prolonged antibiotic treatment has replaced radical surgery and resections done earlier for this condition.
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea, and granulation tissue in EAC and facial nerve palsy indicates malignant otitis externa.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A truck driver came with complaints of a painless indurated genital ulcer after unsafe intercourse. Which of the following can be used to diagnose the condition in a low-resource setting when an active ulcer is present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dark field microscopy

The clinical vignette of a painless, indurated genital ulcer in a truck driver is most likely suggestive of syphilitic chancre / hard chancre caused by Treponema pallidum. The motility of the organism can be demonstrated by dark ground/ field microscopy which can be used in a low economic, low resource setting.

Dark ground microscopy can be used to diagnose syphilis when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present to visualize Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It is generally less sensitive.

Various types of Spirochetes and their appearances under a dark ground microscope:

* Treponemes generally are short, slender with regular and sharp spirals.

* Leptospira have a large number of closely wound spirals and characteristic hooked ends.

* Borrelia is large with irregular and wide open coils.

The image given below shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by dark ground microscopy and the various appearances of other spirochetes respectively.

Other options:

Option B: Fluorescent treponema antibody absorption test (FTA-ABS) is an indirect immunofluorescence test used to detect specific treponemal antibodies. It is not available for routine testing as it is done only in suitably equipped labs.

Option C: VDRL test is a slide flocculation test in which the serum is inactivated at 56°C for 30 minutes and a measured volume of serum is placed on a special cavity slide. The cardiolipin antigen after preparation is added to the serum sample on a slide and is rotated on a VDRL rotator for a specified period of 4 minutes. In a positive test, the cardiolipin antigen reacts with reagin antibodies present in the infected serum and forms visible clumps. In a negative test, cardiolipin continues to remain as uniform crystals in the serum.

Option D: Treponema pallidum immobilization (TPI) test detects the presence of treponemal antibodies in the serum. Similar to the FTA-ABS test, it is also not available for routine testing.

Pearl PF0806: Syphilis - Diagnostic Serology

Nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR)

VDRL- Venereal disease Research Laboratory test

RPR- Rapid Plasma Reagin test

* Quantitative tests(titres)

* Reagin antibody tests; based on cardiolipin antigen

* VDRL can be used to test CSF whereas RPR cannot be used

* RPR does not require preheating of serum unlike VDRL

* VDRL requires light microscope for interpretation whereas RPR can be read macroscopically

* Decrease in titers confirms treatment

* Sensitivity of RPR(86%)>VDRL(76%) in primary syphilis

Treponemal Tests

FTA-ABS- Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption test

TPI-Treponema pallidum immobilization test

TPHA-Treponema pallidum haemagglutination test

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient is not able to see the lateral fields. He was having a mild headache for a few weeks and now presented to the clinic. Visual field examination shows the following finding. What is the probable site of the lesion based on the image displayed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Optic chiasma

The visual field defect in the image is indicative of bitemporal hemianopia, so the probable site of the lesion is the optic chiasma.

Hemianopia or hemianopsia refers to loss of sight in half the visual field. Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma. The most common cause of this is pituitary gland tumours. Other causes include suprasellar aneurysms, chronic arachnoiditis, suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma.

Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia to emphasize the fact that the parts of the visual field that are lost in each eye do not overlap.

Individuals with this condition are able to see in both left and right central visual fields, with both eyes open. However, all information from the most peripheral parts of visual fields (which are seen only by the nasal retinas) is lost.

Other options:

Lesions at the occipital lobe, optic tract and optic radiation would all cause homonymous hemianopia. Here, either the right or left half of the binocular field of vision is lost, due to the loss of the temporal half of one field and the nasal half of the other.
questions.learning: Optic chiasma — The visual field defect in the image is indicative of bitemporal hemianopia, so the probable site of the lesion is the optic chiasma. Hemianopia or hemianopsia refers to loss of sight in half the visual field.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a rural Type-A Primary Health Center (PHC), approximately how many deliveries are performed per month?
questions.explanation: In the Indian public health system, Primary Health Centers (PHCs) are classified based on their caseload to optimize resource allocation. A Type-A PHC is a facility that handles a low volume of deliveries, typically defined as less than 20 deliveries per month. These centers focus primarily on outpatient care and essential maternal health services but refer more complex cases to higher facilities. A Type-B PHC is one that handles a higher load, specifically 20 or more deliveries per month (Option B). Options C and D ( and ) are not the standard cut-off values used in the official classification system. Type-B PHCs are required to have more extensive labor room facilities and staff to manage the increased delivery burden. This classification helps in determining the necessary staffing, equipment, and supply chain needs for each center. Encouraging institutional deliveries at PHCs is a core strategy of the National Health Mission to reduce maternal and infant mortality rates

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the thoracolumbar fascia is incorrect?
options: In the lumbar region, it is in 4 layers
In the thoracic region, it is attached medially to the vertebrae
The anterior, posterior, and middle layers join to form the aponeurotic origin of transversus abdominis
questions.explanation: The thoracolumbar fascia is a critical structural complex in the back, but statement B is incorrect because it consists of three layers in the lumbar region, not four. These are the anterior, middle, and posterior layers which envelop the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and erector spinae muscles. Statement A is correct; the fascia is highly innervated with nociceptive and proprioceptive nerve endings, playing a significant role in chronic low back pain. Statement C is correct, as the fascia in the thoracic region is a thin fibrous layer attached medially to the thoracic spines. Statement D is also correct, as the three layers fuse laterally to form the aponeurotic origin of the transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles. This fascia acts as a "nature's back brace," providing stability to the spine and facilitating load transfer between the upper and lower limbs. Understanding its trilaminar structure is essential for surgical approaches to the posterior abdominal wall

Therefore,

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 51-year-old man complains of abdominal pain and blood-stained stools. The barium study of his intestines shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intussusception

The given clinical scenario and the radiological images are suggestive of intussusception.

In intussusception, the occluding mass prolapsing into the lumen has been termed the coiled spring appearance (barium in the lumen of the intussusceptum and in the intraluminal space). In adults, it develops due to a tumor of the bowel.

The intussusception appears as a sausage-shaped mass in a longitudinal plane or a target mass in the transverse plane on CT and USG.

Ultrasound signs include:

• Target sign (also known as the doughnut sign)
• Pseudokidney sign- this is seen in the longitudinal section of the bowel

• the edematous bowel resembles renal parenchyma and
• the mesentery which is dragged into the intussusception resembles renal hilum

• Crescent in a doughnut sign.

Note: The colographic appearance of intussusception is also described as a claw sign, pincer defect, shouldering effect, and coiled-spring pattern.

Option B: Volvulus presents with constipation, abdominal bloating, nausea, and/or vomiting. It shows coffee bean sign

Option C: Diverticulitis presents with pain in the left iliac fossa

Option D: Ulcerative colitis causes backwash ileitis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with exertional breathlessness and a history of cyanotic spells. On examination, digital clubbing is present, and a harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. A chest X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of cyanotic spells (Tet spells), clubbing, and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border points toward Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). The provided chest X-ray shows the pathognomonic boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot), caused by right ventricular hypertrophy and a narrow pulmonary pedicle. TAPVC (Option B) classically shows a "snowman" or "figure-of-eight" heart. Transposition of the Great Arteries (Option C) would show an "egg-on-a-string" heart and usually presents within days of birth rather than at age 5. Atrial Septal Defect (Option D) is typically acyanotic and shows increased pulmonary vascular markings on X-ray. Thus, the specific radiological sign and history of cyanotic spells confirm TOF
questions.learning: The combination of cyanotic spells (Tet spells), clubbing, and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border points toward Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with fever of 38.5 °C and fundal spots on eye examination. CBC shows a leukocyte count of 20,000/cu mm. How many minor Duke’s criteria are satisfied in this patient for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis (IE) is based on the Modified Duke Criteria. In this case, the patient fulfills three minor criteria, supporting a diagnosis of possible IE. 1. Predisposition: Intravenous drug use is a well-recognized risk factor for infective endocarditis, particularly right-sided involvement. 2. Fever: Documented body temperature ≥ 38 °C fulfills the fever criterion. 3. Immunologic phenomenon: The retinal findings described are consistent with Roth spots, which are classically associated with infective endocarditis. An elevated total leukocyte count is a nonspecific inflammatory finding and is not included as a Duke criterion. At present, major criteria such as positive blood cultures or echocardiographic evidence of vegetations are not available. According to the Modified Duke Criteria, possible infective endocarditis is diagnosed when either one major and one minor criterion, or three minor criteria are present. Therefore, this patient meets the criteria for possible IE. Given the patient’s high-risk profile, urgent blood cultures from multiple sites and transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography are required to confirm the diagnosis. Early recognition is crucial, as right-sided infective endocarditis, common in intravenous drug users, can result in septic pulmonary emboli, valvular destruction, and serious morbidity
questions.learning: The diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis (IE) is based on the Modified Duke Criteria. In this case, the patient fulfills three minor criteria, supporting a diagnosis of possible IE.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 48-year-old man presenting with scrotal swelling, elevated LDH levels, normal AFP levels on tumor marker evaluation, and a characteristic histopathological finding following orchidectomy?
questions.explanation: The histological image and clinical data provided are characteristic of a seminoma, the most common type of germ cell tumor in adults. The pathognomonic histological features seen are large, uniform, polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm (due to glycogen) and "fried-egg" nuclei, organized in nests separated by thin fibrous septa containing lymphocytic infiltrates. Clinically, seminomas often cause elevated Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) but are typically negative for Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP); a high AFP would instead suggest a yolk sac tumor (Option A) or a mixed germ cell tumor. Teratomas (Option B) would show tissues from multiple germ layers (hair, teeth, etc.). Embryonal carcinoma (Option D) features pleomorphic cells in glandular or papillary patterns with more aggressive necrosis. Given the uniform cell population, clear cytoplasm, and the characteristic lymphocytic septa, seminoma is the definitive diagnosis for this middle-aged patient

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person was stabbed in the thigh with a knife, resulting in a wound measuring 1 cm in length and 3 cm in depth. How would you classify this wound?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Penetrating wound

In the given clinical scenario, a person is stabbed in the thigh with a knife, resulting in a wound measuring 1 cm in length and 3 cm in depth is suggestive of a penetrating wound.

A penetrating wound is an injury that occurs when an object, such as a knife, bullet, or any sharp instrument, breaks through the skin and enters deeper tissues of the body. These types of wounds can damage organs, blood vessels, and nerves, depending on the depth and location of the penetration. Penetrating wounds may lead to significant blood loss, infection, or trauma to vital structures, requiring prompt medical attention.

Treatment typically involves controlling bleeding, preventing infection, and repairing any internal damage, often requiring surgical intervention. The severity of a penetrating wound depends on the force of impact, the object involved, and the area affected.

Other options:

Option B: A perforating wound occurs when an object penetrates the body and exits, creating both an entry and an exit wound. These wounds can cause significant internal damage, including injury to organs, blood vessels, and tissues.

Option C: A crush injury occurs when a part of the body is subjected to intense pressure or force, typically from a heavy object. This can lead to tissue damage, fractures, nerve injury, and in severe cases, organ damage or compartment syndrome.

Option D: An incised wound is clean-cut, regular, well-defined caused by sharp lightweight weapons like a knife, razor, scalpel, etc. Incised wounds will have a characteristic head of wound and tailing of a wound.

The edges are well-defined and usually everted, free from contusions and abrasions. It is usually spindle-shaped. The depth is more at the commencement and progressively becomes shallower, known as tailing. Tailing determines the direction of the force applied when creating the wound.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of persistent cough and weight loss. He had a history of contact with multiple sexual partners. He was diagnosed as HIV positive 6 months back and is poorly adherent to his medications. The fungal culture of sputum was negative. On Gomori methamine silver staining, the cells showed darkly stained crescent-shaped cysts. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pneumocystis jerovecii

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii.

P. jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients. It usually occurs when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/μL. Patients usually present with fever and nonproductive cough with progressive shortness of breath. It can also affect other organs like lymph nodes, spleen, and liver.

Laboratory and radiographic findings are also non-specific and show an increase in lactate dehydrogenase levels and symmetric, perihilar, and diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates, respectively. The classic radiographic appearance of symptomatic Pneumocystis pneumonia consists of diffuse bilateral symmetric interstitial infiltrates that are perihilar. CT will show diffuse ground-glass opacities. Giemsa stain, toluidine blue, methenamine silver, and calcofluor white stains demonstrate trophozoites. The cyst wall appears black with Gomori's methenamine silver stain.

Shown below is an image of the staining showing the black-stained crescent-shaped cysts resembling the crushed ping-pong balls of P. jirovecii. The stain used for staining the causative organism is Gomori’s methenamine silver stain.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole combination (commonly known as co-trimoxazole) is the treatment of choice for PCP, and it is administered for 21 days, followed by a course for secondary prophylaxis. Concomitantly, glucocorticoids should also be administered to reduce pulmonary inflammation.

Patients who are susceptible to PCP are also given co-trimoxazole as prophylaxis. For patients who are unable to tolerate co-trimoxazole, IV pentamidine is the drug of choice.

Prophylaxis is indicated for other opportunistic infections like Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection if CD4 counts fall below 50 cells/µL; Coccidioides, if CD count is <250/µL; and Cryptococcus, when the CD count is <100/µL.

Other options:

Option A: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis causes paracoccidioidomycosis, which usually presents with ulcerations in the oral and nasal mucosa, lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary lesions, but it does not form crescent-shaped cysts.

Option B: Histoplasma capsulatum causes histoplasmosis and may be associated with similar symptoms as Pneumocystis jirovecii, but it does not show crescent-shaped cysts on Gomori methenamine silver staining.

Option C: Coccidioides immitis causes coccidioidomycosis, which is characterized by respiratory symptoms, skin lesions, and joint pain. It also does not show crescent-shaped cysts on Gomori methenamine silver staining.
questions.learning: Pneumocystis jerovecii — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. P. jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients.

questions.text: A young female of reproductive age presents for a subcutaneous implant. What is the contraindication for this contraceptive method?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding

A subcutaneous implant is a progestin-containing contraceptive method, and its absolute contraindication is undiagnosed vaginal bleeding.

Implants are thin, flexible, progestin-containing cylinders that are inserted subdermally into the inner aspect of the upper arm, approximately 8 cm above the elbow.

Nexplanon is a single-rod etonogestrel implant that releases at least 30 µg of hormone per day and provides contraception for up to 3 years.

Levonorgestrel implants are a two-rod system containing a total of 150 mg of LNG and provide effective contraception for up to 5 years.

Absolute contraindications of Progestin include:

* Current pregnancy

* Breast cancer

* Acute liver disease

* Liver tumors

* Undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While numerous animals play a role in the transmission of rabies, dogs stand out as the most common ones. Moreover, the impact of this disease is often more in children. Given this understanding, what approach would be both economically efficient and rational to reduce the occurrence of rabies?
options: Testing all the dogs for rabies
Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs
Increase capacity of healthcare workers for surveillance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs

Rabies is primarily transmitted by dogs, and children are disproportionately affected. The most cost-effective and rational strategy to reduce rabies incidence is source control, i.e., targeting the animal reservoir.

• Mass dog vaccination (≥70%) interrupts transmission.
• Control of stray dog population reduces human exposure.
• This approach is far more economical and effective than post-exposure management alone.

questions.explanation: The structure marked in the image, located between the superior constrictor muscle and the tonsil, is the pharyngobasilar fascia. The capsule (Option B) refers to the specialized fibrous layer that immediately surrounds the palatine tonsil.
