questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with following finding. Which of the following clinical tests will aid in diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Grattage Test

The image depicts silvery white scaly plaques on the back which is a charateristic feature of Psoriasis. Grattage test will aid in its diagnosis.

Grattage Test:

* Scratching (grattage) scales in psoriasis makes the scale appear more silver in colour by introducing air–keratin interfaces.

* When the scales are completely scraped off, the stratum mucosum (basement membrane) is exposed and is seen as a moist red surface (membrane of Bulkeley) through which dilated capillaries at the tip of elongated dermal papillae are torn, leading to multiple bleeding points.This classical pinpoint bleeding is known as Auspitz sign.

* Auspitz sign is due to the elongated, dilated, tortuous vessels in the dermal papilla along with supra papillary thinning of epidermis.

However Auspitz sign is neither sensitive nor specific for Psoriasis.

* It is not seen in Pustular, Guttate, Erythrodermic or Inverse psoriasis.

* It is also seen in non-psoriatic scaling disorders like Darier's disease and Actinic Keratosis.

Psoriasis is a group of common chronic inflammatory and proliferative conditions of the skin, associated with systemic manifestations in many organ systems. The most characteristic lesions consist of red, scaly, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques, present particularly over the extensor surfaces and scalp.

Other Options:

Option B: Nikolsky's sign: Firm tangential sliding pressure with a finger will separate normal‐looking epidermis from dermis, producing an erosion. Lateral pressure on the normal skin around the blister results in separation between the layers of epidermis and the epidermis moves under the finger and shears off.

Nikolsky's sign is positive in the following:

* Pemphigus

* Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome(SSSS)

* Pemphigus foliaceus

The following image shows Nikolsky's sign, where the application of gentle lateral pressure causes sliding of the epidermis.

Option C: The Asboe-Hansen sign is a dermatological test that involves applying pressure to a blister to see if it spreads to the surrounding skin. It's used to help diagnose blistering diseases like pemphigus vulgaris and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).

Option D: The standard patch test units are applied in two sets (on either side of the spine) and kept covered. One set of patches is removed and exposed to UVA. After irradiation, the other set of patches are also removed and both the sites are covered again for 48 hours. A positive reaction on the irradiated side only is an indication of photoallergy. Negative reaction is seen in phototoxic reaction.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a sign of irreversible injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blebbing plasma membrane

Blebbing of plasma membrane is a feature of reversible injury

Within limits, a cell can repair derangements and, if the injurious stimulus abates, will return to normalcy. This is called reversible cell injury. Persistent or excessive injury, however, causes cells to pass the rather nebulous “point of no return” into irreversible injury and cell death.

The ultrastructural changes of reversible cell injury include:

* Plasma membrane alterations, such as blebbing, blunting, and loss of microvilli

* Mitochondria - swelling and the appearance of small amorphous densities

* Dilation of the ER, with the detachment of polysomes

* Intracytoplasmic myelin figures

* Nuclear alterations- disaggregation of granular and fibrillar elements

Irreversible cell injury

* Increased eosinophilia, glassy homogeneous appearance

* Whorled phospholipid masses called myelin figures derived from damaged cell membranes

* Discontinuities in plasma and organelle membranes

* Marked dilation of mitochondria with the appearance of large amorphous densities

* Intracytoplsmic amorphous debris, and aggregates of fluffy material probably representing denatured protein.

* Nuclear changes- karyolysis, pyknosis and karyorrhexis
questions.learning: Blebbing plasma membrane Blebbing of plasma membrane is a feature of reversible injury Within limits, a cell can repair derangements and, if the injurious stimulus abates, will return to normalcy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image below shows an image of the anus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perianal abscess

The image shows a smooth swelling on the perineum near the anal opening suggestive of perianal abscess.

Anorectal abscess refers to a collection of pus in the anal or rectal region. More commonly seen in men. Anorectal abscess originates from an infection arising in the cryptoglandular epithelium lining the anal canal. Fistula-in-ano, Crohn's disease, diabetes and immunosuppression are some conditions leading to abscess formation.

Anorectal abscess presents as a painful, throbbing swelling in the anal region with constitutional symptoms like fever.

There are four types of anorectal abscesses:

* Peri-anal (most common)

* Ischio-rectal

* Inter-sphincteric

* Supra-levator

Treatment:

* Most of them can be drained under local anaesthesia as an outpatient procedure in the clinic or emergency room.

* Larger, more complicated abscesses may require drainage in the operating room. A skin incision is created, and a disk of skin is excised to prevent premature closure. No packing is necessary, and sitz baths are started the next day.

Pilonidal sinus refers to non-infected, midline openings in the natal cleft overlying the coccyx. Drivers and hairdressers are more commonly affected and is seen more in men, usually after puberty. Patients complain of intermittent pain, swelling and discharge at the base of the spine. Constitutional symptoms such as fever and fatigue are usually absent. The primary sinus may have one or many openings, all of which are strictly in the midline between the level of the sacrococcygeal joint and the tip of the coccyx. The other sites that they can be affected include the interdigital cleft and axilla.

The image given below shows a pilonidal sinus in the natal cleft(midline opening).
questions.learning: Perianal abscess — The image shows a smooth swelling on the perineum near the anal opening suggestive of perianal abscess. Anorectal abscess refers to a collection of pus in the anal or rectal region.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to the OPD with complaints of amenorrhoea for the past year. She has a history of postpartum hemorrhage and lactational failure. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sheehan's syndrome

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Sheehan's syndrome.

Sheehan's syndrome (SS) is postpartum hypopituitarism secondary to the necrosis of the pituitary gland. It usually results from severe hypotension or shock caused by massive hemorrhage during or after delivery. Patients with SS have varying degrees of anterior pituitary hormone deficiency. The hyperplastic enlargement of the pituitary, which occurs normally during pregnancy, increases the risk of infarction.

Affected women may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to a deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to a deficiency of gonadotropins). Because deficiencies of some or all pituitary-responsive hormones may develop after the initial insult, Sheehan syndrome can be heterogeneous and may not be identified for years.

It can present acutely as pituitary apoplexy, an endocrine emergency, characterized by a sudden onset of headache, nausea, visual deficits, and in severe cases, severe hypoglycemia, hypotension and shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death.

Also, it can present late with the following features:

• Loss of pubic and axillary hair
• Hypothyroidism due to decreased TSH secretion
• Adrenal insufficiency due to low ACTH

Treatment is by hormone replacement - first glucocorticoids, later - thyroid hormone, sex steroids, vasopressin and growth hormones are given. If there is evidence of progressive visual loss, cranial nerve involvement or loss of consciousness, immediate surgical decompression must be carried out. Fertility can be achieved in these women with hMG and hCG. Clomiphene is ineffective.

Option B: Rotor syndrome is a type of hereditary hyperbilirubinemia with autosomal recessive inheritance. Affected individuals have mild jaundice and hyperbilirubinemia.

Option C: Prolactinoma or pituitary adenoids is the condition of hyperprolactinemia diagnosed by a prolactin level >200 μg/L. It usually presents with infertility, amenorrhea, and galactorrhea.

Option D: Acromegaly is characterized by the signs and symptoms pertaining to excessive growth hormone secretion.
questions.learning: Sheehan's syndrome — The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Sheehan's syndrome. Sheehan's syndrome (SS) is postpartum hypopituitarism secondary to the necrosis of the pituitary gland.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Pentavalent vaccine includes which of the following?
options: Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus , HBV, Injectable Polio
Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Haemophilus influenza B, Pneumococcal vaccine
Diphtheria, Tetanus, HBV, Haemophilus influenza B, Pertussis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diphtheria, Tetanus, HBV, Haemophilus influenza B, Pertussis

Pentavalent vaccine is a combination of five vaccines that provide protection against 5 life-threatening diseases such as diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Administration of pentavalent vaccine reduces the number of pricks to a child.

It is given at 6, 10, and 14 weeks in the immunization program, and can replace the need for separate administration of Hepatitis B and DPT vaccines. However, the Hepatitis B birth dose and DPT booster doses should be continued. It is given 0.5ml intramuscularly in the anterolateral aspect of the mid-thigh.

Pentavalent vaccine is a freeze-sensitive vaccine and therefore should be stored and transported at 2- 8° C temperature. It is a very safe vaccine with a few mild side effects like pain, redness and swelling at the injection site, fever, vomiting, abnormal crying, and loss of appetite.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A non alcoholic factory worker in a groundnut factory developed hepatocellular carcinoma. What is the most probable cause in this worker who has been working there for a long time?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aflatoxins

Aflatoxin is the most probable cause in this patient as he is working in a groundnut factory.

Aflatoxins:

* These are a type of mycotoxins produced by Aspergillus species of fungi, such as A. flavus (secretes B1) and A. parasiticus (secretes B1, B2, G1 and G2)

* Frequently present in moldy foods, like groundnuts, corn, and peas.

* These toxins are highly toxic to animals and birds, as well as to human beings.

* Known to cause hepatomas in lower animals, and carcinogenic effects in humans have also been seen.

Risk factors for HCC

* HBV, HCV, aflatoxin, alcohol

* Hereditary hemochromatosis, α1AT deficiency, Wilson disease, metabolic syndrome, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Other options:

BOAA (Beta oxalyl amino alanine) is the toxic compound causing Lathyrism.

Sanguinarine is the toxic compound causing epidemic dropsy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For a woman with a prior pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, what is the recommended folic acid dosage when planning conception?
questions.explanation: The standard periconceptional dose of folic acid for healthy women is 400 mcg (0.4 mg) daily to prevent neural tube defects (NTDs) (Option A). However, for a woman with a high risk—specifically those with a history of a previous pregnancy complicated by an NTD—clinical guidelines mandate a significantly higher dose. The recommended dosage for these women is 4 mg/day (Option D), which is ten times the standard dose . This high-dose supplementation should begin at least one month (ideally three) before conception and continue through the first trimester. Options B (1 mg) and C (2 mg) are insufficient based on international safety standards for secondary prevention. This intervention is proven to reduce the risk of NTD recurrence by over 70%. Therefore, for a woman with a prior affected pregnancy, 4 mg is the definitive and life-saving dosage recommendation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with dry eyes, dry mouth, and dry cough. She requires frequent sips of water while eating. Schirmer test was positive. Laboratory investigations revealed ANA, anti-Ro/SSA, and anti-La/SSB antibodies. What are the characteristic features seen in this condition?
options: Destruction of salivary glands due to neutrophilic infiltration
Destruction of salivary glands and lacrimal glands due to lymphocytic infiltration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Destruction of salivary glands and lacrimal glands due to lymphocytic infiltration

This vignette sketches Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy:

• Xerophthalmia (dry eyes)
• Xerostomia (dry mouth)
• Needs water while eating (saliva is missing)
• Schirmer test positive (↓ tear production)

Serology seals it:

• ANA
• Anti-Ro/SSA
• Anti-La/SSB

A slow, targeted siege:

• CD4+ T cells and B cells infiltrate salivary & lacrimal glands
• Acinar cells are destroyed
• Ducts get replaced by lymphoid tissue
• Over time → glands shrink, dry, and fail

The presentation is classic for Sjögren syndrome, confirmed by positive Schirmer test and anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies.

The characteristic pathology is chronic lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands causing glandular destruction and sicca symptoms.

Neutrophilic destruction, amyloid deposition, or malar rash are not defining features of Sjögren syndrome.

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Lymphocytic infiltration | Mainly CD4+ T cells

| Acinar destruction | Loss of secretory units

| Epimyoepithelial islands | Ductal epithelial hyperplasia

| Glandular atrophy | Chronic stage

| Fibrosis | Late feature

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient sustains a head injury after being struck on the skull by a falling hammer. Subsequent CT imaging demonstrates characteristic findings related to this mechanism of trauma. Based on the nature of the injury and the typical appearance on imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A high-force impact to a small, localized area of the skull—such as being hit by a hammer—characteristically results in a Depressed skull fracture. In this type of injury, a fragment of the skull is driven inward toward the brain. On a head CT (bone window), this appears as an area where the bone is displaced below the level of the surrounding skull vault. Epidural Hematoma (Option A) would show a biconvex lens-shaped bleed. Concussion (Option B) is a functional brain injury that typically shows no visible abnormalities on CT. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option D) would show blood within the sulci and cisterns. Depressed skull fractures are significant because they may be "open" (if the skin is torn) and can cause direct underlying brain contusions or dural tears, leading to an increased risk of infection and post-traumatic epilepsy. If the bone is depressed by more than the thickness of the skull, surgical elevation is often required to minimize complications
questions.learning: A high-force impact to a small, localized area of the skull—such as being hit by a hammer—characteristically results in a Depressed skull fracture. In this type of injury, a fragment of the skull is driven inward toward the brain.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman with a history of ovarian cancer presents with difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a seated position, and combing her hair. On examination, characteristic clinical findings are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms of "difficulty climbing stairs" and "combing hair" indicate proximal muscle weakness. When this weakness is associated with an underlying malignancy (like ovarian cancer), it is a classic paraneoplastic presentation of dermatomyositis. This idiopathic inflammatory myopathy often presents with skin findings such as a heliotrope rash or Gottron papules. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A) and systemic sclerosis (Option C) are autoimmune conditions that can involve muscles, but they are not as specifically linked to this pattern of paraneoplastic proximal weakness as dermatomyositis. Cushing syndrome (Option D) can cause proximal muscle wasting due to steroid excess, but the direct clinical link to ovarian cancer makes an inflammatory myositis much more probable. Dermatomyositis requires evaluation of muscle enzymes (CK) and electromyography for diagnosis. In an older patient, its diagnosis necessitates a thorough screening for internal malignancies, as seen in this patient's history
questions.learning: The patient's symptoms of "difficulty climbing stairs" and "combing hair" indicate proximal muscle weakness. When this weakness is associated with an underlying malignancy (like ovarian cancer), it is a classic paraneoplastic presentation of dermatomyositis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The most potent natural estrogen is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estradiol

Estradiol (E₂) is the most potent natural estrogen with the highest receptor affinity. Estrone is predominant post-menopause, while estriol is weakest and rises in pregnancy.

| Estrogen Type | Source / Predominance | Potency | Key Feature

| ------------- | --------------------- | ------- | -----------

| Estradiol | Ovaries (reproductive years) | Most potent | Highest receptor affinity, main active estrogen

| Estrone | Postmenopausal women | Moderate | Main estrogen after menopause

| Estriol | Pregnancy | Weakest | Predominant during pregnancy

Estradiol is the main estrogen during reproductive years.

Source

• Granulosa cells of ovarian follicles
• Produced from androgens via aromatase enzyme

Major functions

| Function | Effect

| -------- | ------

| Endometrial proliferation | Prepares uterus for implantation

| Secondary sexual characters | Breast development

| Bone metabolism | Prevents osteoporosis

| Cervical mucus | Makes it thin and receptive

Estradiol dominates during the follicular phase of menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the most widespread calculation of Stillbirth Rate, the numerator is defined as foetal deaths weighing over ‘X’ gram at birth, during the year. Which one of the following is the correct value for ‘X’?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1000

The Stillbirth Rate (SBR) is an important indicator of maternal and perinatal health. In the traditional and most widely used definition (Park’s PSM), a stillbirth is defined as the birth of a dead fetus weighing 1000 g or more (or after 28 weeks of gestation) during a given year.

Stillbirth Rate = (Number of stillbirths ≥1000 g ÷ Total births [Live births + Stillbirths]) × 1000

Hence, the correct value of ‘X’ is 1000 g.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child was diagnosed with croup. Which of the following types of stridor will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inspiratory stridor

This child has croup, which would most likely be associated with inspiratory stridor.

In croup, the sudden onset of prominent inspiratory stridor is characteristic, although a softer expiratory stridor may also be present. As the severity increases, a biphasic stridor is heard along with visible suprasternal, intercostal, and subcostal retractions.

Croup, or laryngotracheobronchitis, is a viral infection affecting the upper airway, primarily in children aged 6 months to 6 years. The most common causative organism for croup is the parainfluenza virus. While other viruses like influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and adenovirus can also cause croup, parainfluenza is the predominant cause.

The severity of croup is determined by the Westley croup score.

* Mild croup – Stridor may be present when upset or crying but it is not present at rest. Barking cough, hoarse cry, and either no or only mild chest wall/subcostal retractions are seen.

* Moderate croup- Stridor is present at rest. Mild retractions are at least present. Children may have other symptoms or signs of respiratory distress. The child does not appear agitated.

* Severe croup – Stridor is present at rest. Retractions are severe that include indrawing of the sternum. The child may appear anxious, and agitated.

Hospitalization is done in a child for any of the following:

* progressive stridor,

* severe stridor at rest,

* respiratory distress,

* hypoxia,

* cyanosis,

* depressed mental status,

* poor oral intake

Treatment:

1. Racemic epinephrine nebulization - It causes narrowing of pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa. This lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and promotes the reabsorption of fluid from the interstitial space and thus reduces edema. The indications for the administration of nebulized epinephrine are:

* moderate to severe stridor at rest

* The possible need for intubation

* respiratory distress

* hypoxia

2. Oral dexamethasone - Indicated in all the grades of croup. Corticosteroids reduce laryngeal edema through their anti-inflammatory action. IM dexamethasone and nebulized budesonide have an equal clinical effect. Corticosteroids should not be administered to children with varicella or tuberculosis as they may worsen the disease.

3. A helium-oxygen mixture (heliox) may be considered for severe croup when intubation is being considered. Oxygen recommented for child with spo2 <92% i.e in hypoxia
Note: Antibiotics are not indicated.

The image below shows a steeple sign, seen in croup.

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both

* Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the basic model of a nuclear family life cycle, consider the following phases: 1. Contraction 2. Dissolution 3. Extension 4. Formation Which one of the following best represents the correct sequence of phases in a normal nuclear family?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4 → 3 → 1 → 2

The family life cycle describes the predictable stages through which a nuclear family progresses from its formation to its eventual dissolution. Understanding these stages helps in planning appropriate maternal, child, and geriatric health services.

The normal sequence of phases in a nuclear family is: Formation → Extension → Contraction → Dissolution

• Formation: Begins with marriage and establishment of a new family.
• Extension: Family expands with the birth and upbringing of children.
• Contraction: Children become independent, leave home, marry, and start their own families (“empty nest” phase).
• Dissolution: Ends with the death of one or both spouses, marking the end of the family unit.
questions.learning: 4 → 3 → 1 → 2 The family life cycle describes the predictable stages through which a nuclear family progresses from its formation to its eventual dissolution.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following metabolic abnormalities is most likely to be seen in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypokalemia

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is associated with hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis.

Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e. hypokalemia  hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Persistent vomiting secondary to gastric outlet obstruction results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway.

The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions. Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia. Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine.

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS):

It most commonly presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 3 and 6 weeks of age. It is associated with hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus. This results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. First-born male infants are at the highest risk.

Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting. Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right (not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting.

Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. Ultrasound examination confirms the diagnosis of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) in the majority of cases. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis is a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm.

Management includes the correction of metabolic abnormality before the correction of the pylorus. The hypertrophic pylorus is surgically corrected by Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person was taking an antihypertensive drug and continued taking it despite developing constipation, dry mouth, and dizziness. He was taking it regularly but forgot to take it during a trip abroad and has now developed a hypertensive emergency. Which antihypertensive was he likely taking?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clonidine

Clonidine is a centrally acting α₂-agonist that commonly causes dry mouth, constipation, and sedation. It acts on the brainstem (medulla) to:

• Decrease sympathetic outflow
• Reduce norepinephrine release

Result:

• ↓ Heart rate
• ↓ Peripheral vascular resistance
• ↓ Blood pressure

Abrupt withdrawal leads to rebound sympathetic overactivity, causing severe hypertension or hypertensive emergency.

This withdrawal phenomenon is characteristic of clonidine. This is why clonidine must be tapered slowly, not stopped abruptly.

Calcium channel blockers and RAAS inhibitors do not cause rebound hypertension on sudden cessation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: To prevent recurrence, expectant mothers with a previous fetus with neural tube defect should receive folic acid daily at the dose of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4 mg

Women with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect (NTD) are at high risk of recurrence. To reduce this risk, they should receive high-dose folic acid (4 mg/day), starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, when neural tube closure occurs.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. 4 μg: Far below the recommended daily requirement.
• B. 400 μg: Recommended for low-risk women planning pregnancy, not for women with a previous NTD-affected pregnancy. ⭐
• D. 400 mg: Excessively high and not recommended.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Name the drug that acts on both the marked areas.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Omapatrilat

The drug that acts on both the marked areas is omapatrilat.

Omapatrilat is a dual inhibitor of neutral endopeptidase and Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). It decreases angiotensin II and increases atrial and brain natriuretic peptide, promoting vasodilation, diuresis, and anti-hypertrophic effect.

Other options:

Option A - Sacubitril is a neprilysin inhibitor. It reduces the breakdown of natriuretic peptides such as ANP, BNP, and CNP, thereby increasing their levels. Sacubitril combined with valsartan reduces mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

Option C - Losartan is the angiotensin receptor blocker used in the treatment of hypertension. Hyperkalemia is an important side effect of ARBs. It appears to be a safe and efficacious agent to lower serum uric acid levels in patients with hyperuricemia.

Option D - Nesiritide is a recombinant human brain natriuretic peptide (BNP). It causes vasodilatation and natriuresis. It is administered intravenously and used in acute decompensated heart failure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a patient with endometrial carcinoma receiving pelvic external beam radiation, which pelvic organ is most sensitive to radiation?
questions.explanation: Radio-sensitivity refers to the susceptibility of an organ or tissue to damage from ionizing radiation. Among the pelvic organs listed, the ovary (Option A) is definitively the most sensitive to radiation . Even very low doses of radiation can cause permanent damage to the ovarian follicles, leading to premature ovarian failure and sterility. In contrast, the vagina (Option B), bladder (Option C), and rectum (Option D) are relatively more radio-resistant, although they can still suffer from late-term radiation effects like cystitis or proctitis at higher cumulative doses. Because the oocytes are highly specialized and non-regenerative cells, the ovary serves as the limiting organ for dose planning in younger patients. Therefore, protecting the ovaries or performing an oophoropexy (moving the ovaries out of the radiation field) is a critical consideration in pelvic oncology to preserve endocrine function and fertility
questions.learning: Radio-sensitivity refers to the susceptibility of an organ or tissue to damage from ionizing radiation. Among the pelvic organs listed, the ovary (Option A) is definitively the most sensitive to radiation .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A Patient has muffled heart sounds with low blood pressure. Correct JVP finding is?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of muffled heart sounds, low blood pressure, and distended neck veins (Beck's triad) is diagnostic for cardiac tamponade. In tamponade, the heart is compressed by high-pressure pericardial fluid, which prevents rapid ventricular filling. On the Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP) waveform, the y-descent represents the rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle during early diastole. Because the high intrapericardial pressure resists this filling, the y-descent is characteristically blunted or absent. A steep x-descent (Option A) is often preserved in tamponade, but the "absent y" is the differentiating feature. Conversely, a steep y-descent (Option C, Friedreich's sign) is the hallmark of constrictive pericarditis, where filling is rapid but stops abruptly. Blunted x-descent (Option D) is seen in tricuspid regurgitation. Recognizing these JVP nuances is essential for bedside differentiation between tamponade (an emergency requiring pericardiocentesis) and constrictive pericarditis

questions.text: The following image depicts a particular type of cataract. What history should be elicited from the patient to come to a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blunt trauma

The above image characteristically depicts a rosette cataract. It typically follows closed globe injuries (blunt trauma), and hence is also known as the concussion cataract.

* Late rosette cataract - in posterior cortex; 1-2 years after trauma; smaller and compact than early rosette.

Other options:

Option B: Steroid use is linked with posterior subcapsular cataract.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The stain used for identifying Cryptococcus is _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. India ink stain.

The stain used for identifying Cryptococcus is India ink stain.

Indian ink is a negative staining method that provides a uniformly coloured background. The unstained organisms stand out in contrast to the background. It is useful in the demonstration of organisms with capsules that do not take simple stains. It is also used to stain slender bacteria like spirochetes.

The India ink preparation is employed to detect the presence of Cryptococcus neoformans. It is seen as a globular, encapsulated yeast cell with or without budding, between 5 to 20 μm in diameter in size. Cryptococcus has a polysaccharide capsule which is seen against a black background.

Cryptococcus can be cultured from biologic samples like the CSF, sputum, and skin biopsy on routine fungal and bacterial culture media. Colonies are opaque, white-to-cream coloured, and may turn orange-tan or brown after prolonged incubation. They have a mucoid appearance due to the presence of the capsule around the yeast cells.

The image below shows the fungus Cryptococcus, stained with Indian ink.

Pearl PF0796: Various stains and their applications in microbiology

A. Simple stains: Provides color contrast but gives same color to all bacteria and cells.

Type of stain
Applications

Acidic stains
These include Eosin, acid fuchsin, rose bengal, Congo red, etc. and are mostly used to stain pathological specimens.

Basic stains.

1.    Loeffler’s methylene blue stain is used in counterstaining in quellung reaction of streptococcus pneumoniae.

2.    Polychrome methylene blue is used in McFadyean’s reaction of anthrax bacilli

Neutral stains

1.    Wright and Giemsa stains are Romanowsky stains used to stain peripheral blood and bone marrow smears.

2.    Giemsa stain is used for histopathological diagnosis of malaria and some other spirochete and protozoan blood parasites.

B. Differential stains: Imparts different colors to different bacteria. (These contains more than one stain).

Type of stain
Applications

Gram stain: Used to distinguish cells by cell-wall type.
To differentiate between gram positive (stain purple/violet) and gram negative bacteria (stain pink or red).

Acid-fast stain: Used to distinguish acid-fast bacteria from non-acid-fast cells.
Used in Ziehl–Neelsen staining technique for identification of acid – fast microorganisms such as M. tuberculosis, M. leprae, and Nocardia.

Fluorochrome staining: Used for rapid scanning of the smear, where the AFB appear fluorescent green against a black background
Auramine-rhodamine is used in fluorochrome staining for screening for tuberculosis.

C. Special stains

Type of stain
Applications

Staining volutin-containing organisms
Corynebacterium diphtheriae stained by Albert’s stain. Green colored bacilli showing "Chinese-letter" pattern, containing bluish-black metachromatic granules of cells.

Flagella stain
Salmonella typhimurium stained by modified Ryu stain to show peritrichous flagella

Endospore stain
Used in Schaeffer and Fulton staining technique to stain the endospores, where the primary stain is malachite green, and the counterstain is safranin.

Capsule stain
Used in negative staining (Cryptococcus neoformans), McFadyean’s reaction, Polychrome methylene blue (Anthrax bacilli).

Silver impregnation
Fontana’s silver impregnation method used for staining treponeme and leptospire.

Silver staining
Used in Grocott’s – Gomori’s methenamine silver stain. GMS stain is used to identify pneumocystis jirovecii, which classically appear as crushed ping-pong balls.   Warthin–Starry silver stain for spirochetes.

Calcofluor White Staining
The cell walls of fungi will bind the stain Calcofluor white, which greatly enhances visibility of fungal element in tissue or other specimens. It is especially useful for the identification of Mucor and the causative agents of zygomycosis.   It is also used in staining acanthamoeba

Chance's staining
For Cell wall demonstration
questions.learning: The stain used for identifying Cryptococcus is India ink stain. Indian ink is a negative staining method that provides a uniformly coloured background.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who is unable to perform internal and external rotation of the hip?
questions.explanation: The total inability to perform internal and external rotation of the hip is the pathognomonic physical sign of a Hip Dislocation. In a dislocation, the femoral head is completely out of the acetabulum, which "locks" the joint and prevents any rotational movement. In contrast, with a femoral head fracture (Option A) or acetabular fracture (Option B), rotation is typically possible but extremely painful. Pelvis fractures (Option D) involve the pelvic ring and may not necessarily lock the hip joint itself unless the acetabulum is severely involved. Posterior dislocation is the most common type (often from "dashboard" injuries), presenting with the leg in a "shortened, adducted, and internally rotated" position. Anterior dislocation presents with an "abducted and externally rotated" leg. Emergency reduction under anesthesia is required within 6 hours to minimize the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. This loss of rotation is the critical clinical differentiator from an isolated fracture

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: On neurologic examination, a patient is not able to identify an object but is able to recognize the object from its texture, colour and pattern. Which of the following is likely to have been affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inferior temporal lobe

The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvement would be the inferior temporal lobe.

• Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia. According to De Jong, visual agnosia is further classified into:

• Apperceptive visual agnosia - the visual image appears distorted to the patient and hence they are unable to recognise it. This occurs due lesions in the parieto-occipital region
• Associative visual agnosia - inability to visually identify objects in the absence of visual impairment, with ability to identify the object using other sensory modalities (as suggested in the scenario). This occurs due to lesions of occipito-temporal junction, which is present in the inferior temporal lobe. Prosopagnosia is a type of associatetive visual agnosia which refers to the inability to visually identify faces.

The occipital lobe acts as the primary visual area and a lesion in this region would result in cortical blindness and achromatopsia, which is the inability to visualise colour. In the given scenario, as the patient is also able to identify colour, it indicates that the occipital lobe (Option A) is unaffected and (hence inferior temporal lobe is the better answer).

Stereognosis is the ability to identify an object by a perception of the form and nature of an object without looking at it. In the given scenario, the patient is able to recognize the object from its texture and pattern which indicates that stereognosis is intact. Loss of this ability is known as astereognosis which occurs in lesions of the superior parietal lobule (Options B and C) and dorsal column pathways.
questions.learning: Inferior temporal lobe — The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvement would be the inferior temporal lobe. • Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A primigravida delivers a healthy baby via normal delivery. After how many hours should she initiate breastfeeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Within 1 hour

In this scenario of a healthy mother and infant, breastfeeding should be started within 1 hour.

Breastmilk is the ideal and exclusively food for infants in the first 6 months. It reduces the infant mortality rate, neonatal hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesemia hence  should be started as soon possible.

The standard essential newborn care include:

* Maintain the airway and breathing

* Maintain the body temperature and prevent hypothermia

* Initiate breastfeeding within one hour

* Cleaning of baby and care to prevent infection

* Cord care and care of the eyes

* Administering vitamin K

* Performing a thoroiugh examination.

Pearl PF0003: Baby-friendly hospital initiative (revised 2018)

Ten steps to successful breastfeeding (Revised 2018)

Critical management procedures

1  a. Comply fully with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and relevant World Health Assembly resolutions.

b. Have a written infant feeding policy that is routinely communicated to staff and parents.

c. Establish ongoing monitoring and data-management systems.

2. Ensure that staff has sufficient knowledge, competence, and skills to support breastfeeding.

Key clinical practices

3. Discuss the importance and management of breastfeeding with pregnant women and their families.

4. Facilitate immediate and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact and support mothers to initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth.

5. Support mothers to initiate and maintain breastfeeding and manage common difficulties.

6. Do not provide breastfed newborns any food or fluids other than breast milk, unless medically indicated.

7. Enable mothers and their infants to remain together and to practice rooming-in 24 hours a day.

8. Support mothers to recognize and respond to their infants’ cues for feeding.

9. Counsel mothers on the use and risks of feeding bottles, teats, and pacifiers.

10. Coordinate discharge so that parents and their infants have timely access to ongoing support and care.
questions.learning: Within 1 hour — In this scenario of a healthy mother and infant, breastfeeding should be started within 1 hour. Breastmilk is the ideal and exclusively food for infants in the first 6 months.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient complains of decreased sensation in the lateral three-and-a-half fingers on the palmar side of the right hand, along with difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb. Examination reveals thenar atrophy. Which of the following structures, when affected, lead to this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carpal tunnel

The most likely nerve injured here is the median nerve, which occurs in Carpal tunnel syndrome.

Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common entrapment mononeuropathy caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the fibro-osseous carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. Patients present with pain and paresthesia over the lateral 3 and a half digits. There may be a weakness of thumb opposition. In chronic cases, the thenar eminence is lost due to thenar atrophy. Carpal tunnel syndrome can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, chronic renal failure, acromegaly, hypothyroidism, and gout. The diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds but nerve conduction studies can confirm the diagnosis.

Other tests for CTS -

• Phalen's test - Elicited by holding the wrist flexed fully. The appearance of sensory symptoms within 60 seconds implies a positive test.
• Tinel's sign - Sensory symptoms reproduced by percussing over the median nerve imply a positive test.

The given image shows carpal tunnel syndrome:

Non-surgical Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: In mild to moderate cases of carpal tunnel syndrome, non-surgical management options can be explored to alleviate symptoms and improve function. These conservative treatments include:

1.

Wrist splinting: Wearing a wrist splint at night can help maintain the wrist in a neutral position, reducing pressure on the median nerve and providing relief from nocturnal symptoms.

2.

Activity modification: Identifying and modifying activities that exacerbate symptoms can help in managing carpal tunnel syndrome. For example, taking frequent breaks during repetitive tasks or adjusting the workstation ergonomics can be beneficial.

3.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): Over-the-counter NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, can help manage pain and inflammation associated with carpal tunnel syndrome.

4.

Corticosteroid injections: In some cases, corticosteroid injections into the carpal tunnel may provide temporary relief from symptoms by reducing inflammation and pressure on the median nerve.

5.

Physical and occupational therapy: Therapists can help patients learn exercises to stretch and strengthen the hand and wrist muscles, improving symptoms and function.

If conservative treatments do not provide sufficient relief or the condition worsens, surgical intervention, such as carpal tunnel release surgery, may be considered.

Other options:

Option A: High radial nerve injuries typically cause wrist drop due to weakness in wrist and finger extensors, with sensory loss in the dorsal aspect of the hand, not the lateral three and a half fingers on the palmar side.

Option B: High median nerve injuries can affect sensation in the lateral three-and-a-half fingers on the palmar side and impair thumb flexion and opposition, particularly at the proximal phalanx. There is a loss of pronation due to the paralysis of the pronator teres and pronator quadratus. Paralysis of flexor digitorum superficialis and lateral half flexor digitorum profundus results in loss of wrist flexion. Ape-like hand and pointing index are due to this injury.

Option C: High ulnar nerve injuries result in sensory loss in the medial one-and-a-half fingers (pinky and ring finger) and hand intrinsic muscle weakness, unrelated to thenar muscle involvement.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient develops immune-mediated hemolytic anemia following administration of penicillin, indicating an adverse drug reaction. This immune response represents which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia caused by penicillin is a classic example of a Type 2 (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reaction. In this mechanism, penicillin acts as a hapten and binds to the surface of red blood cells. The immune system then produces antibodies (usually IgG or IgM) that specifically target the penicillin-coated RBCs. This leads to the destruction of the cells via the complement system or phagocytosis by splenic macrophages. Type 1 (Option A) is IgE-mediated and results in immediate anaphylaxis or hives. Type 3 (Option C) involves the deposition of circulating immune complexes in tissues, leading to conditions like serum sickness. Type 4 (Option D) is a cell-mediated (delayed) response, such as contact dermatitis. While penicillin can cause any of these reactions, the specific destruction of blood cells mediated by surface-bound antibodies is uniquely categorized as Type 2. Clinically, this is confirmed by a positive Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) test
questions.learning: Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia caused by penicillin is a classic example of a Type 2 (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reaction. In this mechanism, penicillin acts as a hapten and binds to the surface of red blood cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding shoulder dystocia? I. It can be predicted during early labour. II. Anencephaly is a risk factor. III. Turtle neck sign is present. IV. Episiotomy should always be given. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency in which, after delivery of the fetal head, the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis (or less commonly, the posterior shoulder behind the sacral promontory), preventing delivery of the shoulders. It requires prompt recognition and a series of obstetric maneuvers to prevent fetal hypoxia and birth trauma. The following statements are true:

• II. Anencephaly is a risk factor: Anencephalic fetuses have a small head with relatively normal-sized shoulders, increasing the risk of shoulder dystocia.
• III. Turtle neck sign is present: The turtle sign is the classic clinical sign of shoulder dystocia, in which the delivered fetal head retracts against the maternal perineum after expulsion because the shoulders are impacted.
• IV. Episiotomy should always be given: Although an episiotomy does not relieve the bony obstruction, it is commonly performed to provide additional space for internal maneuvers (e.g., Rubin or Woods screw maneuver). Hence, many traditional examination questions consider it appropriate.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. It can be predicted during early labour: Shoulder dystocia is largely unpredictable. Although several risk factors are recognized, most cases occur without warning, and many women with risk factors deliver without shoulder dystocia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A tall, obese patient with a known history of hypertension is newly diagnosed with metabolic syndrome during a routine health check-up. Which of the following clinical or biochemical findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Increase in uric acid and insulin
Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol
questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome is defined by a cluster of abnormalities, but dyslipidemia is a core diagnostic component. The most characteristic lipid changes are elevated triglycerides and reduced HDL cholesterol, reflecting altered lipid metabolism due to insulin resistance. Among the given options, increase in triglycerides (and often total cholesterol) best represents this defining biochemical disturbance. In fact, raised triglycerides are one of the standard diagnostic criteria for metabolic syndrome (along with waist circumference, BP, glucose, HDL). Although insulin resistance with hyperinsulinemia and raised blood glucose is the underlying mechanism, these are pathophysiological features, not always the most specific “finding” highlighted in exam questions. Why other options are less appropriate: (A) Uric acid → not a diagnostic criterion (B) BP + insulin → incomplete picture (D) Glucose + insulin → mechanism, not defining profile

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following cytokines with their function: 1. IL-5 2. IL-6 3. IL-7 4. IL-8
questions.explanation: 1-D, 2-A, 3-B, 4-C. Interleukins (IL) are essential signaling molecules in the immune system. 1. IL-5 (1-D) is the primary cytokine responsible for the growth, differentiation, and activation of eosinophils, playing a key role in allergic diseases and helminth infections. 2. IL-6 (2-A) is a major pro-inflammatory cytokine that stimulates the liver to produce acute phase reactants like CRP and fibrinogen. 3. IL-7 (3-B) is critical for lymphopoiesis, specifically the survival and maturation of B and T cell precursors. 4. IL-8 (4-C) is a potent chemokine specifically responsible for neutrophil recruitment and chemotaxis to sites of infection. Options A, C, and D are incorrect mathematical pairings. Knowledge of these specific cytokine functions is fundamental to understanding the pathophysiology of inflammation and the targets of modern biologic therapies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient presents with severe dyspnoea. Mitral stenosis with left atrial hypertrophy is seen. Vegetations present on the mitral valve were excised. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the given HPE image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatic valvular disease

The given image depicts Aschoff's body, which is suggestive of rheumatic valvular disease.

• Anitschkow cells or plump macrophages

• Abundant cytoplasm

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A right trochlear nerve lesion causes:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right SO palsy

The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies the superior oblique (SO) muscle of the eye.

• It is the only cranial nerve that exits dorsally from the brainstem.
• Its fibers decussate (cross) within the brainstem before exiting.
• Therefore, each trochlear nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle on the same side after crossing.

A right trochlear nerve lesion results in right superior oblique muscle palsy.

Function of superior oblique:

• Intorsion
• Depression of the adducted eye
• Abduction

Clinical signs:

• Vertical diplopia
• Difficulty looking down while reading or descending stairs
• Compensatory head tilt away from the affected side

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient walks with a stomping gait. When asked to close his eyes and walk, he is unable to do so. Which of the following tracts is probably affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior column tract

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the involvement of the posterior column.

Posterior column carries proprioception which is essential for coordination of motor movements. Loss of this leads to the development of a stomping gait. This is seen in cases of vitamin B12 deficiency leading to subacute combined degeneration, tabes dorsalis or diabetic neuropathy.
questions.learning: Posterior column tract — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the involvement of the posterior column. Posterior column carries proprioception which is essential for coordination of motor movements.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What plasma protein is found in the highest concentration?
questions.explanation: Human plasma contains a variety of proteins that serve essential physiological functions. Among these, albumin is the most abundant, typically accounting for approximately 55% to 60% of the total plasma protein content. It is synthesized in the liver and is vital for maintaining oncotic pressure and transporting various molecules like hormones and fatty acids. Globulins (Option B) are the second most prevalent group, including alpha, beta, and gamma globulins (antibodies), and generally comprise about 35% of plasma proteins. Fibrinogen (Option C) is a large protein involved in blood clotting and is present in much lower concentrations, making up roughly 4%. Bence Jones proteins (Option A) are abnormal light-chain proteins found in the urine and blood of patients with multiple myeloma and are not a standard component of healthy plasma. Therefore, albumin is the correct choice as the highest concentration plasma protein
questions.learning: Human plasma contains a variety of proteins that serve essential physiological functions. Among these, albumin is the most abundant, typically accounting for approximately 55% to 60% of the total plasma protein content.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following drugs can be used in the management of hypertension in pregnancy except for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Enalapril

Enalapril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and it is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Enalapril is an ACE-Inhibitor which is contraindicated in pregnancy due to potential teratogenic side effects like renal dysplasia and renal failure.

ACE inhibitors inhibit the conversion of angiotensin I to the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin-II. When given in the second and third trimesters, they can cause severe fetal malformations such as bony malformations, persistent patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), respiratory distress syndrome, limb contracture, etc.

Choice of anti-hypertensives in pregnancy:

Pregnancy-induced hypertension/pre-eclampsia / severe pre-eclampsia
Labetalol

Acute hypertension/ Hypertensive crisis
IV labetalol, nifedipine, hydralazine

Chronic hypertension in pregnancy
Labetalol > methyl dopa.

Anti-hypertensives to be avoided in pregnancy include:

* ACE inhibitors.

* Angiotensin receptor blockers.

* Diuretics (contraindicated as anti-hypertensive but can be given in congestive cardiac failure).

* Reserpine.

* Sodium nitroprusside (used only as a drug of last resort in refractory severe hypertension).

* Diazoxide.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: If a tumor compresses the structures passing through the opening marked in the given image, which of the following sensations would be affected?
options: Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose

The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure. If a tumour compresses the structures passing through this foramen, it would impair sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose, as this would affect the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face.

The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity. Therefore, if a tumour or lesion compresses the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure, it would likely affect the sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose because these areas are innervated by the branches of the trigeminal nerve that pass through this fissure.

Other options:

Option A: Sensation of the nasopharynx is innervated by other branches of the trigeminal and glossopharyngeal nerve, not by structures passing through the superior orbital fissure.

Option B: While some sensation from the nasal cavity comes from the trigeminal nerve, the specific branches affected by a lesion in the superior orbital fissure are more focused on the anterior areas of the face.

Option D: Sensation of the chin is primarily innervated by the mandibular branch (CN V3) of the trigeminal nerve, which passes through the foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient consumed 90% sodium hydroxide and has complete dysphagia. Which of the following would be the best next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Feeding jejunostomy

• This is a case of acute caustic ingestion.
• Alkali liquefactive necrosis→ leads to deep penetration → severe esophageal injury.
• The patient has complete dysphagia, meaning oral feeding is impossible.

Because the esophagus is severely injured, enteral nutrition must be administered via a route that bypasses it.

The safest option is Feeding jejunostomy (FJ), because → Allows the delay of definitive surgery until inflammation subsides

Why are the other options wrong

A) Esophago-jejunostomy

• A reconstructive surgery; Contraindicated in the acute phase
• Tissue is inflamed and friable → high risk of leak
• Done months later after stricture formation.

B) Stent placement

• Not done in acute caustic burns
• Risk of perforation and worsening injury

D) Gastrojejunostomy

• Requires a functional stomach
• Alkali ingestion often damages the stomach too (pyloric stenosis is a common feature)
• Does not solve the esophageal obstruction
questions.learning: Feeding jejunostomy • — This is a case of acute caustic ingestion. • Alkali liquefactive necrosis→ leads to deep penetration → severe esophageal injury. • The patient has complete dysphagia, meaning oral feeding is impossible.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with features of adenoid facies and symptoms of a mild upper respiratory infection and is diagnosed with chronic adenoid hypertrophy. In view of this diagnosis and the need for definitive management, which surgical procedure is considered the most appropriate treatment for chronic adenoid hypertrophy in this patient?
questions.explanation: Chronic adenoid hypertrophy is a common condition in children and may present with adenoid facies, nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and recurrent upper respiratory infections. When symptoms are persistent and significant, definitive management is surgical removal of adenoids (adenoidectomy). The standard and most commonly accepted technique for adenoidectomy, especially in exam settings, is curettage. In this method, a curette is used to remove hypertrophied adenoid tissue from the nasopharynx. It is simple, effective, widely practiced, and considered the conventional gold standard in many clinical and exam contexts. Why other options are wrong: (A) Coblator : A newer technique using radiofrequency ablation; effective but not the standard answer in most MCQs (B) Microdebrider : Endoscopic-assisted technique; more precise but not traditionally considered first-line in exams (D) Breathing exercise and symptomatic treatment : Not definitive for chronic hypertrophy with structural obstruction
questions.learning: Chronic adenoid hypertrophy is a common condition in children and may present with adenoid facies, nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and recurrent upper respiratory infections.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Most serious contraindication for oxytocin?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is a potent uterotonic agent used for the induction and augmentation of labor. Its most serious and absolute contraindication is any condition where a vaginal delivery is physically impossible or dangerous, such as malpresentation of the fetus (Option A). If oxytocin is administered when the fetus is in a transverse lie or breech (without specific criteria), it can lead to hyperstimulation and catastrophic uterine rupture as the uterus tries to force the baby through an impassable canal. While maternal heart disease (Option B) and premature labor (Option C) are important considerations that require caution, they are often relative contraindications depending on the specific clinical goal. Hypothyroidism (Option D) is not a contraindication for oxytocin use. Therefore, the risk of mechanical obstruction and subsequent uterine rupture makes malpresentation the most critical contraindication. Careful clinical assessment of fetal lie and presentation is mandatory before initiating an oxytocin drip
questions.learning: Oxytocin is a potent uterotonic agent used for the induction and augmentation of labor. Its most serious and absolute contraindication is any condition where a vaginal delivery is physically impossible or dangerous, such as malpresentation of the fetus…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Normal diameter of artery to vein at the optic disc margin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2:3

The normal diameter ratio of the central retinal artery to the central retinal vein at the optic disc margin is 2:3.

The ratio 2:3 means that the artery’s diameter is approximately two-thirds of the vein’s diameter. This is considered the physiological normal. The ratio is assessed during the fundoscopic examination, and significant deviations can indicate pathological conditions:

• Decreased ratio (arteriolar narrowing) may suggest hypertension or arteriosclerosis.
• Increased ratio (relative venous narrowing) is less common but may occur in rare conditions.
questions.learning: 2:3 The normal diameter ratio of the central retinal artery to the central retinal vein at the optic disc margin is 2:3. The ratio 2:3 means that the artery’s diameter is approximately two-thirds of the vein’s diameter.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following according to the latest guidelines is NOT an indication to IE prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrial Septal Defect

According to AHA / ESC guidelines, antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended only for high-risk cardiac conditions.

It is not recommended for most congenital heart diseases, including isolated ASD.

This change was made to:

• Reduce unnecessary antibiotic use
• Prevent antibiotic resistance

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated in high-risk cardiac conditions only.

These include prior IE, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.

An atrial septal defect (isolated, unrepaired) is a low-risk lesion and does not require prophylaxis.

Hence, ASD is not an indication for IE prophylaxis. Prophylaxis is mainly recommended before: Dental procedures involving gingival manipulation

Typical drug:

• Amoxicillin 2 g orally (adults)
questions.learning: Atrial Septal Defect According to AHA / ESC guidelines, antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended only for high-risk cardiac conditions. It is not recommended for most congenital heart diseases, including isolated ASD.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A semen profile showing low sperm count (16 million/ml), reduced motility (40%), and severely abnormal morphology (<1% normal forms) is termed oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT).
questions.explanation: According to the latest WHO criteria for semen analysis, the primary abnormality in this case is a severe defect in sperm morphology. Teratospermia is defined as the presence of less than 4% morphologically normal sperm when assessed using Kruger’s strict criteria. In this patient, the morphology is <1%, which represents severe teratospermia. Oligospermia (Option A) refers to a reduced sperm concentration, defined as a count <15 million/mL. Since this patient’s sperm count is 16 million/mL, it lies within the normal reference range. Asthenospermia (Option C) denotes reduced sperm motility (progressive motility <32% or total motility <40%); the patient’s motility is at the lower limit of normal and does not meet criteria for asthenospermia. Normospermia (Option B) indicates normal semen parameters across all domains, which is clearly not the case here. Although abnormalities of count, motility, and morphology may coexist (OAT syndrome), the isolated and most significant defect here is morphology, making teratospermia the correct diagnosis. Severe teratospermia significantly impairs fertilization, and assisted reproductive techniques such as intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) are often required to achieve pregnancy
questions.learning: According to the latest WHO criteria for semen analysis, the primary abnormality in this case is a severe defect in sperm morphology. Teratospermia is defined as the presence of less than 4% morphologically normal sperm when assessed using Kruger’s strict…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the statements is true about lumbar puncture? 1. LP is urgently indicated if CT scan is negative in suspected SAH 2. Post dural puncture head ache is common in females and older adults 3. Meningitis after LP is an unusual side effect 4. LP is safely done in thrombocytopenia more than 10000
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3

• LP is indicated after a negative CT in suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage to detect xanthochromia (true).
• Meningitis is a rare complication (true).
• PDPH is more common in young females, not older adults, and LP is unsafe at platelet counts around 10,000 (requires ≥50,000). Hence only statements 1 and 3 are correct.
