questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A body was brought in for post-mortem examination, and the following can be seen. What type of wounds are these?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Defense wounds

The given image shows irregular and ragged cut wounds over the palmar surface of the hands and fingers, which is suggestive of defense wounds.

Defense wounds are the wounds that occur as a result of the victim's attempt to save himself from an injury.

It can be active or passive. Active defense wounds occur when the victim tries to grasp the weapon, while passive wounds result when the victim raises the hands, arms, or legs in an attempt to protect the eyes, head, or neck.

The morphology of the wound depends upon the type of weapon and the attack. In a sharp injury due to a single-edged weapon, a single cut may be seen on the palm or the bends of fingers. In the case of a double-edged sharp weapon, cuts are seen on both palm and fingers. The cuts are irregular in-depth and are ragged.

The defense wounds signify homicide, and in females, they often indicate sexual assault.

Other options:

Options B and C: Antemortem and postmortem wounds are of medicolegal importance while evaluating trauma. They can be differentiated by the following features:

Feature
Antemortem wounds
Postmortem wounds

Edges
Swollen edges with wound gapes
Closely approximated with no wound gapes

Hemorrhage
Arterial type of hemorrhage
Venous hemorrhage

Spurting
Spurting of blood seen with firmly coagulated blood
No spurts and no clotting

Vital reaction
Inflammation and repair seen
No signs of inflammation and repair

Option D: Hesitation cuts are a feature of self-inflicted wounds or suicide. It typically appears as multiple, small, and superficial wounds on the skin, at the beginning of an incised wound. The common sites are the throat, wrist, and front of the chest.
questions.learning: Defense wounds — The given image shows irregular and ragged cut wounds over the palmar surface of the hands and fingers, which is suggestive of defense wounds.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True regarding mitochondrial genome:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Maternal inheritance

Mitochondrial genome is maternally inherited.

Mitochondrial inheritance:

• Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum) as an individual’s mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperms contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization.
• Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease.

Pedigree shows mitochondrial inheritance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 33-year-old woman presents with excessive daytime sleepiness and short-term memory difficulties. Her BMI is 43, blood pressure is 170/98 mmHg, and arterial blood gas shows PO₂ 70 mmHg, PCO₂ 53 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 33 mmol/L. Which condition is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: This patient has a Body Mass Index (BMI) of 43 kg/m², marked daytime sleepiness, and arterial blood gas (ABG) evidence of chronic hypercapnia (PaCO2 ≈ 53 mmHg) while awake, which together are diagnostic of Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS), also known as Pickwickian syndrome. Although Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) commonly coexists and contributes to daytime somnolence, the presence of awake hypoventilation with elevated PaCO2 is the defining feature of OHS. Central sleep apnea is characterized by absent respiratory effort during sleep and is not associated with severe obesity or persistent daytime hypercapnia. Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness with features such as cataplexy but does not explain chronic respiratory acidosis, hypercapnia, or hypertension. The elevated serum bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) reflects metabolic compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis. Management includes weight reduction and positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy. If untreated, OHS can progress to pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, and increased mortality

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct regarding “witch’s milk”?
options: It is seen in full-term infants
It is seen only in preterm infants
It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by progesterone
It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by calcitonin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is seen in full-term infants

Witch’s milk refers to transient breast enlargement with milk secretion in newborns. It is a physiological phenomenon caused by the transplacental transfer of maternal estrogens during pregnancy and the subsequent prolactin surge after birth. It is seen in both male and female full-term infants and usually resolves spontaneously without treatment.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. It is seen only in preterm infants: It is more common in full-term infants, not exclusively in preterm infants.
• C. It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by progesterone: The primary cause is maternal estrogen, with prolactin contributing to milk secretion after birth.
• D. It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by calcitonin: Calcitonin has no role in neonatal breast enlargement or milk secretion.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with a two-month history of pain and swelling in his lower leg. Radiography demonstrates an onion-skin periosteal reaction, and biopsy shows PAS-positive small round blue cells. Which of the following chromosomal translocations is most commonly associated with this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. t(11;22)

Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumor that typically affects children and adolescents. It commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones and is characterized by an “onion-skin” periosteal reaction on X-ray. Histologically, the tumor consists of PAS-positive small round blue cells due to abundant intracellular glycogen. The hallmark genetic abnormality is the t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation, which produces the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion gene, an abnormal transcription factor that drives tumorigenesis.

Why not the other options?

• A. t(8;14): Seen in Burkitt lymphoma, involving c-MYC activation.
• B. t(15;17): Seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), producing the PML-RARA fusion gene.
• D. t(9;22): The Philadelphia chromosome, seen in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and some cases of ALL, producing the BCR-ABL fusion gene.
questions.learning: t(11;22) Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumor that typically affects children and adolescents. It commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones and is characterized by an “onion-skin” periosteal reaction on X-ray.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Out of the four given statements, which is true about coughing?

1. Forceful Expiration against closed glottis
2. Slow Expiration against open glottis
3. Begins with a shallow inspiration
4. Remove harmful substances
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. i, iv

Coughing is a type of forceful expiration. During forceful expiration, when pressure builds up, the glottis opens and then the air comes out. The cough reflex is a protective mechanism of the larynx to expel irritants and keep the airway clear.

Coughing begins with a deep inspiration followed by a forced expiration against a closed glottis. This increases the intrapleural pressure to 100 mm Hg or more. The glottis is then suddenly opened, producing an explosive outflow of air at velocities up to 965 km (600 ml) per hour.

Both chemical and mechanical stimuli can initiate the cough reflex. Chemical or mechanical irritation of the respiratory mucosa stimulates the afferent internal laryngeal nerve, which is the branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the vagus nerve. These sensory fibres synapse in the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla oblongata. Complex neural networks here generate the conscious 'urge to cough' while also sending efferent signals to the various muscles involved in generating an effective cough which include the adductors of the vocal cord, the diaphragm, the external intercostals and the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall.

Other Options

Statement ii and iii: It is the forceful expiration, not just a normal expiration or deep inspiration which opens the glottis.
questions.learning: i, iv Coughing is a type of forceful expiration. During forceful expiration, when pressure builds up, the glottis opens and then the air comes out.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 58-year-old develops sudden hypotension and a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border 3 days after an anterior STEMI. There are pulmonary crackles and elevated JVP. The most appropriate immediate confirmation test in this condition is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urgent echocardiography with Doppler

Sudden hypotension with a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border 3 days after an MI strongly suggests a mechanical complication, most classically ventricular septal rupture causing an acute left-to-right shunt with pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. The fastest and most definitive bedside confirmation is urgent transthoracic echocardiography with color Doppler to demonstrate the septal defect and shunt.

Learning Points

• Post-MI mechanical complications often occur 3 to 5 days after infarction.
• Ventricular septal rupture causes a new harsh holosystolic murmur best heard at the LLSB, shock, and pulmonary edema.
• Best immediate confirmation is urgent echo with color Doppler.
• Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe MR with a new systolic murmur at the apex and flash pulmonary edema, and echo is also the key test.

Management is urgent stabilization and early surgical or percutaneous intervention.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with polyuria and polydipsia for six months. Laboratory findings reveal HbA1c 5.5%, normal blood glucose, normal post-prandial glucose, and decreased urine osmolality. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with polyuria (excessive urine output) and polydipsia (excessive thirst), symptoms that can be seen in multiple disorders. However, normal HbA1c and normal blood glucose levels (fasting and postprandial) effectively rule out Diabetes Mellitus (Option A). The key diagnostic clue is the presence of low urine osmolality (dilute urine) despite large urine volumes, which is characteristic of Diabetes Insipidus (DI). DI results from either a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in central DI or renal resistance to ADH in nephrogenic DI, leading to impaired water reabsorption in the collecting ducts. Conn’s syndrome (Option C) is associated with hypertension and hypokalemia, while Addison’s disease (Option D) causes adrenal insufficiency, typically presenting with hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia—none of which match this clinical picture. The diagnosis of DI is confirmed by a water deprivation test, which assesses the kidney’s ability to concentrate urine. Central DI responds to desmopressin, whereas nephrogenic DI is managed with a low-salt diet, thiazide diuretics, and adequate hydration. Accurate differentiation between DM and DI is essential because their treatments differ completely

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mechanism of action of dicumarol?
options: Inhibits vitamin K dependant Clotting factors
questions.explanation: Dicumarol is a naturally occurring oral anticoagulant that belongs to the coumarin class, functionally identical to warfarin. Its mechanism of action is the inhibition of the enzyme Vitamin K epoxide reductase. This inhibition prevents the recycling of Vitamin K, which is a necessary cofactor for the post-translational gamma-carboxylation of several critical proteins. Specifically, it leads to the production of dysfunctional, vitamin K-dependent clotting factors: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X, as well as regulatory proteins C and S. Activating antithrombin III (Option A) is the mechanism of heparin. Inhibiting Factor Xa (Option D) is the mechanism of drugs like rivaroxaban. Inhibiting tissue plasminogen activator (Option C) would be pro-thrombotic rather than anticoagulant. Because dicumarol inhibits the synthesis of new factors rather than inactivating existing ones, its anticoagulant effect has a slow onset (delayed by several days). Monitoring is traditionally performed via the prothrombin time (PT) or INR to ensure therapeutic efficacy and safety
questions.learning: Dicumarol is a naturally occurring oral anticoagulant that belongs to the coumarin class, functionally identical to warfarin. Its mechanism of action is the inhibition of the enzyme Vitamin K epoxide reductase.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: This instrument is contraindicated for?
questions.explanation: Obstetric forceps are instruments designed to assist in the vaginal delivery of the fetal head by providing traction or rotation. Their use is strictly contraindicated in cases of obstructed labor. In obstructed labor, there is a physical mismatch (such as cephalopelvic disproportion) that prevents safe passage; applying forceps in this situation can lead to catastrophic maternal and fetal injuries, including uterine rupture and fetal skull fractures. Regarding the other options, forceps can be used during a Caesarean section (Option A) to help extract a deeply engaged head. Specific types, like Piper forceps, are used for the after-coming head of a breech (Option C). Kielland forceps are used for rotation in occipital posterior positions (Option D). Therefore, only obstructed labor presents a complete contraindication to their use, necessitating an immediate surgical alternative like a C-section
questions.learning: Obstetric forceps are instruments designed to assist in the vaginal delivery of the fetal head by providing traction or rotation. Their use is strictly contraindicated in cases of obstructed labor.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Lesion in the medial lemniscus at the level of pons causes which of the following?
options: Pain and temperature loss in the same side
Pain and temperature loss in the opposite side
Loss of tactile and proprioception on the same side
Loss of tactile and proprioception on the opposite side
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Loss of tactile and proprioception on the opposite side

Lesion in the medial lemniscus at the level of pons causes loss of tactile and proprioception on the opposite side.

Fibers of medial lemniscus ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns of the spinal cord to the medulla, where they synapse in the gracilus and cuneate nuclei.

The second-order neurons from these nuclei cross the midline and ascend in the medial lemniscus to end in the contralateral ventral posterior lateral (VPL) nucleus and related specific sensory relay nuclei of the thalamus.
questions.learning: Loss of tactile and proprioception on the opposite side Lesion in the medial lemniscus at the level of pons causes loss of tactile and proprioception on the opposite side.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The chest X-ray below shows a right-sided lung white-out with contralateral tracheal deviation. In which condition is this finding typically seen?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray shows right-sided white-out (complete opacification) with contralateral (leftward) tracheal deviation. This indicates a space-occupying lesion causing a mass effect, which pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side. White-out lung + trachea shifted away (contralateral) → suggests increased volume/pressure on that side This is typical of large pleural effusion or thoracic mass Why other options are incorrect: (A) Pneumothorax:Would show a hyperlucent (black) hemithorax, not white-out. (B) Consolidation:Causes white-out but usually no significant tracheal shift. (C) Collapse (atelectasis):Leads to tracheal deviation toward the same side (volume loss), not away. Therefore, contralateral deviation with white-out strongly points to a thoracic mass effect (most appropriate option here)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The oxygen carrying capacity of a 18 year old boy with haemoglobin of 14g/dl is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 18

The oxygen carrying capacity of a boy with haemoglobin 14g/dl is 18.

When blood is saturated with 100% O2, the haemoglobin is also 100% saturated and each gram of normal haemoglobin contains 1.39 mL of O2.

However, blood normally contains some inactive haemoglobin derivatives, and the measured value in vivo is thus slightly lower hence, each gram of haemoglobin in vivo contains 1.31 mL of O2 (Hufner’s constant).

According to the above question, when Hb=14g/dl, O2= 1.31*14= 18.34

The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve

• Demonstrates a progressive increase in the percentage of haemoglobin bound with oxygen as blood Po2 increases, which is called the percent saturation of haemoglobin.
• Blood leaving the lungs and entering the systemic arteries usually has a Po2 of about 95 mm Hg, the usual oxygen saturation of systemic arterial blood averages 97 per cent.
• Conversely, in normal venous blood returning from the peripheral tissues, the Po2 is about 40 mm Hg, and the saturation of haemoglobin averages 75 per cent.
questions.learning: 18 The oxygen carrying capacity of a boy with haemoglobin 14g/dl is 18. When blood is saturated with 100% O2, the haemoglobin is also 100% saturated and each gram of normal haemoglobin contains 1.39 mL of O2.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Cytotoxic and expired drugs are disposed by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incineration

Cytotoxic and expired drugs are collected in a yellow bag and then disposed of by incineration.

Expired cytotoxic drugs are to be returned to the manufacturer and subjected to incineration, encapsulation, or plasma pyrolysis. Other discarded medicines can be disposed by incineration.
questions.learning: Incineration Cytotoxic and expired drugs are collected in a yellow bag and then disposed of by incineration. Expired cytotoxic drugs are to be returned to the manufacturer and subjected to incineration, encapsulation, or plasma pyrolysis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle is not involved in the inversion of foot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Peroneus longus

Peroneus longus muscle is not involved in the inversion of the foot. It causes eversion and plantar flexion.

Inversion of the foot is a movement in which the medial border of the foot is elevated so that the sole faces medially.

• Tibialis anterior - Causes dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot
• Tibialis posterior - Causes plantar flexion and inversion of the foot
• Extensor hallucis longus - Causes extension of the great toe, dorsiflexion of the foot, and inversion of the foot (minimal action)

Eversion of the foot is a movement where the lateral border of the foot is elevated so that the sole faces laterally. Peroneus longus, peroneus brevis, and peroneus tertius are the muscles involved.

These movements take place, mainly at the talocalcaneal and the talocalcaneonavicular joints, and partly at the transverse tarsal joint.
questions.learning: Peroneus longus Peroneus longus muscle is not involved in the inversion of the foot. It causes eversion and plantar flexion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor of adequacy of shock therapy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urine output

Urine output is the most reliable bedside indicator of end-organ perfusion and the best clinical monitor of adequacy of shock resuscitation. Since the kidneys are highly sensitive to hypoperfusion, restoration of adequate urine output reflects successful improvement in renal blood flow, cardiac output, and tissue perfusion. Target urine output:

• Adults: ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour
• Children: ≥1 mL/kg/hour
• Burn patients: 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour (adults), 1 mL/kg/hour (children)

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Central venous pressure (CVP): CVP reflects right atrial pressure/preload, but is a poor predictor of tissue perfusion or fluid responsiveness.
• B. Pulmonary wedge pressure (PCWP): PCWP estimates left ventricular filling pressure and is mainly used in selected critically ill patients; it is not the best routine monitor of shock resuscitation.
• D. Restoring blood pressure/pulse vital parameters: Normal blood pressure and pulse do not necessarily indicate adequate tissue perfusion, as compensatory mechanisms may maintain vital signs despite ongoing organ hypoperfusion.
questions.learning: Urine output Urine output is the most reliable bedside indicator of end-organ perfusion and the best clinical monitor of adequacy of shock resuscitation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man who follows a strict vegetarian diet presents with gradually worsening fatigue, numbness and tingling in both feet, and difficulty walking for the past six months. Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Megaloblastic anemia

A strict vegetarian presenting with anemia and neurological symptoms (paresthesias and gait difficulty) most likely has vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, resulting in megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, causing macrocytic megaloblastic anemia, and also leads to demyelination of the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration), producing neurological manifestations.

The patient has:

• Strict vegetarian diet (risk factor for vitamin B₁₂ deficiency)
• Fatigue due to anemia
• Numbness and tingling
• Difficulty walking (posterior column involvement)

These findings are characteristic of megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B₁₂ deficiency.

Why not the other options?

• A. Aplastic anemia: Presents with pancytopenia due to bone marrow failure, without neurological symptoms.
• B. Sideroblastic anemia: Characterized by microcytic anemia with ring sideroblasts and iron overload; neurological symptoms are not typical.
• D. Iron deficiency anemia: Causes microcytic hypochromic anemia, fatigue, koilonychia, and pica, but does not cause neurological deficits.
questions.learning: Megaloblastic anemia — A strict vegetarian presenting with anemia and neurological symptoms (paresthesias and gait difficulty) most likely has vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, resulting in megaloblastic anemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old primigravida at 10weeks gestation comes to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Nausea and vomiting began one day back and now the patient is unable to tolerate fluids. She complains of pain in the right upper quadrant which started a few hours back. On examination, her temperature is 100.2 F, the pulse is 118 bpm and her BP is 110/70 mm of Hg. She has swelling of her lower limbs up to the ankles bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows a gravid uterus corresponding to 10 weeks of gestation and tenderness in the right upper quadrant, with mild guarding and is diagnosed as acute appendicitis. What is the next step of management? Complete blood count * Hemoglobin: 11g/dL * Leukocytes: 13,000 cells/μL * Platelets: 150,000 cells/μL Liver function tests * Aspartate transaminase (AST): 40U/L * Alanine transaminase (ALT): 48U/L Urinalysis * Protein: negative * Pus cells: 1-2/HPF * Bacteria: none USG Abdomen: Reveals a 7mm diameter, aperistaltic, non-compressible, dilated, blind-ending structure arising from the base of the caecum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Do appendicectomy

Based on the given clinical vignette, the next step of management is Laparoscopic appendicectomy at the earliest. Laparoscopic appendicectomy can be done before 28 weeks of gestation.

Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical non-gynecological cause of acute abdomen in pregnancy.

The diagnosis of acute appendicitis in pregnancy is difficult due to

* Nausea and vomiting may be considered normal, especially in the first trimester of pregnancy

* Leukocytosis is a physiological finding in pregnancy

* A gravid enlarging uterus can push the appendix upward and outward, causing the pain to localize in the right flank or right upper quadrant.

Acute appendicitis in pregnancy is associated with miscarriage, preterm delivery, increased risk of peritonitis, perinatal and maternal mortality.

USG abdomen is used to confirm. MRI abdomen can be done if USG is inconclusive.USG Abdomen would reveal a >6mm diameter, aperistaltic, non-compressible, dilated appendix seen as a blind-ending structure arising from the base of the caecum

Other options:

Option B,C,D are not appropriate because they do not treat the urgent cause of the pathology.
questions.learning: Do appendicectomy — Based on the given clinical vignette, the next step of management is Laparoscopic appendicectomy at the earliest. Laparoscopic appendicectomy can be done before 28 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Astrocytomas are associated with all of the following syndromes, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cowden’s disease

Astrocytomas are associated with several inherited tumor-predisposition syndromes:

• (a) Neurofibromatosis type 1 — Correct association

• Classically associated with optic pathway pilocytic astrocytomas.

• (b) Neurofibromatosis type 2 — Correct association

• NF2 can be associated with gliomas including astrocytomas, although vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas are more characteristic.

• (c) Cowden disease — Incorrect → Answer

• Cowden syndrome is caused by PTEN mutation and is classically associated with dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte–Duclos disease) rather than astrocytoma.

• (d) Li-Fraumeni syndrome — Correct association

• Due to TP53 mutation and associated with CNS tumors including astrocytoma/glioblastoma.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In which condition is cherry red post mortem lividity observed?
questions.explanation: Post mortem lividity (livor mortis) usually appears as a bluish-purple discoloration of the dependent parts of the body. However, certain poisonings produce a distinct color change in the blood that is reflected in the lividity. Cherry red lividity is pathognomonic for carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. This occurs because CO binds to hemoglobin with high affinity to form carboxyhemoglobin, which is a bright cherry-red color. Opioid poisoning (Option A) usually shows dark bluish-purple lividity due to asphyxia. Hydrogen sulfide poisoning (Option C) can produce a greenish or dark lividity due to the formation of sulfhemoglobin. Phosphorus poisoning (Option D) does not have a specific characteristic lividity color like CO. Other "reddish" lividities include cyanide poisoning (bright red/brick red) and cold exposure (pinkish red). Identifying the specific hue of livor mortis is a vital forensic tool for narrowing down the cause of death before internal autopsy begins
questions.learning: Post mortem lividity (livor mortis) usually appears as a bluish-purple discoloration of the dependent parts of the body. However, certain poisonings produce a distinct color change in the blood that is reflected in the lividity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a recent history of pneumonia develops a pleural effusion. On pleural fluid analysis, which finding is most characteristic of a parapneumonic effusion?
options: Pleural protein/plasma protein ratio less than 0.5
Pleural LDH less than 2/3rd of plasma LDH
Pleural LDH less than 0.6 of plasma LDH
questions.explanation: A pleural fluid pH of less than 7.2 is a critical indicator of a complicated parapneumonic effusion. This acidic state occurs because of increased metabolic activity by bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space, leading to lactic acid accumulation. According to Light’s Criteria, parapneumonic effusions are exudative, meaning they must have a pleural/serum protein ratio and a pleural/serum LDH ratio . Thus, Options A, B, and D are incorrect as they describe transudative characteristics. Complicated effusions often feature low glucose ( mg/dL) and high LDH levels ( U/L). Recognizing a low pH is essential because it serves as an absolute indication for chest tube drainage (thoracostomy) to prevent the development of a trapped lung or loculated empyema
questions.learning: A pleural fluid pH of less than 7.2 is a critical indicator of a complicated parapneumonic effusion. This acidic state occurs because of increased metabolic activity by bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space, leading to lactic acid accumulation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which factor is the most likely cause of an acute asthma attack in a patient being treated for glaucoma who presents to the emergency department?
questions.explanation: Timolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist commonly administered as topical eye drops to treat open-angle glaucoma by reducing aqueous humor production. Despite topical administration, it can be absorbed systemically through the nasolacrimal duct into the blood. In susceptible individuals, systemic beta-blockade triggers bronchoconstriction by antagonizing receptors in the lungs, leading to an acute asthma exacerbation. Betaxolol (Option B) is a cardioselective blocker and is much less likely to cause pulmonary side effects. Latanoprost (Option C) and Bimatoprost (Option D) are prostaglandin analogs that lower intraocular pressure without affecting the adrenergic system, and they do not cause asthma. Therefore, Timolol is the classic causative agent for medication-induced asthma in glaucoma patients. To reduce this risk, patients are taught punctal occlusion to minimize systemic absorption
questions.learning: Timolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist commonly administered as topical eye drops to treat open-angle glaucoma by reducing aqueous humor production.

• a minimum of five or six groups of well-preserved cells, with each group containing approximately 10–15 cells
•  six clusters of benign cells on at least two slides prepared from separate FNA biopsy samples
• 10 clusters of follicular cells, with each cluster containing at least 20 cells .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Kidney damage and Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) value between 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² are found in which stage of Chronic Kidney Disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage 4 (severe)

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as kidney damage and/or a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) persisting for ≥3 months. CKD is classified into five stages based on the estimated GFR (eGFR) according to the KDIGO guidelines.

A patient with an eGFR of 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² has Stage 4 CKD (Severe reduction in GFR).

Why not the other options?

• A. Stage 2 (Mild): GFR 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² with evidence of kidney damage.
• B. Stage 3A (Mild to moderate): GFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m².
• D. Stage 5 (Kidney failure): GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or dialysis-dependent.

| Stage | eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) | Description

| ----- | --------------------- | -----------

| G1 | ≥90 | Normal/high GFR (with evidence of kidney damage)

| G2 | 60–89 | Mild decrease

| G3a | 45–59 | Mild to moderate decrease

| G3b | 30–44 | Moderate to severe decrease

| G4 ⭐ | 15–29 | Severe decrease in GFR

| G5 | <15 | Kidney failure (ESKD)
questions.learning: Stage 4 (severe) Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as kidney damage and/or a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) persisting for ≥3 months.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: For which of the following condition is the V-Y procedure used as a treatment modality ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ectropion

V-Y procedure is done for Cicatricial ectropion.

Ectropion is the eversion of the lid margin and eyelashes away from the globe.

Cicatricial ectropion is commonly the result of burns, trauma and chronic inflammations of the skin which shorten the anterior lamina of the eyelid which pull the eyelid away from the globe.

Treatment of cicatricial ectropion requires release and relaxation of the scarred tissues, and an elongation of the skin muscle lamina by some form of surgery called as blepharoplasty. However, localized areas of scarring can be released by Z or V–Y plasty.

A V incision is made just below the eyelid with the base of the triangle in line with the ectropion which is pulled up to repair the ectropion. The V incision is now in the shape of a Y which is closed and the normal structure is retained.

Types:

* Involutional/senile- affects the lower lid of elderly patients.

* Cicatricial- caused by the scarring or contracture of the skin and underlying tissues

* Paralytic- caused by ipsilateral facial nerve palsy

* Mechanical- caused by tumors on or near the lid margin that mechanically evert the lid

* Congenital

Pearl PF1603: Surgical Modalities Used in Correcting Ectropion

Ectropion

Procedure

Involutional ectropion

• Medial conjunctivoplasty
• Horizontal lid shortening
• Byron–Smith-modified Kuhnt–Szymanowski operation
• Lateral tarsal strip technique

Paralytic ectropion

• Horizontal lid tightening
• Palpebral sling operation

Cicatricial ectropion

• V-Y operation
• Z-plasty (Elschnig’s operation)
• Excision of scar tissue and full-thickness skin grafting

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Villages A and B have different age distributions. Which indicator is most appropriate for comparing the death rates between these two villages?
questions.explanation: When comparing mortality across populations with different age structures, the Age Standardized Death Rate is the most reliable indicator. In this scenario, Village B has a significantly larger elderly population (10,000 people aged 60+) compared to Village A (7,000). Because older people naturally have higher death rates, a direct comparison using the Crude Death Rate (Option A) would be biased, likely showing higher mortality in Village B simply due to its age composition rather than poor health quality. Standardization mathematically "removes" the influence of age by applying observed death rates to a common standard population. Specific death rates (Option C) provide details for a single group but not an overall comparison. Proportional mortality (Option D) measures the percentage of deaths from a specific cause and does not assess overall death risk. Standardization allows epidemiologists to make a fair, "apples-to-apples" comparison between disparate communities to identify true health disparities

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which source and cell produce testosterone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cholesterol and Leydig cells

Testosterone production is mainly contributed by Leydig cells from cholesterol.

Testosterone is also synthesized from androstenedione secreted by the adrenal cortex. Luteinizing hormone(LH) helps in the secretion of testosterone by increased formation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) via the G-protein- coupled LH receptor and Gs. 99% of the testosterone in plasma is bound to protein, 65% is bound to gonadal steroid–binding globulin (GBG) or sex steroid–binding globulin, and 33% to albumin.

Actions of testosterone:

* Development of secondary sexual characters in males.

* Increases protein synthesis and decreases protein destruction.

* Maintain spermatogenesis along with FSH.

* Libido

In some target cells testosterone is primarily converted into dihydrotestosterone(DHT) by 5α reductase. DHT helps in the development of male external genitalia, enlargement of the prostate and penis at the time of puberty, facial hair and acne development, and the temporal recession of the hairline.

questions.text: What would be the diagnosis in case the axis aligns with the "?" mark as depicted in the below diagram?

questions.text: A 13-year-old boy presents with involuntary dancing movements of his right hand. He was diagnosed with rheumatic fever. What constitutes the ganglia involved in the presenting complication?

Correct answer: D. Caudate nucleus and putamen

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Sydenham's chorea, a complication of rheumatic fever. The choreic movements are caused by the destruction of D2 neurons of the striatum. The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen.

The image given below shows Sydenham's chorea in a patient.

Nomenclature of basal ganglia:

• Corpus striatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen+ globus pallidus
• Lentiform nucleus: Putamen + globus pallidus
• Neostriatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen

questions.text: Genetic testing for BRCA 1/BRCA 2 is indicated for all of the following except:

Genetic counselling is the process of discussing various genetic testing such as BRCA testing and multiple gene panel testing.

* Bilateral breast cancer

* Family history (maternal or paternal) of two or more individuals with breast and ovarian cancer

* A close relative with early-onset (<50 years) breast or ovarian cancer

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman, with a history of burn injury to her lower limb 5 years ago, now presents with an ulcer developing in the burn scar (as shown in the image). What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The development of a new ulcer within a long-standing, chronic burn scar (especially 5 years or more after the initial injury) is highly diagnostic for a Marjolin’s Ulcer. This is a type of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma that arises in areas of chronic inflammation or previous trauma. Venous ulcers (Option B) typically occur in the "gaiter area" above the medial malleolus and are associated with varicose veins. Arterial ulcers (Option C) occur on distal pressure points and are extremely painful. Cellulitis (Option D) is an acute bacterial skin infection and would not present as a chronic, non-healing ulcer in an old scar. Marjolin's ulcers are characterized by their rapid growth, everted edges, and a high risk of regional lymph node metastasis compared to standard skin cancers. The definitive diagnostic step is a wedge biopsy of the ulcer edge. Management requires wide surgical excision with adequate margins, often involving skin grafting or amputation depending on the location and depth of invasion
questions.learning: The development of a new ulcer within a long-standing, chronic burn scar (especially 5 years or more after the initial injury) is highly diagnostic for a Marjolin’s Ulcer.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All of the following ions have decreased concentration on the luminal side of proximal convoluted tubule except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chloride

The concentration of chloride on the luminal side is more when compared to sodium, glucose, and amino acids.

In the first half of the proximal tubule, sodium is reabsorbed by co-transport along with glucose, amino acids, and other solutes. As sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, it preferentially carries glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate along with it. Thus, their concentrations decrease markedly along the length of the proximal tubule, and a solution having a higher concentration of chloride is left behind. The concentration of chloride here is around 105 mEq/L.

In the second half of the proximal tubule, sodium gets re-absorbed along with chloride since there is only a little glucose and amino acids yet to be re-absorbed. The second half of the proximal tubule has a concentration of chloride ≈140 mEq/L. This higher chloride concentration favors its own diffusion from the lumen into the renal interstitial fluid.

Although the amount of sodium in the tubular fluid decreases markedly along the proximal tubule, the concentration of sodium and the total osmolarity remain relatively constant. This is because the proximal tubule is highly permeable to water and water reabsorption increases to keep pace with the sodium reabsorption.
questions.learning: Chloride — The concentration of chloride on the luminal side is more when compared to sodium, glucose, and amino acids. In the first half of the proximal tubule, sodium is reabsorbed by co-transport along with glucose, amino acids, and other solutes.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with facial edema progressing to generalized edema. Urinalysis shows heavy proteinuria, light microscopy appears normal, and electron microscopy demonstrates effacement of podocyte foot processes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (accounting for about 80% of cases). It classically presents with sudden-onset edema, starting peri-orbitally (facial) and progressing to anasarca. The diagnosis is confirmed by three key pathological findings: massive proteinuria, a completely normal appearance on light microscopy (hence the name "minimal change"), and the pathognomonic effacement (flattening) of podocyte foot processes visible only on electron microscopy. FSGS (Option A) shows focal scarring on light microscopy and is more common in adults or steroid-resistant cases. Membranous glomerulonephritis (Option C) shows basement membrane thickening. PSGN (Option D) is a nephritic syndrome (hematuria/hypertension), not a pure nephrotic syndrome. MCD is highly responsive to steroid therapy, which is the standard of care. Therefore, the electron microscopy findings provide the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (accounting for about 80% of cases). It classically presents with sudden-onset edema, starting peri-orbitally (facial) and progressing to anasarca.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the phase marked C to D in the given nerve action potential?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. K+ efflux

The phase C to D in the given nerve action potential is caused by K+ efflux as a result of the opening of the  K+ channels, resulting in repolarization.

The sequence of events occurring during an action potential is shown below

• Point A represents the resting state where both channels are closed.
• Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus resulting in Na+ influx (option A). The initiation of action potential occurs only after a certain potential is reached, which is called the threshold potential represented by point B.
• After this, the sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs to reach point C.
• At point C, Na+ channels close and K+ channels open, causing repolarization due to K+ efflux.
• Point D represents continued depolarization due to K+ efflux.
• At point E, Na+ channels are reset and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus. During this phase, the K+ channels remain open and slowly return to the closed state, causing after-hyperpolarization. As a stronger stimulus is required to reach the threshold potential, the excitability of nerve fibre is reduced at point E.
• As both channels close, the membrane returns to resting membrane potential back to point A.

Point B-D is a part of the refractory period. During this period, the application of even a stronger stimulus will not elicit an action potential.

The refractory period is divided into an absolute refractory period and a relative refractory period. During the absolute refractory period, the nerve will not be excited no matter how strong a stimulus is given. However, during the relative refractory period, stronger than normal stimuli can cause excitation.
questions.learning: K+ efflux — The phase C to D in the given nerve action potential is caused by K+ efflux as a result of the opening of the K+ channels, resulting in repolarization.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding Hirschsprung disease are true except:
options: Failure of migration of ganglion cells.
Colonic segment proximal to the affected area is constricted.
Failure of passage of meconium in the postnatal period.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colonic segment proximal to the affected area is constricted.

Hirschsprung disease is caused by failure of neural crest cell migration, leading to absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel (aganglionosis). This results in loss of coordinated peristalsis and functional obstruction.

Key concepts:

• The affected distal segment is spastic and constricted due to aganglionosis
• The proximal segment becomes dilated due to accumulation of intestinal contents (megacolon)
• Newborns typically present with failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours
• There is absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex
questions.learning: Colonic segment proximal to the affected area is constricted. Hirschsprung disease is caused by failure of neural crest cell migration, leading to absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel (aganglionosis).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy presents with right-sided nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis for the past 6 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. JNA

A teenage boy with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis is classic for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA).

·         Occurs in adolescent males

·         Highly vascular benign tumor arising from nasopharynx (sphenopalatine foramen area)

·         Presents with:

o    Recurrent epistaxis

o    Progressive unilateral nasal obstruction

Pathophysiology:

·         Tumor is fibrovascular → prone to profuse bleeding

·         Locally aggressive → can extend to pterygopalatine fossa, orbit, intracranial space

Biopsy is contraindicated due to risk of severe bleeding

Why other options are incorrect:

·         Allergic rhinitis: Bilateral symptoms, no epistaxis

·         Coagulation disorder: Generalized bleeding, not localized obstruction

·         Antrochoanal polyp: Nasal obstruction but no recurrent epistaxis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 36-year-old man presents with persistent dull pain in the upper abdomen. He gives a history of a severe episode of abdominal pain five weeks ago following heavy alcohol consumption. On examination, he is jaundiced and has a firm, palpable mass in the epigastric region. A CT scan reveals a well-circumscribed, fluid-filled lesion near the pancreas. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a firm epigastric mass developing four to six weeks "after an episode of acute pancreatitis" (heavy drinking event) is the classic presentation for a "Pancreatic Pseudocyst". A pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic fluid walled off by granulation and fibrous tissue rather than a true epithelial lining. The dull pain and jaundice result from the cyst compressing adjacent structures like the bile duct. Choledochal cysts (Option B) are congenital dilations of the bile duct and would usually present earlier in life. Gastric duplication cysts (Option C) and mesenteric cysts (Option D) are much rarer and would not be temporally related to a clear episode of pancreatitis. Most pseudocysts resolve with conservative management. However, if they are large, symptomatic, or infected, they may require drainage (endoscopic or surgical cystogastrostomy)
questions.learning: The clinical history of a firm epigastric mass developing four to six weeks "after an episode of acute pancreatitis" (heavy drinking event) is the classic presentation for a "Pancreatic Pseudocyst".

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During neurological examination, the clinician observes concentric rings with multiple colors around the periphery of the patient’s iris. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of "concentric rings" around the outer edge of the iris in a 30-year-old woman with an unsteady gait and labile moods is diagnostic of Kayser-Fleischer (K-F) rings. These rings are golden-brown or greenish deposits of copper in the Descemet membrane of the cornea, which occur in Wilson's disease—a disorder of impaired biliary copper excretion. The patient's neurological symptoms result from copper accumulation in the basal ganglia. Neurofibromatosis 1 (Option C) is associated with Lisch nodules, which are small, raised pigment spots on the iris. Neurofibromatosis 2 (Option A) and cataracts (Option D) do not produce these specific corneal rings. The K-F ring is a pathognomonic clinical finding that requires confirmation via slit-lamp examination. Early diagnosis of Wilson's disease is critical as it is treatable with copper-chelating agents. Therefore, the combination of specific ocular and neurological signs confirms the diagnosis
questions.learning: The presence of "concentric rings" around the outer edge of the iris in a 30-year-old woman with an unsteady gait and labile moods is diagnostic of Kayser-Fleischer (K-F) rings.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient undergoes endoscopic evaluation for recurrent abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits. Which anatomical structure is indicated by the arrow in the provided image?
questions.explanation: The given histological image represents a section of the duodenum, which can be identified by the presence of finger-like villi in the mucosa and prominent glandular structures in the submucosa. The arrow is pointing to clusters of mucous-secreting glands located beneath the mucosal layer. These are Brunner’s glands, a distinctive feature of the duodenum. Brunner’s glands secrete an alkaline mucus rich in bicarbonate ions, which plays a crucial role in neutralizing the acidic chyme entering from the stomach. This protective mechanism helps prevent damage to the intestinal lining and provides an optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (B) Interstitial cells of Cajal: These are microscopic pacemaker cells and are not visible as large glandular clusters (C) Crypts of Lieberkühn: Present in the mucosa, not in the submucosa (D) Peyer’s patches: Lymphoid aggregates found in the ileum, not in the duodenum
questions.learning: The given histological image represents a section of the duodenum, which can be identified by the presence of finger-like villi in the mucosa and prominent glandular structures in the submucosa.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the image of the anal region showing a painful abscess commonly resulting from obstruction of an anal gland, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided image and clinical description identify a perianal abscess (Option C). This is the most common type of anorectal abscess, occurring when an anal crypt gland becomes blocked and subsequently infected. It presents as a very painful, red, and swollen lump immediately adjacent to the anal verge. Hemorrhoids (Option A) are swollen vascular cushions; while they can be painful if thrombosed, they do not present as an acute fluctuant abscess. A pelvirectal abscess (Option B) is deeper and more severe, often presenting with systemic symptoms and high-seated rectal pain rather than a visible external lump. A pilonidal sinus (Option D) occurs in the natal cleft between the buttocks, further away from the anus. The primary treatment for a perianal abscess is immediate incision and drainage. Over 50% of these cases may eventually develop a fistula-in-ano. Therefore, the visual evidence of a localized abscess confirms the diagnosis
questions.learning: The provided image and clinical description identify a perianal abscess (Option C). This is the most common type of anorectal abscess, occurring when an anal crypt gland becomes blocked and subsequently infected.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presented with a white pupillary reflex for which enucleation was done. The histopathological examination of the specimen showed Flexner Winterstein rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

The most likely diagnosis with a histopathological finding of Flexner Winterstein rosettes in a 7-year-old child with a whitish pupillary reflex is retinoblastoma. Flexner Winterstein rosettes refer to an arrangement of columnar cells around a central lumen, which is highly characteristic of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of immature retinal neural cells and is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14. It is a tumour of a group called small round blue cell tumours because the immature retinal neural cells are seen as small round cells with large nuclei.

White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Image showing leukocoria of left eye

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

The histopathological image of retinoblastoma is shown below.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of Vincristine, Carboplatin, Etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when

• the tumor involves more than half of the retina
• the optic nerve is involved
• glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

In the stage of extraocular extension, the globe bursts through the sclera, usually near the limbus or near the optic disc. This is followed by rapid fungation and involvement of extraocular tissues results in marked proptosis. Distant metastasis occurs through the lymphatic spread and the direct extension by continuity to the optic nerve and brain.

Other options:

Option B - Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Patients usually present with headaches, ataxia, and signs of brainstem involvement.

Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin.

Option C - Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. The child usually presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. There are 4 subtypes - embryonal, alveolar, botyroid, and pleomorphic. Cells show light microscopic features of striated muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin.

Option D - Astrocytoma of the retina and optic nerve head is rare. It is usually asymptomatic and is most frequently seen in tuberous sclerosis. Fundus examination reveals a yellowish or white plaque, nodule, or mulberry-like lesion. These lesions are semitransparent peripherally and calcified centrally.

Image showing calcified astrocytoma:
questions.learning: Retinoblastoma — The most likely diagnosis with a histopathological finding of Flexner Winterstein rosettes in a 7-year-old child with a whitish pupillary reflex is retinoblastoma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following incisions is most appropriate when ligating the anterior ethmoidal artery to control anterior epistaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lynch-Howarth incision

The anterior ethmoidal artery is a key arterial supply to the anterior nasal septum and lateral wall. When severe anterior epistaxis is uncontrolled by packing or cautery, surgical ligation may be required.

Best surgical approach: Lynch–Howarth incision

• Medial orbital incision along the anterior lacrimal crest
• Provides access to anterior ethmoidal artery at frontoethmoidal suture line
• Used for ligation/cauterization to control refractory epistaxis

Why other options are incorrect

B. Sublabial incision: used for maxillary sinus/Caldwell-Luc

C. Gullwing incision: eyelid reconstructive procedures

D. Weber-Ferguson incision: maxillary tumor access

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 62-year-old patient with a history of diabetes and hypertension came with post-menopausal bleeding. Which of the following you will do to evaluate the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endometrial sampling

Endometrial sampling is done to evaluate a patient presenting with postmenopausal bleeding.

Postmenopausal bleeding is defined as any bleeding from the genital tract after 12 months of menopause in a woman not on hormone replacement. Any vaginal bleeding occurring after 6 months of amenorrhea in a menopausal woman should also be considered as postmenopausal bleeding and investigated. All postmenopausal women with unexpected uterine bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial malignancy since age is a significant risk factor for this.

Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is a better first-line investigation. Since TVS is not included in the options, endometrial sampling is the next best answer.

Endometrial sampling is indicated if:

• The endometrial thickness is >4 mm
• The endometrium shows diffuse or focal increased echogenicity (heterogeneity)
• The endometrium is not adequately visualized on transvaginal sonography
• The woman has persistent bleeding, as it can be a sign of endometrial cancer even when the endometrial thickness is less than 4mm.

The image below gives a summary of the evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding, as per the FOGSI guidelines.

Other options:

Option A: Pap smear should be offered to all women above the age of 21 years who are sexually active for at least 3 years. Colposcopic examination and selective biopsy are considered in patients with abnormal Pap smears.

Option B: Visual inspection with iodine is done where the facilities for Pap screening do not exist. This involves painting the cervix with Lugol's iodine. It is used to detect any abnormal cytology in the cervix and vagina, such as in cases of carcinoma cervix.

The normal vaginal and cervical epithelium contains glycogen, therefore stains mahogany brown on being painted with Lugol's iodine. The abnormal cells remain unstained. These areas need to be biopsied and sent for histopathological examination.

Option C: The colposcopic study is challenging in postmenopausal women because of narrow vaginas, senile vaginitis, indrawn and poorly visible squamocolumnar junction, and atrophic cervix.
questions.learning: Endometrial sampling Endometrial sampling is done to evaluate a patient presenting with postmenopausal bleeding. Postmenopausal bleeding is defined as any bleeding from the genital tract after 12 months of menopause in a woman not on hormone replacement.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A point-of-care diagnostic test with a sensitivity of 98% shows a negative test result in a patient. What does this imply?
options: The patient would need another point-of-care diagnostic test for the same clinical condition.
Patient is less likely to have the disease.
Patient has been wrongly ruled out due to false negativity.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patient is less likely to have the disease.

A negative result in a diagnostic test with a sensitivity of 98% implies that the patient is less likely to have the disease.

Sensitivity is the proportion of all people with the disease who test positive. It is the probability of the test being positive when the disease is present. The sensitivity of a test is given by those who have the disease and test positive (true positives) out of the total diseased population.

Other statements:

Option A: The patient would not need another point-of-care diagnostic test for the same clinical condition as the sensitivity of the diagnostic test is 98%.

Option B: Prevalence refers to the number of old and new cases at a given point in time or over a period of time in a given population. It cannot be derived from the given data.

Option D: The higher the sensitivity of a diagnostic test, the lower will be the number of false negatives. Since the test has a 98% sensitivity, the patient most likely does not have the disease.
questions.learning: Patient is less likely to have the disease. A negative result in a diagnostic test with a sensitivity of 98% implies that the patient is less likely to have the disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An adolescent girl complaints of dropping objects from hands precipitated during morning hours and exams. There is no history of loss of consciousness. One of her cousins has been diagnosed with epilepsy. EEG was suggestive of epileptic spikes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

The given clinical scenario describes an adolescent girl with myoclonic jerks (a history of dropping objects) with preserved consciousness. This, along with abnormal EEG findings strongly suggests juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome) is the most common generalized epilepsy in young adults. It starts in early adolescence with one or more of the following features: bilateral myoclonic jerks in the morning, causing patients to drop things, generalized tonic-clonic or clonic-tonic-clonic seizures upon awakening, and juvenile absence seizure.

Consciousness is usually preserved. Precipitating factors include sleep deprivation, alcohol, and photic stimulation. EEG shows 4 to 5Hz polyspike and slow wave discharges. A family history of epilepsy is often present.

The treatment options for JME include sodium valproate, levetiracetam, and topiramate. Benzodiazepine, lamotrigine, perampanel, phenobarbital, primidone, and zonisamide can be considered as add-on drugs. Complete remission is uncommon and has a high risk of seizure recurrence, hence antiepileptics are continued lifelong in a majority of the patients.

Other options:

Option B: Atypical absence seizures have been associated with myoclonic components and head drop. They are precipitated by drowsiness and EEG shows 1 to 2 Hz spike and slow wave discharges.

Option D: In benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, the child typically wakes at night due to a focal seizure with preserved awareness. Buccal and throat tingling and tonic or clonic contractions on one side of the face are seen, with drooling and preserved consciousness. EEG shows typical wide-based centrotemporal spikes.
questions.learning: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy — The given clinical scenario describes an adolescent girl with myoclonic jerks (a history of dropping objects) with preserved consciousness.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32 year old female presents with grey-white vaginal discharge and on gram stain of the discharge, clue cells are seen. Clue cells are
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epithelial cells covered by bacteria

Clue cells are epithelial cells with a fuzzy border or granular cytoplasm caused by small gram-negative bacilli adhering on their surface is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.

Bacterial vaginosis is a polymicrobial infection caused by Mobiluncus curtisii, Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma hominis, and Haemophilus vaginalis. It has a malodorous (fishy smell) vaginal discharge with minimal vulval irritation.

Amsel's Criteria is helpful in diagnosing bacterial vaginosis when 3 of the following 4 are present

• Thin, white homogenous vaginal discharge
• A pH of vaginal fluid >4.5
• Fishy odor of discharge accentuated by adding 10% KOH-Whiff test
• Presence of Clue cells on microscopy.

Treatment is oral metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days. Alternatively, Ampicillin 500 mg or cephalosporin 500 mg bid for 7 days is also effective.
questions.learning: Epithelial cells covered by bacteria Clue cells are epithelial cells with a fuzzy border or granular cytoplasm caused by small gram-negative bacilli adhering on their surface is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a neonate who presents with mild, intermittent upper abdominal pain, a scaphoid abdomen, reduced breath sounds bilaterally, and the findings shown on the provided X-ray?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a neonate with a "scaphoid abdomen" (hollowed out) and decreased breath sounds is the classic physical finding for a Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH). The scaphoid appearance occurs because the abdominal organs have migrated into the thoracic cavity through a defect in the diaphragm. The most common type is the Bochdalek hernia (Option A), which occurs posterolaterally, usually on the left side. The provided X-ray (Option R) displays the characteristic "gaseous bowel loops" filling the hemithorax and displacing the mediastinum to the opposite side. Pneumonia (Option B) would show solid infiltrates without bowel loops. Gastric volvulus (Option C) involves twisting of the stomach within the abdomen. Eventration (Option D) involves a weak, elevated diaphragm but the abdominal organs remain under the diaphragmatic thin sheet. CDH is a life-threatening emergency causing pulmonary hypoplasia. Immediate management involves intubation and gastric decompression before surgical repair
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a neonate with a "scaphoid abdomen" (hollowed out) and decreased breath sounds is the classic physical finding for a Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 39-year- old man who repeatedly washes his hands 15–20 times daily due to persistent fears of contamination, resulting in significant impairment in his occupational functioning?
questions.explanation: The patient’s behavior fulfills the core diagnostic criteria for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) (Option B). OCD is characterized by the presence of obsessions (intrusive, persistent thoughts of contamination) and compulsions (repetitive behaviors like excessive hand washing) aimed at reducing the distress caused by the obsessions. These symptoms are time-consuming and lead to significant impairment in social or occupational functioning. Bipolar disorder (Option A) involves cycles of depression and mania, while Mania (Option D) is characterized by elevated mood and racing thoughts, not contamination obsessions. Schizophrenia (Option C) involves hallucinations and delusions. Because the patient's symptoms are specifically centered on a contamination ritual that he feels compelled to perform to neutralize his anxiety, OCD is the definitive psychiatric diagnosis. Management typically involves selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and cognitive-behavioral therapy

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a town of 20,000 populations, total 456 births were there in a year out of which 56 were dead born. The total death were 247 out of which 56 deaths were within 28 days of life and another 34 had dies after 28 days and before completing the first birthday. Calculate the infant mortality rate of the area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 225

The infant mortality rate is 225 per 1000 live births.

Infant mortality rate (IMR) is defined as the ratio of infant deaths registered in a given year to the total number of live births in the same year. IMR is usually expressed as a rate per 1000 live births. Infants include those under the age of 1 year.

Calculation:

• IMR = (Number of deaths of children under 1 year of age in a year x 1000)/(Number of live births in the same year).
• In the given question, Out of total 456 births, 56 were dead born. Therefore, the number of live births= 456-56 = 400.
• In the same year, it is given that the number of deaths before 28 days is 56, and the number of deaths after 28 days but before 1 year. Therefore, the total number of deaths of children under the age of 1 year is 56 + 34 = 90
• IMR = (90x1000)/400 = 900/4 = 225
• Hence, the IMR is 225 per 1000 live births.
questions.learning: 225 The infant mortality rate is 225 per 1000 live births. Infant mortality rate (IMR) is defined as the ratio of infant deaths registered in a given year to the total number of live births in the same year.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient who wears contact lenses presents with two months of eye watering, redness, and a foreign body sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a contact lens wearer with chronic discomfort and foreign body sensation is highly suggestive of an immune response to the lens material or deposits. The pathognomonic visual finding shown in the image—large, flattened papillae on the superior tarsal conjunctiva, often described as a "cobblestone" appearance—is diagnostic of Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC). GPC is effectively a mechanical and allergic reaction. Acute trachoma (Option A) presents with follicles and scarring, often linked to Chlamydia infection in endemic areas. Follicular conjunctivitis (Option B) shows small, translucent lumps (follicles) rather than these large papillae. Spring catarrh (Option D), or Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis, also shows cobblestone papillae but is typically seen in young boys without a contact lens history. Because the patient specifically has a contact lens risk factor and classic papillary changes, GPC is the correct diagnosis. Management involves discontinuing lens wear and using topical antihistamines
questions.learning: The clinical history of a contact lens wearer with chronic discomfort and foreign body sensation is highly suggestive of an immune response to the lens material or deposits.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with head and neck cancer was told by his oncologist that needs radiotherapy at a total dose of 70 Gy over a 7 week period for his tumor. He was scheduled to receive a dose of 1.8-2Gy per fraction, once daily over 5 days a week, for 7 weeks. What is this type of radiotherapy called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regular Fractionated radiotherapy

Since the patient needs 70Gy in total for his tumour and his dose per fraction is at 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week, for 7 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

Radiotherapy:

The total dose of radiation needed for a tumour is usually given as fractions over the entire treatment period as it maximises the effects of the radiation on the malignant cells and minimises the damage on the healthy cells.

The reasons for this are due to :

1. Re-distribution: Cells are more resistant to damage in the late S2 phase while sensitive in the M and G2 phase. Only some tumour cells will be in the sensitive phase of the cell cycle when the radiation is given. Hence, giving another dose at a later time helps in killing the other cells who were in the resistant part of the cell cycle, thus increasing the success rate of the therapy.

2. Re-oxygenation: Hypoxic cells are less sensitive to the indirect effects of radiation. The tumour cells which are closer to oxygen sources are killed first and in the intervening time, the other relatively hypoxic cells can improve their oxygenation so that the next fraction of radiation is effective on them.

3. Repair: The ability to repair DNA is more for healthy cells than malignant cells and thus when a radiation dose has been received, the healthy cells repair their DNA faster than the malignant cells. The malignant cells whose DNA is not fully repaired are highly susceptible to the next dose of radiation.

Types of fractionation:

* In the case of Head and neck cancer, the conventional schedule of radiotherapy involves the delivery of 70 Gy in 1.8-2 Gy fractions(total around 35-36 fractions) over 7 weeks, treating 5 days per week.

* However, this dose can be delivered at 1.10-1.25 Gy/fraction for 56 fractions over the same time period of 7 weeks which is called hyperfractionation(Option B). This delivers a lower dose with more fractions and the efficacy improves as the healthy cells have more ability to repair themselves in the intervening time.

* Accelerated fractionation(Option C) is when the same 70 Gy, is given at around 1.6-1.8 Gy/fraction but it is delivered more than once daily, decreasing the total treatment time to around 6 weeks. These aim to decrease tumor proliferation which can lead to failure of the therapy.

Note:

* Shorter schedules remain useful for small-volume treatments: 50 Gy in 16 fractions over 3 weeks or 55 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks.

* Accelerated schedules although is easier to implement than hyperfractionation result in a lesser survival gain.

Option D: Brachytherapy is a method of treatment in which sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.

The following isotopes are used in brachytherapy:

* I-125 and Iridium-192 - are used in low-dose rate (LDR) brachytherapy.

* Cobalt-60 - is used for high-dose rate (HDR) brachytherapy.

Afterloading is the process of placing the radioactive material into the target region. This is either done manually by the oncologist, or by using remote afterloading devices.

Remote afterloading devices enable us to eliminate direct contact with radioactive sources while administration. It provides protection from radiation exposure to healthcare professionals by securing the radiation source in a shielded safe manner.
questions.learning: Regular Fractionated radiotherapy Since the patient needs 70Gy in total for his tumour and his dose per fraction is at 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week, for 7 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is brought by her mother with concerns about asymmetrical breast development. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reassure and reassess

Breast asymmetry is a common physiological finding during puberty. In adolescent girls with isolated asymmetrical breast development and no red-flag features (e.g., mass, pain, skin changes, nipple discharge, or lymphadenopathy), the appropriate management is reassurance and follow-up, as breast development usually becomes symmetrical over time.

Why not the other options?

• A. Biopsy of the larger breast: Not indicated in physiological pubertal breast asymmetry.
• B. Mammography: Not recommended in adolescents due to dense breast tissue and low likelihood of malignancy.
• D. Breast ultrasound: Reserved for a palpable breast mass or other suspicious clinical findings, not for isolated asymmetry.
