questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient collapses soon after delivery. There is profuse bleeding and features of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amniotic fluid embolism

The given clinical scenario with a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) points to amniotic fluid embolism as the most likely etiology.

Amniotic fluid embolism presents with a classic triad of hemodynamic and respiratory compromise, along with DIC. Usually, it presents during the late stages of labor or immediate postpartum. Gasping for air, seizures, and cardiorespiratory arrest are other features. Clinical features are variable.

Diagnostic criteria for amniotic fluid embolism include:

• Sudden onset cardiorespiratory arrest, or both hypotension and respiratory compromise
• Overt DIC
• Onset during labor or within 30 minutes of delivery of the placenta
• No fever ≥38°C

Since there are no specific diagnostic tests, a clinical diagnosis has to be made. Other causes for a similar presentation such as myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and anaphylactic shock needs to be ruled out.

Risk factors include rapid labor, meconium-stained liquor, and uterine tears. Post-term pregnancy, maternal age, and eclampsia are other predisposing conditions. The currently accepted mechanism is the entry of fetal material into the maternal circulation which leads to the activation of proinflammatory mediator systems. This results in pulmonary vasoconstriction and hypertension. The tissue factor present in fetal material also activates factor VII resulting in DIC.

The condition can be fatal and management includes cardiopulmonary resuscitation and advanced cardiac life support.

Other options:

Option B: Post-partum hemorrhage is the loss of ≥500mL of blood after the third stage of labor. Symptoms and signs of hypovolemia are commonly seen.

Option C: Peripartum cardiomyopathy presents with features of heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months of delivery. Probable causes include viral myocarditis, malnutrition, and hormonal interactions.

Option D: Rupture of the uterus is a disruption in the continuity of all the uterine layers anytime after 28 weeks of pregnancy. Clinical features depend on the specific cause and include abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fainting attacks, and rapid pulse rate.
questions.learning: Amniotic fluid embolism — The given clinical scenario with a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) points to amniotic fluid embolism as the most likely etiology.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true regarding memantine?

1. Its therapeutic effect is due to its action on NMDA.
2. It is reserved for moderate-to-severe diseases.
3. It is used as monotherapy and should not be used with other cholinesterase inhibitors.
4. It is given at a daily dose of 15–30 mg/day.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2

1 and 2 are true statements regarding memantine.

Memantine is a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist. It inhibits glutamate excitotoxicity. It delays the progression of dementia in Alzheimer's disease. Commonly, it is started in patients with moderate-to-severe disease.

It can be given both as monotherapy or can be given along with cholinesterase inhibitors. It can be started at a dose of 5 mg once daily and then progressively increased up to 10 mg twice daily for a minimum of 6 months.

It can cause dizziness and headache. Since it is excreted in the kidney, careful dose adjustments should be made in patients with renal failure.
questions.learning: 1, 2 1 and 2 are true statements regarding memantine. Memantine is a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All are correct statements about muscle tension curves, except:
options: Passive tension increases with muscle stretch
Active tension is highest at optimal length
Total tension equals sum of passive and active tension
Passive tension is highest at resting muscle length
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Passive tension is highest at resting muscle length

The muscle length–tension relationship describes how muscle force varies with sarcomere length.

• Active tension: Produced by actin–myosin cross-bridge formation.
• Maximum at optimal sarcomere length (ideal overlap of actin and myosin).
• Passive tension: Produced by elastic elements of muscle (titin, connective tissue).
• Increases progressively as the muscle is stretched beyond resting length.
• Total tension:
• Total tension = active tension + passive tension

Passive tension is not highest at resting length; it is minimal at resting length and increases with stretch.
questions.learning: Passive tension is highest at resting muscle length — The muscle length–tension relationship describes how muscle force varies with sarcomere length. • Active tension: Produced by actin–myosin cross-bridge formation. • Maximum at optimal sarcomere length…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Transport of iron into enterocytes is done by which of the following proteins:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Divalent metal transporter - 1

Transport of iron into enterocytes is done by divalent metal transporter-1 protein.

Iron absorption occurs in the duodenum. Iron in our gut exists in 2 forms, they are nonheme and heme iron.

Luminal nonheme iron is mostly in the Fe3+ (ferric) state and is reduced to Fe2+ (ferrous) iron by ferrireductases. Fe2+ iron is then transported across the apical membrane by divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1).

Given below is an image of iron absorption that shows divalent metal transporter-1 protein in intestinal mucosal cells.

Heme iron is moved across the apical membrane into the cytoplasm through heme transporters.

In the duodenal cells, Fe2+ iron can follow one of two pathways: transport to the blood or storage as mucosal iron. The nonstorage form of Fe2+ iron is transported from the cytoplasm into circulation by the protein ferroportin (Option B).

Once in circulation, Fe2+ is again oxidized back to Fe3+ iron by hephaestin and ceruloplasmin. The newly absorbed Fe3+ iron binds rapidly to transferrin (Option A), which delivers iron to red cell progenitors in the marrow.

Hepcidin (Option C), is a protein secreted from the liver that plays a major role in the regulation of iron absorption. When the body’s iron stores are adequate, it downregulates the expression of ferroportin and thereby decreases iron absorption.
questions.learning: Divalent metal transporter - 1 Transport of iron into enterocytes is done by divalent metal transporter-1 protein. Iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After parotidectomy patients complains of loss of sensation while shaving. Which nerve is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Great auricular nerve

After parotid surgery, the nerve involved in the loss of sensation while shaving is the great auricular nerve.

The great auricular nerve (GAN) originates from the second and third nerve roots of the cervical plexus (C2-C3). It supplies the skin over the lower pinna, pre-auricular region, and angle of the mandible (image below). The main trunk passes over the sternocleidomastoid and into the anterosuperior portion of the parotid glands and branches into the anterior and posterior GAN. The anterior branch of GAN is often injured during parotid surgery during the initial elevation of the skin flap.

When GAN is injured, it can cause reduced sensations in the earlobe, pre-auricular skin, and the angle of the mandible that can interfere with habits such as shaving, wearing earrings, etc.

Other options:

Option A: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve (V3 of trigeminal) supplies the posterior part of the temple, tragus, and adjoining auricle. It does not supply the area where a person is likely to shave. However, the injury to the auriculotemporal nerve resulting in aberrant regeneration would result in Frey's Syndrome (gustatory sweating).

Option C: Though the facial nerve is the most common nerve affected during parotidectomy, any damage would result in facial paralysis and not loss of sensation of the face.

Option D: The mandibular nerve is a branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) that supplies the skin over the mandible, lower lip, and cheek. However, they are not injured during parotidectomy.
questions.learning: Great auricular nerve After parotid surgery, the nerve involved in the loss of sensation while shaving is the great auricular nerve. The great auricular nerve (GAN) originates from the second and third nerve roots of the cervical plexus (C2-C3).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Congenital lactic acidosis is due to the defect of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pyruvate dehydrogenase

Congenital lactic acidosis commonly results from a deficiency of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex, which converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle in mitochondria.

When PDH is defective, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and is instead converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, leading to accumulation of lactic acid and metabolic acidosis. Patients often present with neurological deficits, developmental delay, hypotonia, and persistent lactic acidosis.

Thus, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency impairs aerobic glucose metabolism and causes congenital lactic acidosis.

Why not others:

• Transketolase: Enzyme of the HMP shunt (pentose phosphate pathway), not involved in pyruvate metabolism.
• Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase: Deficiency causes Maple syrup urine disease, not lactic acidosis.
• Isocitrate dehydrogenase: TCA cycle enzyme; defects are mainly associated with certain tumors, not congenital lactic acidosis.
questions.learning: Pyruvate dehydrogenase Congenital lactic acidosis commonly results from a deficiency of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex, which converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle in mitochondria.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient presented with cough, fatiguability, and weight loss. He was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) on bronchoscopy. The resected specimen had a hilar lymph node that was 1cm in size and showed a black pigment. What is the black pigment likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anthracotic pigment

The black-colored pigment in the hilar lymph node of the resected bronchoscopic specimen is likely to be an anthracotic pigment.

The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles. The inhaled carbon particles are engulfed by the lung macrophages and then transported to the hilar lymph nodes. This accumulates and causes the blackening of the lung tissues or anthracosis.

It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution with carbon particles, such as coal mines. It is also the most common exogenous pigment found in the human body as a result of air pollution in urban areas. The aggregates of the carbon dust may induce fibroblastic reaction or emphysema that may lead to a condition called coal worker's pneumoconiosis.

The following image shows anthracosis with deposition of black carbon particles, within the cytoplasm of macrophages.

Option B: Melanin is brown-black in color which occurs as a result of oxidation of tyrosine in melanocytes, as shown in the following histopathology of a lymph node.

Option C: Lipochrome or lipofuscin (brown lipid) is seen as a yellow-brown pigment in histopathological sections of the liver and heart of normal aging patients, patients with severe malnutrition, and cancer cachexia. It is derived through lipid peroxidation and indicates free radical injury and lipid peroxidation. The following image shows a cardiac myocyte with fine yellow-brown lipofuscin granules in the perinuclear region.

Option D: Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment seen in conditions associated with iron overload such as hemochromatosis. The following image shows extensive intra-alveolar hemosiderin deposition following pulmonary hemorrhage.
questions.learning: Anthracotic pigment — The black-colored pigment in the hilar lymph node of the resected bronchoscopic specimen is likely to be an anthracotic pigment. The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: During the examination of a patient with a suspected right forearm fracture, the patient is asked to make a fist. A characteristic change in finger alignment is observed. What is the name of this clinical sign?
questions.explanation: The image shows the index finger remaining extended while the other fingers are flexed into a fist. This is the classic Pointing Index Sign, also called the "Index finger sign" seen in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) palsy — a branch of the median nerve. AIN injury causes paralysis of FDP to index finger and FPL, so when making a fist, the index finger cannot flex at the DIP joint and remains pointing straight out. This is commonly associated with supracondylar fractures or forearm fractures compressing the AIN. Why Other Options are Wrong: (A) Froment's Sign : Tests ulnar nerve integrity; patient cannot pinch paper between thumb and index finger without flexing the thumb IP joint (FPL compensation). No index pointing involved. (C) Benediction Sign : Also a median nerve palsy sign but seen at rest, where index and middle fingers remain extended due to FDS/FDP weakness. Different nerve level injury. (D) Policeman Tip Deformity : Associated with Erb's palsy (C5-C6 brachial plexus injury), showing shoulder adduction, internal rotation, and elbow extension : an entirely different deformity
questions.learning: The image shows the index finger remaining extended while the other fingers are flexed into a fist. This is the classic Pointing Index Sign, also called the "Index finger sign" seen in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) palsy — a branch of the median nerve.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Poisoning with which of the following drugs causes hypothermia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chlorpromazine

Hypothermia is a characteristic feature of poisoning with phenothiazines (e.g., chlorpromazine) due to depression of the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center, along with peripheral vasodilation. Although alcohol intoxication can also cause hypothermia, chlorpromazine is the classic drug tested in toxicology MCQs.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Digoxin: Poisoning typically presents with cardiac arrhythmias, nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances (yellow vision), and hyperkalemia, not hypothermia.
• C. Iron: Iron poisoning causes gastrointestinal bleeding, metabolic acidosis, shock, and hepatic failure, not hypothermia.
• D. Alcohol: Alcohol can cause hypothermia by causing vasodilation and CNS depression, but chlorpromazine is the classical drug associated with hypothermia in poisoning questions.
questions.learning: Chlorpromazine Hypothermia is a characteristic feature of poisoning with phenothiazines (e.g., chlorpromazine) due to depression of the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center, along with peripheral vasodilation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arises from 6th pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ductus arteriosus

Ductus arteriosus arises from the 6th pharngeal arch.

Pharyngeal arches appear in the 4th or 5th week of development and contribute to the formation of the head and neck region. They are formed as a series of 6 thickenings in the cranial most part of the foregut (the future pharynx). They are craniocaudally numbered from I to VI. The 5th pharyngeal arch disappears, so only 5 arches remain.

* The first pharyngeal arch is also known as the mandibular arch.

* The second pharyngeal arch is also known as the hyoid arch.

* The 3rd, 4th, and 6th pharyngeal arches have no special names.

Other options:

Medial pterygoids,Lateral pterygoids,Tensor veli palatini- all arise from first pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with a history of vomiting within 3 hours of consumption of food at a party. Which of the following organism is most likely to cause these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Staphylococcus aureus

Vomiting 2 hours after the consumption of food is likely food poisoning by Staphylococcus aureus.

Staphylococcus aureus can grow in carbohydrate and protein food sources, producing enterotoxins. There are 15 types, all of which are superantigens. They are preformed toxins that are relatively heat stable. They stimulate the vagus nerve,  vomiting centre of the brain and intestinal peristaltic activity. Type A enterotoxin is responsible for most cases of food poisoning.

The common sources of infection are the foods that are not cooked after handling. These include sliced meats, puddings, pastries, and sandwiches. Ingestion of such contaminated food causes food poisoning within 30 minutes to 6 hours after consumption. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and diarrhoea.
questions.learning: Staphylococcus aureus Vomiting 2 hours after the consumption of food is likely food poisoning by Staphylococcus aureus. Staphylococcus aureus can grow in carbohydrate and protein food sources, producing enterotoxins.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding the effect of Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase deficiency?

1. Decrease in reduced glutathione
2. Decreased NADPH
3. Decreased lipid peroxidation
4. Decreased RBC membrane damage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 & 2 are correct.

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathione and decreased NADPH.

G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt. Defective enzyme function reduced the ability of red cells to protect themselves against oxidative injuries, thereby increasing lipid peroxidation and lead to hemolysis.

• G6PD reduces NADP to NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate.
• This NADPH then provides reducing equivalents needed for conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione.
• This reduced glutathione acts as a cofactor in reactions that neutralize compounds such as H2O2, thereby protecting against oxidant injury.
• Exposure of G6PD deficient red cells to oxidative stress leads to crosslinking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains, which then becomes denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates called ‘Heinz bodies’, thereby producing membrane damage.
• When these inclusion bearing RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these Heinz bodies.
• The resultant cells are called ‘Bite cells’.

Clinical features:

• Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
• Hemolytic anaemia
• Hemoglobinemia
• Hemoglobinuria

The episode of hemolysis is self-limiting, since only the older RBCs are at risk for lysis, leaving the G6PD-replete younger RBCs in circulation. The recovery phase is heralded by reticulocytosis.
questions.learning: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathione and decreased NADPH. G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, dizziness on standing, and hyperpigmentation of the skin. Blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Laboratory tests show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. She is diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency. Which of the following findings is not expected in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased protein breakdown

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) results from deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. Aldosterone deficiency causes renal sodium loss, volume depletion, hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, while increased ACTH production leads to hyperpigmentation.

Why is D correct?

• Increased protein breakdown is a feature of cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome), not cortisol deficiency.
• In Addison disease, the absence of cortisol reduces its normal catabolic effects on protein metabolism.

Why not the other options?

• A. Low blood pressure – expected due to volume depletion and reduced vascular responsiveness.
• B. Decreased extracellular fluid volume – occurs because of aldosterone deficiency and sodium loss.
• C. Decreased sodium–potassium ratio – results from hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 4-year-old male child developed sore throat and difficulty in swallowing and mild fever. On examination, the clinical picture shown below is seen. Which of the following sentences is false regarding the vaccine that could have prevented this condition?
options: Its administered on the anterolateral aspect of thigh
A prior adverse reaction with temperature above 37 degrees is a contraindication
Cellular pertussis component in the vaccine is not recommended after 7-years of age
The diphtheria toxoid dose in adults is much lesser than the pediatric dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A prior adverse reaction with temperature above 37 degrees is a contraindication

The image shows a dirty white pseudomembrane classic of diphtheria. A prior adverse reaction with a temperature above 37 is not a contraindication.

Precautionary measures are taken when the temperature is above 40 degrees, but it is not considered a contraindication for subsequent doses of DPwT.

Anaphylaxis is a contraindication for subsequent vaccination with diphtheria, pertussis, or tetanus vaccine. Encephalopathy following vaccination is a contraindication for pertussis vaccine. DT is given for successive doses.

Events such as inconsolable cry, fever more than 40.5°C, seizures with or without fever are considered as precautions, and not contraindications for DTwP.

The cellular component of pertussis is not recommended after 7 years.

• Unvaccinated child 5-7 years: Give DPT 1, 2 and 3 at 1-month intervals. Administer booster dose of DPT at a minimum of 6 months
after administering DPT-3 up to the age of 7 years.
• Unvaccinated child above 7 years: Administer Tdap (Tetanus and diphtheria toxoids and acellular pertussis) at 0, and Td (Tetanus, Diphtheria vaccine) at 1 and 6 months, respectively.

The adult dose of diphtheria toxoid is almost 12 times lesser in comparison with the pediatric dosage.

Note: IAP guidelines state that "temperature more than >40.5°C is a precaution and not contraindication". Park's 27th Ed states that "temperature above 40°C is a contraindication to DPT". This topic is controversial, however, IAP guidelines are commonly followed by practitioners.
questions.learning: A prior adverse reaction with temperature above 37 degrees is a contraindication The image shows a dirty white pseudomembrane classic of diphtheria. A prior adverse reaction with a temperature above 37 is not a contraindication.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not reversed with the administration of atropine?
options: Muscle weakness due to neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and it effectively counteracts parasympathetic overstimulation at smooth muscle, cardiac tissue, and exocrine glands. Therefore, it is useful in conditions such as bradycardia (Option A), excessive salivation (Option C), and bronchoconstriction (Option D), which are mediated by M₂ and M₃ muscarinic receptors. However, muscle weakness caused by neuromuscular blocking agents is mediated by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Nm) located at the neuromuscular junction. Atropine has no action on nicotinic receptors, and thus cannot reverse skeletal muscle paralysis or weakness. Reversal of neuromuscular blockade requires an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as neostigmine, which increases acetylcholine levels at the neuromuscular junction to competitively overcome the blockade. Atropine is administered concurrently with neostigmine only to prevent muscarinic side effects (such as bradycardia, bronchospasm, and salivation) caused by increased acetylcholine. Therefore, atropine cannot directly improve skeletal muscle strength, as it does not act on the receptors responsible for neuromuscular transmission
questions.learning: Atropine is a competitive antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and it effectively counteracts parasympathetic overstimulation at smooth muscle, cardiac tissue, and exocrine glands.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How is cerebral perfusion pressure calculated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mean arterial pressure - intracranial pressure

Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is calculated as mean arterial pressure (MAP) - intracranial pressure (ICP).

However, ICP values are not readily available. In this case, CPP may be calculated as MAP - central venous pressure (CVP), and if CVP > ICP.

The brain depends on continuous perfusion for oxygen and glucose delivery, thus its survival. The blood flow to the brain is normally about 55 mL per 100 g of brain tissue. If the cerebral flow reduces to less than 20 mL per minute, the brain undergoes ischemia.

Blood flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP). Normally the CPP is 75-105 mmHg, MAP is 90-110 mmHg and ICP is 5-15 mmHg.

According to Monro Kellie doctrine, the cranium is a rigid box containing a nearly incompressible brain. In cases of head trauma, there is an expansion of cranial content, in the form of hematomas and brain swelling. This increase in cranial pressure is accommodated initially by the exclusion of fluid components, venous blood, and cerebrospinal fluid. Further increase in the cranial pressure leads to an uncontrolled rise in ICP resulting in a compromise in cerebral perfusion and eventually cerebral herniation.

Acute rise in ICP causes Cushing reflex, a triad of widened pulse pressure (increasing systolic, decreasing diastolic) bradycardia, and irregular respirations.

Thus, in cases of head injury with intracranial bleeding, cranial decompression is performed to avoid further complications due to the raised ICP.
questions.learning: Mean arterial pressure - intracranial pressure Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is calculated as mean arterial pressure (MAP) - intracranial pressure (ICP).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents to you with anemia early in her pregnancy. She is 7 weeks pregnant as seen on ultrasound. Her hemoglobin level is 9 g/dL. When should the iron supplements be started for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8 to 10 weeks

The iron supplements for the 7-week pregnant mother presenting with anemia should be started at 8 to 10 weeks.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention defined anemia in pregnant women using a cut-off value. The pregnant mother is said to be anemic when the level of hemoglobin is less than 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters and less than 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester.

Anemia in the first trimester is treated by oral iron therapy. According to the Anemia Mukt Bharat program, pregnant women with mild and moderate anemia are treated with two iron and folic acid tablets. Each tablet contains 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid. These tablets are taken daily and are supplied by the healthcare worker. Hence, in this mother iron supplementation should be started by 8-10 weeks.

Drawbacks of oral therapy are intolerance presenting as epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, or diarrhea, and unpredictable absorption rate. The improvement in hemoglobin levels is generally evident within 3 weeks of oral iron therapy. The hemoglobin concentration is expected to rise at about 0.7 gm/100 mL/week.

Contraindications to oral therapy are intolerance, and severe anemia in advanced pregnancy. The best time to start corrective iron therapy in pregnancy depends on the individual patient's needs and the presence of anemia. For most pregnant women without anemia, it is recommended to start iron supplementation between 12-16 weeks of gestation to meet the increased iron demands during pregnancy.

If a pregnant woman is found to be anemic, the iron supplementation should be started as soon as the anemia is diagnosed, regardless of the gestational age. Early diagnosis and treatment of anemia are crucial to reduce the risk of complications for both the mother and the baby.

In the case of severe anemia or intolerance to oral iron supplements, intravenous iron therapy may be considered, depending on the clinical situation and the patient's response to oral therapy.
questions.learning: 8 to 10 weeks The iron supplements for the 7-week pregnant mother presenting with anemia should be started at 8 to 10 weeks. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention defined anemia in pregnant women using a cut-off value.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Match the structures shown in the image:
options: A- Apocrine sweat gland; B- Eccrine sweat gland; C- Sebaceous gland; D- Erector pili muscle
A- Eccrine sweat gland; B- Apocrine sweat gland; C- Sebaceous gland; D- Erector pili muscle
A- Sebaceous gland; B- Apocrine sweat gland; C- Eccrine sweat gland; D- Erector pili muscle
A- Eccrine sweat gland; B- Sebaceous gland; C- Apocrine sweat gland; D- Erector pili muscle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A- Eccrine sweat gland; B- Apocrine sweat gland; C- Sebaceous gland; D- Erector pili muscle

The correctly matched option (B)- A- Eccrine sweat gland; B- Apocrine sweat gland; C- Sebaceous gland; D- Erector pili muscle.

Human skin contains various structures, including sweat and sebaceous glands. Eccrine sweat glands, which are crucial for temperature regulation, are distributed across most of the body and are identified early in fetal development. These glands have a coiled secretory portion in the lower dermis and a duct that opens directly onto the skin surface. They are most concentrated on the palms, soles, and forehead.

Apocrine sweat glands, found in areas like the axillae, genital, and mammary regions, differ from eccrine glands in that they release secretion via decapitation, where parts of the cell pinch off. They are connected to hair follicles and have a larger lumen compared to eccrine glands. Their primary function remains unclear, and they have a lower secretory output.

Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, providing skin lubrication and waterproofing. These glands are associated with hair follicles and are absent in non-hairy skin.

The erector pili muscle, a smooth muscle bundle, extends from the dermis to the follicle wall and is involved in hair erection.
questions.learning: A- Eccrine sweat gland; B- Apocrine sweat gland; C- Sebaceous gland; D- Erector pili muscle The correctly matched option (B)- A- Eccrine sweat gland; B- Apocrine sweat gland; C- Sebaceous gland; D- Erector pili muscle.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948, if the sickness of an insured person is duly certified by an Insurance Medical Officer, periodical cash payment benefit is payable for a maximum period of how many days in any continuous period of 365 days, as Sickness Benefit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 91 days

The Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act, 1948 provides Sickness Benefit as a cash compensation to insured persons who are temporarily unable to work due to certified illness. The benefit is payable at approximately 70% of wages for a maximum of 91 days in two consecutive benefit periods (365 days), provided the insured person fulfills the required contribution conditions.

High-Yield Pearls

• Sickness Benefit: Cash benefit at \~70% of wages. ⭐
• Maximum duration: 91 days in a continuous period of 365 days. ⭐
• Requires certification by an Insurance Medical Officer.
• Available only if the insured person has made the prescribed contributions during the relevant contribution period.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following levels of hypoglycaemia corresponds to a blood glucose level of 50 mg/dL leading to cognitive impairment and need for corrective treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Level 2

• Level 2 hypoglycemia is defined as a blood glucose level <54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L), regardless of symptoms. It is considered clinically significant and generally requires prompt corrective treatment.
• A blood glucose of 50 mg/dL therefore falls under Level 2 hypoglycemia.

Why not other options?

• Level 0: No longer part of the standard ADA classification.
• Level 1: Glucose <70 but ≥54 mg/dL.
• Level 3: Severe hypoglycemia characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance, irrespective of glucose level.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A female patient presented with pain and redness in great toe. Serum uric acid level is 9.4mg/dl. The physician prescribed a drug for the treatment. Which of the following enzyme is likely to be inhibited by this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Xanthine oxidase

This patient with the classic symptoms of gout will most likely be prescribed Allopurinol - a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

Allopurinol is the first-line agent for the treatment of chronic gout in the period between attacks and it tends to prolong the intercritical period.

Allopurinol is not used in the management of acute gout. Urate-lowering drugs such as allopurinol, probenecid, lesinurad are not initiated during acute attacks.

The treatment options for an acute attack includes-

* NSAIDs: Indomethacin, naproxen, ibuprofen, and diclofenac are highly effective

* Colchicine: It acts by inhibiting neutrophil migration and reducing inflammation. It is used orally and is most effective if given early in an attack.

* Glucocorticoids: Systemic glucocorticoids may be used in polyarticular involvement. If the disease is limited to one joint, intraarticular triamcinolone may be given.

As per the latest 2020 ACR - American College of Rheumatology Guidelines for the management of gout, the following are the recommendations:

* Any patient with radiological evidence of tophi/ damage due to gout (or) with two or more flares reported in a year should be started on Urate Lowering drugs.

* Allopurinol - a xanthine oxidase inhibitor is the first-line drug to be started for all patients and the target level for serum urate should be less than 6mg/dl.

* Febuxostat can be considered in patients with renal compromise.

* For acute management of flares, colchicine, NSAIDs should be preferred. Glucocorticoid shots can be used in patients who have an intolerance to oral medications.

* Continue these drugs for 3-6 months if acute flare continues despite treatment.

* If urate target is not achieved or if flares/ tophi continue to be seen, pegloticase can be considered.

Lithium was first used therapeutically in the mid-19th century in patients with gout.

Note: Pegloticase should never be used to lower uric acid levels in asymptomatic/ incidentally discovered individuals.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following jugular venous pressure (JVP) waves corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. c wave

The c wave of jugular venous pressure wave corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase in the cardiac cycle.

During isovolumetric contraction, the ventricles start contracting with valves closed. This leads to bulging of the tricuspid valve. This bulging increases pressure in the right atrium which is transmitted to the right internal jugular vein. This appears as a c wave in jugular venous pressure (JVP) tracing.
JVP measured in the internal jugular vein (IJV) is a reflection of the right atrial pressure. IJV is preferred because it is not valved and is in direct line with superior vena cava and right atrium.

The waveforms seen in a normal JVP are:

• a wave corresponds to atrial contraction and occurs just after the P wave (on ECG) and just before the first heart sound.
• c wave represents the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during ventricular systole.
• x descent corresponds to the atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.
• v wave represents atrial filling during ventricular systole and peaks at the second heart sound.
• y descent represents passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after tricuspid valve opening.

The Wiggers diagram given below correlates JVP with other aspects of cardiac cycle.
questions.learning: c wave The c wave of jugular venous pressure wave corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase in the cardiac cycle. During isovolumetric contraction, the ventricles start contracting with valves closed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old alcoholic patient presents with a history of waxing and waning jaundice for the past 2 months. His CT examination reveals, dilatation of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct. What is the most probable diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Periampullary carcinoma

In the given scenario, a characteristic history of waxing and waning jaundice along with a dilated common bile duct and pancreatic duct on CT scan, points to a diagnosis of periampullary carcinoma.

Periampullary carcinoma arises from the vicinity of the ampulla of Vater. Patients with hereditary polyposis syndromes, such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) have a higher risk of developing it.

Clinical features:

• Jaundice: It intermittently waxes and wanes because, whenever the tumor undergoes necrosis and sloughing, obstruction to bile ducts is partially relieved.
• Weight loss
• Pain: It depends on the location of the tumor and may involve back pain as well due to the involvement of retropancreatic nerves, pancreatic duct obstruction or stasis, and disruption of nerve sheath by the tumor.
• Nausea/vomiting
• Pruritus
• Fever
• Gastrointestinal bleeding

In suspected periampullary disease, a three-phase CT scan should be done routinely.

Management includes resection, along with chemotherapy/ chemoradiotherapy.
questions.learning: Periampullary carcinoma — In the given scenario, a characteristic history of waxing and waning jaundice along with a dilated common bile duct and pancreatic duct on CT scan, points to a diagnosis of periampullary carcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which electrolyte abnormality will lead to cardiac arrhythmia in patients with severe vomiting?
questions.explanation: Severe vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), resulting in metabolic alkalosis. This alkalosis causes an intracellular shift of potassium, which, combined with increased renal potassium excretion to compensate for the bicarbonate load, leads to profound hypokalemia. Low serum potassium disrupts the cardiac membrane potential and repolarization, making it a major risk factor for life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Typical ECG changes in hypokalemia include flattened T waves, prominent U waves, and a prolonged QT interval, which can lead to Torsades de Pointes. Hyponatremia (Option B) can occur due to volume loss but is less likely to cause direct arrhythmias. Hyperkalemia (Option C) typically results from renal failure or acidosis, not vomiting. Hypocalcemia (Option D) causes QT prolongation and tetany but is not the primary drive for arrhythmias in the setting of gastric acid loss. Treatment focuses on replacing potassium and correcting the underlying fluid deficit

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the colon specimen image shown below from a 14-year-old boy, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The gross specimen shows a colon covered in "hundreds of small adenomatous polyps," which is the classic appearance of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP). FAP is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a mutation in the APC gene. In a 14-year-old boy, the discovery of extensive polyposis is pathognomonic. While FAP inevitably leads to "Colon cancer" (Option B) by age 40 if untreated, the primary diagnosis of the specimen itself is the polyposis syndrome. Juvenile polyps (Option C) are usually solitary and hamartomatous rather than numerous and adenomatous. Ulcerative colitis (Option D) presents with diffuse mucosal inflammation and ulcers, not hundreds of discrete polyps (though inflammatory pseudopolyps can occur, they look different). Total proctocolectomy is the mandatory treatment for FAP because the risk of malignancy is 100%. Screening of first-degree relatives via colonoscopy is also essential

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
In atrial fibrillation, choose the correct statements:

1. Novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs) used in the treatment of moderate to severe MS
2. Anticoagulants should be given in patients with ischemic stroke due to atrial fibrillation
3. NOACs are contraindicated in prosthetic valves
4. All patients with atrial fibrillation who are not candidates for cardiac surgery can be started on beta-blockers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3 correct

Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

Novel Oral Anticoagulants (NOACs) also known as direct oral anticoagulants are a new class of anticoagulants that include oral thrombin inhibitor (dabigatran) and oral factor Xa inhibitors like rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban. They are easier to use, achieve reliable anticoagulation, and do not require dosage adjustment based on blood tests. They have a lower risk of intracranial hemorrhage compared to warfarin and are used as alternatives to warfarin for patients who have atrial fibrillation.

Anticoagulation with warfarin or NOACs should be given in patients with ischemic stroke due to atrial fibrillation. In patients with small or moderate-sized infarcts and no intracranial bleeding, warfarin can be started soon (after 24 hours) after admission. The risks of transformation to hemorrhagic stroke are minimal. NOACs should be started after 48 hours as they have a more rapid anticoagulant effect.

Statement 3: NOACs are contraindicated in patients with prosthetic mechanical heart valves due to a lack of sufficient evidence.

Statement 1: NOACs are not used in the treatment of moderate to severe mitral stenosis (MS) due to limited clinical evidence supporting their efficacy and safety in MS. Warfarin is the recommended anticoagulant for patients with MS and mechanical prosthetic valves.

Statement 4: Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are the first line drugs used to acheive rate control in atrial fibrillation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During ward rounds, you see a patient who is admitted with a ca esophagus. What is the most likely presentation in this patient?
options: Dysphagia of solids followed by liquids
Dysphagia of liquids followed by solids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dysphagia of solids followed by liquids

Dysphagia of solids followed by liquids is the most likely presentation in a patient with ca esophagus.

Initially, patients have difficulty swallowing solids. Later, as the tumor grows and narrows the esophageal lumen, dysphagia progresses to liquids. This progression occurs because solid foods require a wider lumen to pass through, and the narrowing caused by the tumor becomes more critical as it advances.

Carcinoma esophagus is one of the most common malignancies manifesting in mid to late adulthood. It can be a squamous cell or adenocarcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) affects the upper two-thirds of the esophagus while adenocarcinoma affects the lower third. Tobacco smoking and alcohol are the risk factors for SCC. Obesity and gastroesophageal reflux disease increase the risk of adenocarcinoma.

Dysphagia can be the most common presenting feature but may present late. Other features such as regurgitation, weight loss, vomiting, and odynophagia can be seen. Lymph node involvement indicates a poor prognosis.

Endoscopy is the first line of investigation done. CT is useful to rule out metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion through the wall of the esophagus, adjacent organs, and lymph node metastasis.

Management options include radical esophagectomy, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and palliative chemoradiation or endoscopic treatments.

Other options

Option B: Dysphagia of liquids followed by solids is typically seen in motility disorders, such as achalasia cardia, where there is functional obstruction rather than a mechanical obstruction.

Option C: Chest pain may occur in the CA esophagus, but it is not the most common presenting symptom. It usually arises in advanced cases or due to tumor invasion into surrounding structures.

Option D: A neck mass might occur in metastatic disease (e.g., supraclavicular lymphadenopathy), but not the typical initial presentation.
questions.learning: Dysphagia of solids followed by liquids Dysphagia of solids followed by liquids is the most likely presentation in a patient with ca esophagus. Initially, patients have difficulty swallowing solids.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In an elderly male experiencing recurrent fainting episodes, the electrocardiogram shows P waves at a rate of 75 beats per minute and qRS complexes at a rate of 35 bpm. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stokes Adam syndrome

In this clinical scenario, elderly male experiencing recurrent fainting episodes, with P waves at 75 bpm and qRS complexes at 35 bpm.

The presence of P waves at a rate of 75 bpm suggests normal atrial activity, while qRS complexes at a rate of 35 bpm indicate a significant bradycardia. This combination of findings is consistent with a severe AV block, suggesting a diagnosis of Stokes-Adams syndrome.

Stokes-Adams syndrome, also known as Adams-Stokes syndrome, refers to episodes of syncope (fainting) caused by sudden, temporary interruptions of the heart's electrical activity, leading to a lack of blood flow to the brain. This interruption often results from complete heart block (third-degree AV block) or other severe bradyarrhythmias.

Prompt recognition and management, including consideration of pacemaker therapy, are essential in such cases to prevent further syncopal episodes and potential complications.

Other options:

Option B: Second-degree AV block: Second-degree AV block is characterized by intermittent failure of atrial impulses to conduct to the ventricles. This condition may present with a variety of patterns, such as Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) or Mobitz type II. While second-degree AV block can lead to symptomatic bradycardia and syncope, the specific ECG findings described in the question are more consistent with a complete heart block or severe bradycardia.

Option C: First-degree AV block:First-degree AV block is identified by a lengthened PR interval on the ECG, reflecting delayed electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles. It typically does not result in symptomatic bradycardia or syncope.

Option D: Electrical alternans: Electrical alternans refer to a phenomenon in which the amplitude of certain ECG waves, such as the QRS complex or T wave, alternates from beat to beat. It is often associated with pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, or severe left ventricular dysfunction, rather than bradyarrhythmias leading to syncope.

Pearl PF1792: Types of Heart block

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The average daily dietary nutrient intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97-98%) healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group is known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Recommended dietary allowance

The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is defined as the average daily intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97–98%) healthy individuals in a specific age and sex group.

It is derived from the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) and includes a safety margin to cover individual variability.

RDA=EAR+2SD

In contrast, Adequate Intake is used when RDA cannot be determined, and dietary goals are population-level recommendations rather than individual requirements.
questions.learning: Recommended dietary allowance — The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is defined as the average daily intake level sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97–98%) healthy individuals in a specific age and sex group.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Resistance to the airflow through the tube shown below is primarily because of :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diameter

The airway device shown in the image is an endotracheal tube and the resistance to the airflow through it primarily depends on diameter(Internal diameter).

* The size of an endotracheal tube usually refers to the internal diameter in mm. Rarely the French scale is used where the size corresponds to the external diameter multiplied by 3.

* For adults, usually, a 7-mm is used for women and a 7.5 or 8-mm ETT is used for men.

* Generally, high-volume, low-pressure cuffed tubes are used in adults, and cuffless tubes are used in neonates and infants.

* Besides age, the choice of an endotracheal tube also depends on the presence of airway pathologies and the reason behind the placement of the tube.

* Smaller-sized tubes lead to increase airway resistance and increased work breathing.

* Larger tubes have a higher risk of laryngeal and tracheal trauma and sore throat.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following does not suggest a medical cause of mental illness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Auditory hallucination

Auditory hallucination is not suggestive of a medical cause of mental illness.

Hallucinations are perceptions in the absence of stimuli to account for them.

Auditory hallucinations are the hallucinations most commonly seen in the psychiatric setting. Nonauditory hallucinations often suggest that there is a neurologic, medical, or substance withdrawal issue rather than a primary psychiatric issue.

Features of the medical cause of mental illness:

* Acute onset (within hours or minutes, with prevailing symptoms) First episode

* Older age

* Current medical illness or injury

* Significant substance abuse

* Nonauditory disturbances of perception

* Neurologic symptoms—loss of consciousness, seizures, head injury, change in headache pattern, change in vision

* Classic mental status signs—diminished alertness, disorientation, memory impairment, impairment in concentration and attention, dyscalculia, concreteness

* Other mental status signs—speech, movement, or gait disorders

* Constructional apraxia—difficulties in drawing clocks, cubes, intersecting pentagons, Bender–Gestalt test
questions.learning: Auditory hallucination Auditory hallucination is not suggestive of a medical cause of mental illness. Hallucinations are perceptions in the absence of stimuli to account for them.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient receiving the antipsychotic haloperidol develops acute dystonia. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Acute dystonia (involuntary muscle contractions, such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis) is a common and distressing extrapyramidal side effect of high-potency first-generation antipsychotics like Haloperidol. The next best step and standard acute treatment is the administration of an anticholinergic agent, such as Benztropine or Procyclidine, which rapidly reverses the muscle spasm. Fluphenazine (Option C) is another high-potency antipsychotic that would likely worsen the dystonia. Increasing the dose of haloperidol (Option D) is strictly contraindicated and would exacerbate the condition. Changing to clozapine (Option B) is a long-term strategy for refractory patients but is not the immediate treatment for an acute dystonic episode. After reversing the dystonia, the overall treatment plan should be reviewed, often by switching the patient to an atypical antipsychotic with lower extrapyramidal risk. Bedside recognition and rapid pharmacological reversal are essential for patient comfort and safety
questions.learning: Acute dystonia (involuntary muscle contractions, such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis) is a common and distressing extrapyramidal side effect of high-potency first-generation antipsychotics like Haloperidol.

questions.text: Bindi Leukoderma is caused by which chemical?

• There is also evidence that azo dyes, by virtue of structural similarity to tyrosine, can directly inhibit melanogenesis by competing with that amino acid for binding with tyrosinase enzyme.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the parasite.
questions.explanation: The parasite depicted in the image is the trophozoite form of Giardia lamblia. It is characteristically described as having a "pear-shape" or "tennis-racket" shape, with two large nuclei that give it a "monkey-face" appearance. It has four pairs of flagella and a large ventral sucking disc used for attachment to the intestinal mucosa. Trichomonas vaginalis (Option B) is also pear-shaped but has only one nucleus and a characteristic undulating membrane. Trypanosoma (Option C) is a spindle-shaped blood parasite. Cyclospora (Option D) is a spherical coccidian parasite seen in stool. Giardia is a major cause of malabsorptive diarrhea and steatorrhea (foul-smelling, fatty stools) worldwide. It is usually acquired by drinking contaminated water from lakes or streams ("beaver fever"). Diagnosis is made by identifying cysts or trophozoites in the stool or through an ELISA for fecal antigens

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In the case of ototoxicity induced by diuretics, which specific structure within the cochlea is most susceptible to damage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stria vascularis

Loop diuretic-induced ototoxicity (e.g., furosemide, ethacrynic acid) primarily affects the stria vascularis of the cochlea, disrupting endolymph production and the endocochlear potential, leading to sensorineural hearing loss, which is often reversible but may become permanent with high doses or concomitant aminoglycoside use.

Why not the other options?

• A. Outer hair cells: Primarily damaged by aminoglycosides and noise-induced hearing loss, not loop diuretics.
• C. Inner hair cells: Less commonly affected; not the primary target of diuretic ototoxicity.
• D. Macula and crista: Vestibular sensory organs involved in balance, not the principal site of diuretic-induced cochlear toxicity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The patient presents with miosis,anhidrosis and mild drooping of eyelids and a small pupil that remains small even in darkness. The likely diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horner syndrome

The clinical scenario with a small sized pupil which does not dilate in response to darkness is due to sympathetic palsy  seen in Horner syndrome (miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis).

In a normal eye, the pupil dilates in response to dim light and constricts in response to bright light. Pupillary dilation is brought about by the contraction of dilator pupillae mediated by sympathetic innervation. Pupillary constriction is due to the contraction of sphincter pupillae mediated by parasympathetic innervation.

The difference in pupillary diameter is called anisocoria. A difference of up to 0.5 mm is common even in normal individuals.

Pearl PF0622: Horner's syndrome

Horner's Syndrome:

Horner's syndrome occurring due to occulo-sympathetic paresis is characterized by the classic triad of:

* Mild ptosis (due to paralysis of Muller's muscle).

* Miosis (due to paralysis of dilator pupillae).

* Reduced ipsilateral sweating (anhydrosis).

Other features include:

* Mild enophthalmos,

* Loss of cilio-spinal reflex,

* Heterochromia, i.e., the ipsilateral iris is lighter in colour,

* Pupil is slow to dilate, and there occurs slight elevation of lower eyelid.

Cocaine test (2% to 4%): Small pupils fail to dilate in Horner's syndrome.

In congenital Horner's syndrome, the additional features seen are heterochromia iridis and unilateral straight hair.

Pearl PF1404: Causes of small and dilated pupils

Causes of small pupils include

* Pontine hemorrhage

* Horner's syndrome

* Old age

* Argyll Robertson pupil

* Drugs and poisons (opiates, organophosphates)

Causes of dilated pupils include

* Holmes–Adie (myotonic) pupil

* Third nerve palsy

* Atropine

* Carbon monoxide

* Ethylene glycol
questions.learning: Horner syndrome — The clinical scenario with a small sized pupil which does not dilate in response to darkness is due to sympathetic palsy seen in Horner syndrome (miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the finding in the given ultrasound image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phrygian cap

The ultrasound examination of the gallbladder shows a Phrygian cap. It is a normal anatomical variant.

Phrygian cap refers to an anatomical variant of the gallbladder, where, the fundus of the gallbladder folds on itself, or is separated from the body by a partial or complete septum. A true septum is uncommon and is usually an apparent septum due to the gallbladder wall folding. It is an incidental finding that may be seen on CT, MRI, or ultrasound. It causes no symptoms.

The Phrygian cap is named so, due to the resemblance of the ultrasonographic appearance to a hat or cap that is worn by the inhabitants of ancient Phrygia circa 1200 BC.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A doctor asks a patient about her age, and the patient responds, "You know doctor, I'm from a village, I was married at a very young age of 12 years and my husband was just 5 years older than me. Then I had two kids when I was around 18 or something. Now I am 38, but I look like their older sister". What is most likely thought disorder displayed by patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Circumstantiality

Circumstantiality best describes this patient’s thought disorder, as she provides irrelevant and unnecessary details when asked her age before eventually giving the actual answer.

Circumstantiality refers to a formal thought disorder in which a patient gives irrelevant and unnecessary details. This is before finally getting to the point or the correct answer. It may be seen in schizophrenia, obsessional disturbances, and certain cases of dementia. An example is given below.

Doctor: "How did you get that bruise?"

Patient: "I woke up and had a cup of coffee, read the newspaper, and went for a walk. It was a wonderful day in the park. I returned home and watched the TV. I took a nap in the afternoon after lunch. I slipped and fell in the bathroom. The fall gave me this bruise."

A formal thought disorder is a disturbance in the formulation of thoughts and their expression. It is characterized by loosened associations, illogical constructs, and neologisms. Derailment, neologism, perseveration, and thought blocking are some examples.

Other options:

Option A: Clang association is a formal thought disorder where the thoughts are associated with the sound of words through rhyming, rather than the meaning of the words. It is usually seen in schizophrenia or mania. An example is "I am Sam...I like jam...I travel in a tram"

Option B: Flight of ideas refers to a rapid succession of multiple associations, where the thoughts appear to abruptly shift from one idea to another. It is usually seen in mania. An example is "I like mangoes, the weather is nice, India is great"

Option D: Tagentiality is a formal thought disorder where the patient says something that is related to the general topic. Although, the actual answer is not given. An example is as below.

Doctor: "How has your appetite been lately?"
Patient: "I usually have dinner with my wife, but now I eat alone"

Pearl PF1257: Disorders of thought and perception

DISORDERS OF THOUGHT

DISORDER OF STREAM OF THOUGHT

(A) Disorder of tempo

(i) Flight of Ideas

Continuous flow of rapid speech that jumps from topic to topic

•

"I like mangoes, the weather is nice, India is great"

(ii) Retardation of thinking

Slow speed of speech and a prolonged latent period before a response

•

"I went to the market (pause)......... the shop was closed"

(iii) Circumstantialities

Inclusion of irrelevant details and going on in a roundabout manner, but their thought ultimately reaches the answer

•

Doctor: "How did you get that bruise?"

•

Patient: "I woke up and had a cup of coffee, read the newspaper and went for a walk. It was a wonderful day in the park. I returned home and watched the TV. I took a nap in the afternoon after lunch. I slipped and fell in the bathroom. The fall gave me this bruise."

(iv) Clang associations

Jumping from one word to another irrelevant rhyming word

•

I am Sam...I like jam...I travel in a tram"

(B) Disorder of continuity

(i) Perseveration

Repetition of out of context words, phrases, or ideas beyond the point of relevance.

•

Q1. What's your name?: "Rahul"

•

Q2. Where are you from?: "Rahul"

•

Q3. How old are you?: "Rahul"

(ii) Thought blocking

A sudden disruption of thought or a break in the flow of ideas

•

"I went to the market (extreme silence)...................."

DISORDER OF FORM OF THOUGHT

(i) Tangentiality

In response to a question, the patient gives a reply that is appropriate to the general topic but does not answer the question exactly. The speech moves away from the actual answer.

• Doctor: "Have you had any trouble sleeping lately?"
• Patient: "I usually sleep in my bed, but now I'm sleeping on the sofa"

(ii) Derailment

A breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of goal-directedness. The words make sentences, but the sentences do not make sense.

• "Some people just don't understand why I had breakfast in America during the first world war"

(iii) Neologisms

Bringing in new words that do not exist.

• The world is not 'gooder' for people like me"

(iv) Desultory thoughts

Speech is grammatically correct, however, sudden unrelated ideas force their way in from time to time.

• My actual problem is that the people never understand me and my stomach feels like an empty bucket"

(v) Word salad

Using a mixture of unintelligible meaningless words and sentences

• Tree bus rain food home car tiger"

DISORDER OF POSSESSION OF THOUGHT

(A) Obsession and compulsion

(i) Obsessions

Recurrent and persistent thoughts, impulses. or images that cause distress to oneself.

• Fear of dirt or contamination
• Fear of becoming ill
• Constant thoughts of a certain number
• Need for symmetry or exactness
• Worry about whether something has been done "right"
• Forbidden sexual or religious thoughts

(ii) Compulsions

Repetitive behaviors or actions that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession

• Washing hands
• Blinking eyes
• Counting items, such as currency
• Checking to see if doors are locked
• Arranging items in a certain way
• Requiring constant approval from people around them

(B) Thought alienation

(i) Thought insertion

Thoughts are being inserted into the patient's mind and they recognize them as being foreign and coming from without any stimulus

•

"I have repeated thoughts of killing my neighbors and I believe aliens are putting these ideas into my head at night"

(ii) Thought withdrawal

Delusion that someone or something is removing from one's mind and the patient has no power over this.

•

"Lately, I am losing all my memories and I believe that the 'government agents' are stealing them when I go to sleep"

(iii) Thought broadcasting

Belief that one's thoughts are quietly escaping from one's mind and that other people might be able to access them and hear or see them.

•

"I believe my exact thoughts appear on the TV and the internet and I think I can broadcast them globally"

(iv) Thought echo

Patient hears the 'echo' of his own thoughts in the form of a voice after he has made the thought.

•

"I thought of making a sandwich in the morning and surprisingly a voice, from nowhere, told me to make a sandwich out loud"

DISORDER OF CONTENT OF THOUGHT

(i) Phobias

Persistent fear of an object or situation, typically disproportional to the actual danger posed, in which the sufferer goes to great lengths in avoiding it

•

Arachnophobia - fear of spider

•

Barophobia - fear of gravity

•

Cynophobia - fear of dogs

•

Hemophobia - fear of blood

•

Nosocomephobia - fear of hospitals

(ii) Religious preoccupations

Thoughts involving religious themes or subject matter.

•

"I get instructions from God on how to make my country great"

(iii) Ideas of hopelessness

Thoughts of complete despair where the patient strongly believes that the circumstances will never get better for him.

•

"I am never going to pass my final exams, no matter how hard I study"

(iv) Antisocial urges

Thoughts of indulging in some behaviors or actions that harm or lack consideration for the well being of others.

•

"I have these urges to go rob a bank or blackmail my neighbors for their money"

(v) Derealization

Alteration in the perception or experience of the external world so that it seems unreal

•

"The world and everything around is nothing but just a dream"

(vi) Depersonalization

Feeling as if one is disconnected from reality, feeling detached from one's own thoughts and one's own physical body

•

"I sometimes drift into a dream-like state where I lose contact with my own self"

(vii) Delusions

False beliefs that are strongly held and unchangeable in the face of refuting evidence and that are not consistent with the person's educational, social and cultural background.

The three main criteria for a belief to be considered a delusion are:

•

Certainty (held with complete confidence)

•

Incorrigibility (not changeable by proof to the contrary)

•

Impossibility or falsity of content (implausible, bizarre or patently untrue)

DISORDERS OF PERCEPTIONS

•

Illusion: Misinterpretation of real external stimuli.

•

Hallucination: False sensory perception, externally.

•

Pseudohallucination: False sensory perception from within and having an insight.
questions.learning: Circumstantiality Circumstantiality best describes this patient’s thought disorder, as she provides irrelevant and unnecessary details when asked her age before eventually giving the actual answer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following should be the treatment of choice for renal cell carcinoma with tumor less than 4 cm in size?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Partial nephrectomy

Partial nephrectomy (also known as nephron-sparing surgery) is the treatment of choice for tumors <4 cm.

Indications for partial nephrectomy:

• Tumors < 4cm
• Well-selected tumors between 4-7 cm
• Bilateral tumors
• Tumor in solitary kidneys
• Patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction.

Recently, partial nephrectomy is also increasingly being performed for stage T1b tumors.

Treatment of renal cell carcinoma:

RCC is a radio and chemoresistant tumor.

Staging
Description
Management

Stage 1
Tumor <7 cm, confined to the kidney
Partial nephrectomy

Stage 2
Tumor >7 cm, confined to the kidney
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 3
Tumor extends into the major veins or adrenal gland with intact Gerota’s fascia or regional lymph nodes involved.
Radical nephrectomy

Stage 4
Tumor invades beyond Gerota fascia (including contiguous extension into the ipsilateral adrenal gland)

• Debulking surgery
• mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus, sirolimus
• Tyrosine kinase inhibitors: sunitinib, sorafenib

Radical nephrectomy consists of the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes. The adrenal gland is no longer removed except in cases of obvious tumor involvement. Lymphadenectomy is indicated only in high-risk patients with large primary tumors and enlarged lymph nodes.

Cryoablation is indicated in the T1a stage of RCC if surgery cannot be performed. It is also indicated in advanced/metastatic tumors.

Note: Sunitinib and sorafenib are also used in GIST and hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with lower abdominal pain and diarrhea. The stool examination finding is shown below. Which of the following is most likely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Entamoeba histolytica

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of amoebic dysentery caused by Entamoeba histolytica and the given image shows hematophagous trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica.

Clinical features of intestinal amebiasis:

* Acute intestinal amebiasis- dysentery, lower abdominal discomfort, and flatulence.

* Chronic amebiasis- low-grade symptoms such as occasional diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue.

A granulomatous lesion called an ameboma may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas of the colon which can resemble an adenocarcinoma of the colon.

Option A - Giardia is often asymptomatic, but in some cases can lead to fat malabsorption, dull epigastric pain, and flatulence.

Option B - Shigella causes bacillary dysentery which is characterised by fever and generalised abdominal tenderness.

Option D - Campylobacter presents with fever, pain, and watery diarrhea. The stool contains leucocytes and blood.

Metronidazole is used in the treatment of amoebiasis like amoebic colitis and amoebic liver abscess. It is well absorbed from the small intestine and only a small amount of the unabsorbed drug reaches the colon, which is insufficient to kill the cysts.

Hence, luminal agents like diloxanide furoate, nitazoxanide or iodoquinol are required for the eradication of cysts and trophozoites in the intestine.
